title: Visual Testing (VT) & Remote Visual Inspection (RVI): The Complete 2026 Guide — ASME V Art 9, Borescope, Drones
snippet: Definitive 5,000-word guide to visual testing and RVI for welds, vessels, pipework and turbines. Covers direct vs remote VT, borescope/videoscope, drones & ROVs, illumination > 1,000 lux, Jaeger J1 vision, ASME V Article 9, AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15, ISO 17637.
content:
Visual Testing (VT): The Complete 2026 Guide

Visual testing (VT) is the original, most-performed, and most-underrated non-destructive testing method. By the simplest possible means — the human eye, often augmented with mirrors, magnifiers, illumination, and increasingly with borescopes, videoscopes, drones and remote visual inspection (RVI) systems — VT detects surface conditions: cracks, corrosion, mechanical damage, weld profile, distortion, paint, coatings, foreign objects and dimensional irregularities. Every other NDT method is a follow-up to VT; ASME Section V Article 9 mandates VT as the prerequisite for any other examination. Modern VT extends from direct eye-on-part inspection at arm's length to high-definition videoscopy of jet-engine combustion chambers, deep-water ROV inspection of subsea wellheads, and AI-augmented drone-based bridge surveys. The method is governed by ASME V Article 9, ASTM E165 (cross-referenced), AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15 and 8.9, API 510/570/653 in-service codes, ISO 17637 (welds) and ISO 18238 (vision). This 2026 complete guide — written by ASNT Level III practitioners — covers physics, equipment, step-by-step procedure, codes, certifications, applications, common defects, advantages, costs and 2024-2026 innovations.

Physics & Principles of Visual Testing

VT relies on the physiology and physics of human vision augmented by optical instruments. Three vision parameters govern detection capability:

Visual acuity — the ability to resolve fine detail at a defined distance — is the primary qualifier. Code-compliant VT personnel are required to demonstrate near-vision acuity of Jaeger J1 (lines 0.4 mm at 300 mm) or equivalent (e.g. Snellen 20/25). Acuity is tested annually for code-compliant work per ASME V T-922 and ISO 9712 — eye exam, with corrective lenses if needed.

Color vision — verified via Ishihara plates or equivalent at hire and at least every 5 years — ensures the inspector can distinguish typical defect colors (oxide colors on heat-tinted stainless, paint colors, corrosion product colors).

Contrast sensitivity — the ability to detect a small luminance difference from background — depends on illumination level. ASME V T-952 mandates ≥ 1,000 lux at the inspection surface (some codes require 1,500 lux for fine work). Direct-VT illumination must be reasonably uniform without glare or shadow.

Beyond direct vision, three optical phenomena underpin equipment-aided VT:

Optical magnification via hand-held magnifiers (3-10×), loupes, or microscopes — extends practical resolution to ≤ 0.05 mm. Reflection via mirrors for hidden surfaces (e.g. inside-of-tube inspection during fabrication). Endoscopy via flexible (fiberscopes) or rigid (borescopes) tube assemblies, or video-equipped tip articulating videoscopes — extends visibility into pressure vessel interiors, pipework, gear cases, turbines and any cavity inaccessible to direct eye-on-part. Modern videoscope optics deliver > 1080p HD resolution at probe-tip distances of 5-150 mm, with stereo measurement (laser-shadow or stereo dual-lens) for sizing defects.

Remote Visual Inspection (RVI) extends VT to environments inhospitable to humans — pressure-vessel interiors during downtime, jet engines without disassembly, subsea oilfield infrastructure, nuclear reactor internals — using crawler robots, ROVs, drones and articulating snake-arm cameras.

Visual Testing Equipment

Equipment ranges from a flashlight and mirror (a significant capital item) to a high-end industrial videoscope with stereo measurement (a significant capital item). The table below summarizes the typical 2026 spec.

Equipment ClassExamples / SpecIndicative Cost
Inspection flashlight (LED)Streamlight Stinger, Maglite ML150 — 700-1,500 lumens, > 4-hour runtimea modest cost
Mirror set (inspection)Telescoping handle, 38 mm + 50 mm + 75 mm circular + rectangular tipsa modest cost
Magnifier / loupe5×, 10×, 20× with built-in LED — Bausch & Lomb 81-41-71a modest cost
Inspection USB microscopeDino-Lite AM7915 — 1.3-5 MP, 20-220× magnification, image capturea modest cost
Weld gauge set (Cambridge / Hi-Lo / fillet)Reaches all weld dimensions per AWS D1.1 Figure 5.5a modest cost
Pit gauge / depth micrometer0-25 mm depth, 0.025 mm resolutiona modest cost
Ultrasonic thickness gauge (for VT-supplement)Olympus 38DL Plus, Tritex Multigauge 6000 — 0.5-300 mm rangecost varies by specification
Pen-style borescope (rigid)4-10 mm diameter, 175-200 mm working length, fixed lensa modest cost
Flexible fiberscope4-12 mm diameter, 1-3 m working length, manual articulationcost varies by specification
Industrial videoscope (handheld)Olympus IPLEX NX, GE Mentor Visual iQ, Karl Storz — 6.0-8.4 mm probe, 4-way articulation, HD camera, stereo measurementcost varies by specification
RVI crawler / snake-armGE Inuktun Versatrax, Olympus IPLEX GXcost varies by specification
Inspection ROV (subsea)SaaB Seaeye Falcon, VideoRay Defender — to 1,000 m depthcost varies by specification
Drone (inspection-grade)DJI Matrice 30T, Skydio X2, FlyAbility Elios 3 — collision-tolerant, IR + 4K camerascost varies by specification
Light meter (lux)Extech LT300, Konica Minolta T-10A — verifies ≥ 1,000 lux per ASME V T-952a modest cost
DSLR / mirrorless inspection cameraSony A7 IV + 90 mm macro lens — for permanent indication recordcost varies by specification
Vision chart (Jaeger / Snellen)Standard near-vision chart for annual eye exama modest cost

A field VT kit (flashlight + mirror + 5× loupe + weld gauge + pit gauge + camera + log book) runs a modest cost. A professional RVI / videoscope program runs cost varies by specification.

Step-by-Step Visual Testing Procedure

  1. Pre-job planning & documentation review. Review the qualified VT procedure (per ASME V T-921 / ISO 17637). Confirm: scope of inspection, required acceptance criteria (AWS D1.1, ASME B31.3, API 510/570/653), reporting format, lighting requirement, surface preparation expectation. Verify the inspector's current annual eye exam is on file.
  2. Personnel preparation. Verify inspector has current ASNT Level II VT (or ISO 9712 / equivalent). Allow eyes to adapt to ambient conditions for at least 1 minute. If transitioning from bright sunlight to a dim vessel interior, allow 5-10 minutes dark-adaption.
  3. Surface preparation. Surface must be sufficiently clean to allow detection of relevant features. Per ASME V T-953 the surface is normally as-fabricated unless contractually specified otherwise. Remove loose scale, slag, weld spatter that could mask defects. For coated/painted in-service work, may require localized paint removal in any suspect area before measurement.
  4. Illumination & access setup. Verify illumination ≥ 1,000 lux at the inspection surface with a calibrated light meter. Some codes (e.g. ASME V T-952 for direct VT) accept 1,000 lux but 1,500 lux is preferred for fine fatigue cracks and corrosion pitting. Position direction of light to maximize defect visibility — generally low-angle grazing light reveals surface relief defects better than perpendicular flood-light. Ensure inspector can position eye within 600 mm of surface and at ≥ 30° angle for direct VT.
  5. Direct visual examination. Systematically scan the surface — top to bottom, left to right, in overlapping strips no more than 250 mm wide. Use 5×-10× loupe for fine inspection of weld toes, geometric transitions, suspected indications. Use a mirror to view hidden surfaces (inside of nozzles, back of fillets). Note every relevant feature: cracks, undercut, overlap, porosity, slag, spatter, arc strikes, mismatch (Hi-Lo), reinforcement profile, throat dimension, leg length.
  6. Measurement of relevant indications. Use weld gauge set for profile dimensions per AWS D1.1 Figure 5.5: reinforcement, undercut depth, fillet leg length and throat, Hi-Lo, concavity, convexity. Use pit gauge or depth micrometer for corrosion pits, mechanical damage. Use UT thickness gauge for wall-thinning if accessible.
  7. Remote visual examination (if applicable). For inaccessible surfaces (vessel interiors, piping bores, turbine internals), deploy borescope or videoscope: pre-clean the access port, articulate the probe to systematic positions (typically 360° rotation every 250 mm advance), record video of full coverage, freeze-frame for measurements via stereo or shadow technique. Verify probe-tip resolution against a reference scale before each shift.
  8. Indication marking & mapping. Mark all relevant indications with a paint marker. Photograph with a scale included. Sketch indication map showing weld ID, indication type, location and dimension. Record in inspection log.
  9. Accept / reject determination. Apply governing acceptance criteria. Common references: AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 (statically loaded), Table 8.2 (cyclically loaded), ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2, API 510/570 in-service criteria. Cracks of any size — almost universally rejected.
  10. Reporting. Issue VT report listing procedure number, inspector certification level, area covered, lighting, equipment used, indications mapped, accept/reject decisions, Level II signature, Level III review for procedure qualification.

Standards & Codes Governing Visual Testing

ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code Section V Article 9 — primary North American procedural standard. Defines direct visual examination (eye to surface < 600 mm at ≥ 30°), remote visual (lighting, resolution, recording), surface preparation, vision acuity (Jaeger J1 + colour Ishihara), illumination (≥ 1,000 lux at surface). Invoked by Section VIII (vessels), B31.1, B31.3, Section III nuclear, Section IX welding. Article 9 is paired with the in-service codes API 510, 570, 653.

ASME Section V Mandatory Appendix III covers Remote Visual Inspection (RVI) specifically, including borescope and videoscope resolution and recording requirements. Mandatory Appendix IV covers system performance verification.

AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15 defines the visual acceptance criteria for structural welds — the most-cited dimensional criteria in the world. Clause 8.9 covers fabrication-level VT. Tables 8.1 and 8.2 list specific accept/reject limits for cracks, undercut, fillet leg length, weld profile, etc.

ISO 17637 — Visual Testing of Fusion-Welded Joints. ISO 18238 covers vision requirements (acuity, illumination, colour). EN 13018 — VT general principles (largely superseded by ISO 17637 in 2016).

ASTM E165 cross-references VT as a prerequisite to PT. ASTM E1316 defines terminology. ASTM E3022 is the lighting standard (applies to UV but also informs VT lighting).

API 510 / 570 / 653 in-service inspection codes invoke VT as the principal in-service surface NDT method. NACE / AMPP SP 0294 / RP 0292 covers visual coating-condition inspection.

VT Inspector Certification Pathways

VT has the lowest formal-training threshold of any NDT method but the most onerous physical-eye-test requirement — annual vision verification mandatory.

ASNT SNT-TC-1A / CP-189: Level I VT requires 8 hours of training plus 70 hours of supervised OJT. Level II adds 16 hours (24 total) and 140 hours OJT. Level III requires the basic, method and specific exams plus 4 years documented experience. The vision exam is mandatory annually: Jaeger J1 or equivalent + Ishihara colour. Loss or expiration of vision certification immediately disqualifies. See the ASNT certification roadmap.

ISO 9712 / PCN / CSWIP: Level II VT requires 24 hours training + 1 month supervised experience (70 hours minimum), external exam, vision test, 5-year recertification.

AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI): The dominant U.S. weld VT certification — requires high-school education, 5 years of welding/inspection experience (or less with associate/bachelor degree), passing a 6-hour fundamentals + practical + code-book exam. Recertified every 9 years with annual vision exam. Many fabricators require CWI in addition to ASNT Level II VT. See our CWI certification guide.

For inspectors who specify and review VT — the pressure-vessel, piping and storage-tank inspector — the API certifications are the natural progression: API 510 Pressure Vessel, API 570 Piping, API 653 Storage Tank.

Applications by Industry

Oil & Gas: Pre-weld fit-up inspection, in-process root-bead VT, cap-pass VT, in-service vessel/piping VT during turnaround. ASME B31.3 mandates VT before any further NDT. API 510 / 570 / 653 use VT as the principal in-service surface method.

Power Generation: Steam-turbine blade VT during overhaul (borescope), boiler tube external VT, HRSG internals VT via crawler.

Aerospace: Engine borescope inspection between flights and at overhaul intervals — combustion chamber, turbine blades, compressor airfoils. Airframe surface VT during heavy maintenance (C/D-check) finds skin fatigue cracks, corrosion, lightning-strike damage. See our aircraft engine component inspection.

Nuclear: Reactor pressure-vessel internals VT via underwater RVI cameras, RPV closure-head bolt VT, control-rod-drive VT. Some primary system inspections require < 0.4 mm resolution at probe-tip working distance per Mandatory Appendix IV.

Manufacturing: Production-line VT of castings, forgings, machined parts — increasingly automated with machine vision.

Marine & Shipbuilding: Hull external VT (dry-dock, ROV-based wet inspection), tank internal VT, anchor-chain VT.

Bridge & Civil Infrastructure: Drone-based VT of bridges, towers, wind-turbine blades. See our bridge inspection guide and wind turbine blade inspection.

Common Defects Detected by VT

Defect TypeIndicationSeverityTypical Acceptance (AWS D1.1 Cyclic)
Surface crackSharp line, may have associated rust staining or oxide tintCriticalNot permitted
UndercutGroove melted into base metal at weld toeModerate≤ 0.25 mm for material ≤ 25 mm; ≤ 1 mm length
Overlap (cold lap)Weld metal flowing over base metal without fusionHighNot permitted
Excessive convexity / concavityReinforcement out of specLow-ModeratePer AWS D1.1 Figure 5.4
Insufficient throat / legFillet dimension under-specHighNot permitted
Hi-Lo (mismatch)Misalignment of joining surfacesModerate≤ 25 % of thinner member to max 3 mm
Surface porosityRound open pits, isolated or clusteredLow-ModerateLimits per AWS Table 8.1 / 8.2
Arc strikeLocalized hardened/discolored spot, often crack-proneHighNot permitted — must be ground & re-inspected
Weld spatterLoose globules adjacent to weldCosmeticRemoved prior to acceptance
Corrosion pittingLocalized loss of material, > 1 mm deepHigh at > 50 % wallPer API 510/570 fitness-for-service
General corrosion (uniform wall thinning)Visible flattening / discoloration; confirmed by UTModerate-HighPer remaining-wall criteria
Mechanical damage (gouge, dent)Sharp profile changeHigh at sharp transitionsPer fitness-for-service
Heat tint (austenitic stainless)Surface oxide color blue/brownModerate (degrades corrosion resistance)Must be removed by pickling/passivation

Advantages & Limitations of Visual Testing

Advantages: Fastest of any NDT method — 1-5 minutes per joint. Cheapest — a modest cost per joint consumables. No surface chemistry, electrical power or radiation hazard. Universally applicable to any material — steel, aluminum, plastic, composite, ceramic. Detects surface conditions invisible to other NDT methods — coatings, profile, geometric mismatch. Mandatory prerequisite to any other NDT (ASME V T-921). RVI extends reach to internal cavities. Easy to document with photo evidence. Inspectors can be qualified relatively quickly (8-24 hours classroom).

Limitations: Only detects surface and externally-visible defects (no subsurface capability). Sensitive to operator vision and fatigue; long inspection days produce errors. Cracks < 25 μm wide are typically invisible to unaided eye (require magnification). Borescope and videoscope have limited depth of field. RVI in confined spaces requires permit-to-work and gas-test entry. Color-tint detection on stainless requires good lighting and may require specific lamp temperature (3,000-4,000 K). Critically dependent on lighting quality and surface cleanliness. Highly subjective without rigorous procedure and calibrated tools.

VT vs PT vs Liquid Penetrant Coating Inspection

CriterionVTPTCoating-Lift VT
Detection sensitivity (surface crack width)25 μm unaided, 5 μm at 10×0.5 μm (Level 4)50 μm (visible after coating defect)
Required equipmentFlashlight, magnifier, gauge3 consumables + UV / lightingCoating-thickness gauge + magnifier
Cycle time per 200 mm weld2-5 min30-45 min5-10 min
Surface prep effortLight (clean)HighNone
Sub-surface detectionNoneNoneNone
Cost / inspectiona modest costa modest costa modest cost

VT is always the first-line inspection done; PT is the follow-up for crack-suspect areas; coating-lift VT (per NACE / AMPP SP 0294) is used for in-service surface corrosion under coatings. See the penetrant testing complete guide and the magnetic particle testing complete guide for full method-by-method tradeoffs.

Cost & ROI of Visual Testing

Field VT is the cheapest NDT inspection by labor and consumables. Typical 2026 rates: butt-weld VT on structural steel, a modest cost per joint. Pressure-vessel internal VT during turnaround, a modest cost per vessel (3-8 hours). Borescope inspection of a 100-cm-long heat-exchanger tube, a modest cost per tube. Jet-engine borescope inspection, a modest cost per engine. ROV subsea wellhead VT, cost varies by specification per day day-rate. Drone-based bridge inspection, cost varies by specification per day. ROI of converting in-house from manual VT to videoscope-assisted RVI typically breaks even at 3,000+ vessel-internals inspections per year, driven by avoided scaffolding (cost varies by specification per vessel) and reduced confined-space-entry permits. Atlantis NDT's reporting software reduces VT documentation time by 60-75 % via mobile photo capture tagged to weld ID and procedure.

Recent Innovations in Visual Testing (2024 - 2026)

4K-resolution videoscopes — Olympus IPLEX NX, GE Mentor Visual iQ — deliver > 1080p HD with stereo-shadow measurement to 0.1 mm at 25 mm working distance, completely replacing fibre-optic eyepiece-view scopes for any code-compliant work.

AI-assisted defect detection — CNN-based real-time indication classification on videoscope video streams. GE's AI VT module flags candidate cracks, corrosion and burn-through during borescope walk-through; Level II adjudication remains required by code.

Collision-tolerant inspection drones — FlyAbility Elios 3, DJI Matrice 30T — enable confined-space and indoor inspection without permit-required entry. Used heavily for storage-tank internals, boiler interiors, ship cargo holds. AAA-payload capacity now supports 4K + thermal + lidar.

Photogrammetric 3D reconstruction from drone-captured photo sets — used to build dimensioned 3D models of bridges, towers, refineries — feeds directly into the Atlantis Digital Twins platform for asset visualization.

Articulating snake-arm cameras — for jet engines and turbomachinery without disassembly — now feature 2 m working length and 4-way articulation.

Remote video-recorded VT permits Level III review remotely — eliminating the travel cost of senior inspectors and speeding up turnaround. Combined with the Atlantis NDT reporting platform, indications are tagged, time-stamped, weld-ID-linked, and shared with the owner's integrity engineer in real-time.

Direct VT Procedure Qualification & Inspector Vision Records

Visual testing's deceptive simplicity masks rigorous qualification requirements. Every code-compliant VT procedure must be qualified — typically by Level III approval and demonstration on a representative test piece showing that the smallest specified defect is detected under the procedure's lighting and access conditions.

Essential variables per ASME V T-921: surface preparation, lighting type and intensity, access geometry (direct vs remote), required equipment (mirrors, magnifiers, gauges), inspector vision requirements, recording and acceptance criteria. Any change in an essential variable requires re-qualification.

The inspector vision record is the single most important personnel document. Per ASME V T-922 and ISO 9712, every VT inspector must demonstrate annually: (1) near-vision Jaeger J1 (or equivalent Snellen 20/25) on a standard near-vision chart at 300 mm with corrective lenses if needed, (2) colour-vision Ishihara plates at hire and at least every 5 years. The record is maintained by the certifying authority (the company Level III for ASNT, the central body for ISO 9712). Loss of vision certification immediately suspends the inspector from code work — no exceptions.

For high-stakes nuclear and aerospace work, the requirement is often stricter: ASME Section XI (in-service inspection of nuclear power plants) requires Jaeger J2 (lines 0.6 mm at 300 mm — slightly easier than J1) per IWA-2321 with annual re-test, plus a demonstration of resolution at the actual working distance using a custom resolution target.

Remote Visual Inspection: Borescope, Videoscope & ROV Technical Detail

RVI is the fastest-evolving area of VT. Three main equipment classes.

Rigid borescopes use a series of relay lenses inside a stainless steel tube. Diameter 4-10 mm; working length 175-500 mm typical (extreme cases to 2 m for industrial applications). Optical resolution < 0.05 mm at the tip working distance of 25-50 mm. Pen-style economy models use a simple eyepiece; professional models couple to a video camera. Used for: cylinder bore inspection, blind-tapped hole inspection, gun barrel inspection, jet engine intermediate inspection.

Flexible fiberscopes use a coherent bundle of optical fibers (typically 6,000-30,000 fibers, each < 10 μm diameter) to transmit the image through a bendable shaft. Diameter 4-12 mm; working length 1-3 m. Resolution limited by fiber count (typically 0.5 mm at tip), so quickly being replaced by videoscopes. Still used where electromagnetic interference precludes electronic videoscope use.

Videoscopes place a CMOS / CCD sensor and LED light source at the probe tip, transmitting digital video back through a flexible shaft. Diameter 6-12 mm typical; working length 1-3 m. 4-way articulation at the tip. HD or 4K resolution. Stereo measurement via two cameras at the tip, or shadow measurement via offset LED — both give 0.1 mm dimensional accuracy at 25 mm tip-to-target distance. The market leaders: Olympus IPLEX NX, GE Mentor Visual iQ, Karl Storz, Yateks. Capital cost varies with capability for handheld; cost varies by specification for advanced articulated systems with 3D mapping.

Inspection ROVs and crawlers extend RVI to environments where a handheld probe cannot reach — submerged subsea infrastructure (SaaB Seaeye, VideoRay), large vessel interiors (GE Inuktun crawlers, snake-arm devices). HD camera plus auxiliary lighting plus often UT thickness gauging in a single platform. ROVs deploy from a surface vessel or platform to depths of 1,000-3,000 m for offshore inspection. See our offshore platform inspection guide.

Drone-Based Inspection: Regulations, Capability & Workflow

Drone-based VT has matured rapidly. The dominant 2026 platforms: DJI Matrice 30T (commercial workhorse, RTK GPS, IR + 4K camera), Skydio X2 (semi-autonomous obstacle avoidance), FlyAbility Elios 3 (collision-tolerant indoor / confined-space inspection with lidar SLAM).

The standard external-asset drone-VT workflow: pre-job site survey, flight-permission filing (FAA Part 107 in U.S., CASR Part 101 in Australia, EASA Part-UAS in EU); pre-flight: charge batteries, calibrate compass, verify return-to-home setpoint, set geofence; flight: fly a planned grid pattern at 5-15 m standoff capturing overlapping 80 % nadir + 20 % oblique images; post-flight: stitch images via photogrammetry software (Pix4D, Agisoft Metashape) into a dimensioned 3D model; review: a Level II VT inspector reviews the imagery in-office, flags candidate indications, dispatches a follow-up ground team to suspect areas. The drone replaces 60-80 % of scaffolding and rope-access labor.

For confined-space indoor inspection (storage tank interiors, boiler interiors, ship cargo holds), the collision-tolerant Elios 3 carries a 4K camera plus a lidar SLAM module that builds a real-time interior 3D map. Indoor flights bypass the permit-to-work requirements for human entry — a typical 30-meter-diameter tank that previously required 8 hours of confined-space-entry inspection can be drone-scanned in 30 minutes. ROI: typically > 90 % labor savings on first-year program.

VT Standards Comparison Across Codes & Acceptance Tables

The single biggest source of VT field error is using one code's acceptance criteria when a different code applies. The dominant 2026 visual acceptance tables:

AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 (statically loaded non-tubular connections): explicit limits for crack (none permitted), undercut depth (0.25 mm for thicker material), porosity (cluster < 6 mm), fillet leg dimension (per design + 1.5 mm tolerance). Most-cited table for structural welding worldwide.

AWS D1.1 Table 8.2 (cyclically loaded): tighter limits for fatigue applications — undercut allowed only at toes parallel to the principal stress, etc.

ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2 Normal Fluid Service: visual criteria refer to BPVC Section IX qualification plus specific dimensional limits on weld profile.

ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2 Severe Cyclic / Category M: tighter limits including no crack, no LOF, no overlap, undercut depth restrictions.

API 510 Section 5.5 (in-service vessel VT): focus on corrosion features, mechanical damage, distortion, leakage — different paradigm from new-construction VT.

API 570 Section 5.5 (in-service piping VT): similar in-service focus.

API 653 Section 6 (storage tank VT): roof, shell and floor visual inspection with sketch and photo documentation.

Always confirm which code applies before quoting acceptance.

VT Case Study: 30-Year Refinery Pressure Vessel Re-Rating

A 30-year-old refinery surge drum (1995-vintage, 4.5 m ID × 12 m long, ASME Section VIII Div 1) underwent a 2026 fitness-for-service re-rating using a drone-plus-RVI internal VT campaign. External drone inspection (DJI M30T) captured 4K imagery of all 600 m² of vessel shell and head exterior in 90 minutes, with photogrammetric reconstruction into a 3D digital twin. Internal inspection used an Elios 3 confined-space drone (no human entry) followed by handheld Olympus IPLEX NX videoscope inspection of 24 nozzle bore welds and 6 internal-baffle attachment welds. Total indications identified: 3 hairline cracks at saddle support welds (later confirmed by MT), 14 corrosion-pit clusters (mapped and UT-thickness-verified), localized blistering at one HAZ. The vessel was re-rated for 5 more years of service at ≈ a modest cost inspection cost vs an alternative full-scaffold internal-entry inspection at a modest cost plus 5 additional turnaround days. The captured 3D model is loaded to the Atlantis Digital Twins platform for ongoing integrity-trend monitoring. This is a typical 2026 ROI of drone + RVI VT on a major pressure-equipment asset.

Procurement, Service Sourcing & Buyer Checklist for VT

VT is the most-commoditized NDT method, which makes vendor differentiation harder for buyers — and the cost of a poor VT inspector higher because every other NDT method depends on first-line VT accuracy. The five-item buyer checklist:

(1) Personnel certification. ASNT Level II VT (or ISO 9712 Level II) for every inspector, with current annual vision exam (Jaeger J1 / Snellen 20/25 + Ishihara). For weld inspection in fabrication, an additional AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) certificate is broadly expected — see our CWI certification guide. For in-service pressure equipment inspection, supervising inspector should hold API 510, API 570 or API 653 as applicable.

(2) Equipment kit. Verify the field kit contains calibrated weld gauge set, pit gauge, calibrated lux meter, mirror set, magnifier (at least 5×), pen-style borescope, DSLR or equivalent camera with macro lens. For RVI work, additionally a code-compliant videoscope (resolution demonstrable to Mandatory Appendix III requirements) and a probe-tip resolution reference target.

(3) Written procedure. VT procedure listing the essential variables (surface preparation, lighting, vision, equipment, acceptance) signed by Level III. For each project, a project-specific Annex documenting acceptance code reference (e.g. AWS D1.1 Table 8.1, ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2, API 510).

(4) Lighting and access plan. For new-construction work: confirm shop lighting at the inspection location ≥ 1,000 lux. For field/in-service work: portable LED inspection lights and a lux meter — verify illumination at each weld before inspection.

(5) Reporting format. Verify the deliverable format: hand-sketched indication maps are obsolete; modern code-compliant reporting uses mobile photo-tagged indication records with weld ID, GPS coordinates, dimensional measurements and accept/reject disposition. The Atlantis NDT reporting platform is purpose-built for this workflow.

Typical 2026 VT crew day rates: a modest cost U.S., a modest cost Middle East, a modest cost India / SE Asia. CWI-supervised structural weld VT: a modest cost per joint. Pressure-vessel internal VT during turnaround: a modest cost per vessel. Drone-based external VT of a refinery tower: cost varies by specification per day with photogrammetric 3D model deliverable. Subsea ROV VT: cost varies by specification per day-rate. For asset owners, ROI of investing in higher-quality VT (better-certified inspectors, more rigorous lighting/access, mobile digital reporting) typically pays back in the first turnaround through avoided rework, faster downstream NDT scheduling, and improved fitness-for-service documentation for ASME and API code compliance.

Atlantis NDT operates VT and RVI crews including drone-based external inspection and collision-tolerant indoor drone (FlyAbility Elios 3) coverage for confined spaces. See our service-area pages: Houston, Sabine Pass, Galveston, Hyderabad and Midland.

Frequently Asked Questions about Visual Testing

Q1: What lighting level is required for code-compliant VT?

A: Minimum 1,000 lux at the inspection surface per ASME V T-952. 1,500-2,000 lux preferred for fine work (fatigue cracks, corrosion pitting). Measure with a calibrated lux meter held at the surface.

Q2: What is direct vs remote visual examination?

A: Direct = eye to surface < 600 mm at angle ≥ 30°. Remote = via borescope, videoscope, mirror, camera or any other optical aid. ASME V Article 9 covers both; Mandatory Appendix III specifically governs RVI resolution and recording.

Q3: What vision requirements must VT personnel meet?

A: Annual near-vision acuity Jaeger J1 (lines 0.4 mm at 300 mm) or equivalent Snellen 20/25 — with corrective lenses if needed. Colour-vision Ishihara plates at hire and at least every 5 years. Failure of either disqualifies the inspector from code work until re-tested and passed.

Q4: How do I qualify a VT procedure to ASME V?

A: Write procedure per T-921 covering scope, lighting, surface condition, equipment, vision aids, acceptance criteria. Demonstrate on representative test piece showing required indication is visible. Level III approval mandatory.

Q5: What is the minimum probe-tip resolution for borescope inspection?

A: Per ASME V Mandatory Appendix III, probe-tip resolution must be demonstrated against a 1 mm or 0.4 mm reference at the working distance specified in the procedure. Modern HD videoscopes easily achieve < 0.1 mm at 25 mm WD.

Q6: Can drones be used for code-compliant VT?

A: Yes — provided the resolution, lighting, recording and Level II review meet ASME V Article 9 and Mandatory Appendix III. Drones are increasingly used for bridges, tanks, towers and flare stacks where access is hazardous.

Q7: What is the relationship between VT and other NDT methods?

A: VT is the mandatory prerequisite to any other NDT method per ASME V T-921 (and any owner-specified procedure). Any surface treatment defect (slag, scale, paint over-coverage) that would interfere with PT/MT/UT/RT must be addressed before those methods are applied.

Q8: What weld profile gauges should I carry?

A: Cambridge gauge (universal — covers convexity, concavity, fillet leg, throat, undercut depth). Hi-Lo gauge (root mismatch and reinforcement). Bridge cam (fillet leg). Fillet weld gauge set (multiple leg dimensions). Pit gauge / depth micrometer for corrosion.

Q9: When is direct VT inadequate and RVI required?

A: Any time the inspector cannot achieve eye-to-surface distance < 600 mm at angle ≥ 30°. Pressure-vessel interiors, piping bores, turbine internals, heat-exchanger tubes, gear-case interiors are all RVI applications.

Q10: What is heat tint on stainless steel and why does it matter?

A: Surface oxide color formed during welding — light straw (260 °C) to dark blue (430 °C). Heat tint indicates chromium oxide depletion and locally reduced corrosion resistance. ASME B31.3 normal-fluid service requires removal by pickling/passivation for stainless service.

Q11: Can a CWI certification substitute for ASNT VT Level II?

A: Per ASME V T-921, only an ASNT Level II VT (or equivalent ISO 9712 / NAS 410) is recognized for code VT. AWS CWI is widely accepted for welding-visual inspection by fabrication standards but ASME-stamped work requires ASNT or equivalent Level II VT in addition.

Q12: How do I record evidence of a VT finding?

A: Photograph with a measurement scale included. For RVI, freeze-frame video and save in a tamper-evident archive (DICONDE compliant for nuclear/aerospace). Use Atlantis NDT's mobile reporting platform to tag photos to weld ID, GPS location, timestamp, inspector ID and procedure revision.

Q13: What is the difference between AWS visual acceptance and ASME visual acceptance?

A: AWS D1.1 (structural) has explicit dimensional acceptance tables (Tables 8.1 statically and 8.2 cyclically loaded). ASME B31.3 (process piping) references ASME V Article 9 and Section IX without specific dimensional tables — relies on procedure-specified acceptance. Both reject any crack.

Q14: Can I do VT on hot surfaces?

A: Up to about 150 °C with normal PPE; above that, use heat-resistant mirrors or remote camera. RVI is the standard for hot equipment (still-warm vessels, in-operation pipework).

Q15: How does VT interface with API 510 / 570 / 653 in-service inspection?

A: Each of these in-service codes mandates VT as the primary external survey of the vessel/piping/tank, with UT thickness used for wall-loss measurement and PT/MT for crack-confirmation. The API inspector schedules and approves VT, but the work itself is typically performed by an ASNT Level II VT under the API inspector's direction.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is an ASNT Level III-led inspection technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with engineering operations in Hyderabad, India. We help oil & gas operators, EPCs, fabrication shops, and asset owners modernize their inspection programs across all surface and volumetric NDT methods. Our offerings include the Atlantis NDT Reporting Software, an Odoo 18 ERP pre-configured for NDT operations, and the Atlantis Digital Twins platform that overlays live inspection data on a 3D model of the asset. We also provide ASNT Level III consulting, training and procedure development for ASME Section V, ISO, API and AWS code work. Speak to a Level III directly: +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com.

title: UT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 Exam-Quality MCQs with Answers
snippet: Free 2026 UT Level II practice exam with 30 multiple-choice questions, full explanations, ASME V Article 4 and ISO 17640 references, and study plan.
content:
This 2026 practice question bank for Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Level II certification covers the full body of knowledge tested by ASNT (SNT-TC-1A and CP-189), PCN, and CSWIP examination boards. The questions below reflect the format and difficulty of the actual closed-book general examination, the open-book specific examination, and the practical demonstration. All questions are referenced to ASME BPVC Section V Article 4, ISO 17640, EN 12668, and ASNT SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7.

UT Level II Exam Format Overview

Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7, the minimum exam composition for UT Level II is:

  • General Examination: 40 closed-book multiple-choice questions on UT principles, equipment, and physics. Minimum score 70%.
  • Specific Examination: 20 open-book questions on the employer's written procedures, applicable codes, and equipment. Minimum score 70%.
  • Practical Examination: Hands-on demonstration on at least one specimen. Minimum score 70%.
  • Composite Score: Average of all three must be at least 80%.

For PCN Level 2, the structure is similar but the general paper has 40 questions and the specific paper has 30 questions across two methods. See our ASNT vs PCN comparison for full details.

UT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: Per ASME Section V Article 4, the minimum number of calibration reflectors required on a DAC curve is:

  • A. One
  • B. Two
  • C. Three
  • D. Four

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 T-434.2.1 requires a minimum of three points on the DAC: 1/4T, 1/2T, and 3/4T side-drilled holes to establish the distance amplitude correction curve for weld inspection.

Question 2: The velocity of a longitudinal wave in steel is approximately:

  • A. 3,250 m/s
  • B. 5,920 m/s
  • C. 7,500 m/s
  • D. 1,480 m/s

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Longitudinal wave velocity in carbon steel is approximately 5,920 m/s (5.92 mm/microsecond). This value is used in time-of-flight calculations and thickness measurements.

Question 3: Snell’s Law is used to calculate:

  • A. Beam divergence
  • B. Refraction angles between two media
  • C. Attenuation coefficient
  • D. Pulse repetition frequency

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Snell’s Law (sinθ1/V1 = sinθ2/V2) calculates the refracted angle when an ultrasonic beam crosses an interface between two materials of different acoustic velocities. It is fundamental to angle beam wedge design.

Question 4: The first critical angle for a perspex-to-steel interface is approximately:

  • A. 27.5°
  • B. 57.7°
  • C. 90°
  • D. 33°

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The first critical angle is the incident angle at which the refracted longitudinal wave reaches 90°, leaving only the refracted shear wave in the second medium. For perspex (2,730 m/s) to steel (5,920 m/s longitudinal), this is approximately 27.5°.

Question 5: Per ISO 17640, testing level B is used for:

  • A. Reduced testing
  • B. Basic testing
  • C. Enhanced testing
  • D. Special testing

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ISO 17640 defines four testing levels: A (reduced), B (basic), C (enhanced), and D (special). Level B is the most commonly specified level for general weld inspection in pressure equipment, while level C provides enhanced sensitivity.

Question 6: A 60° angle beam shear wave probe is most commonly used for:

  • A. Thickness measurement
  • B. Lamination detection
  • C. Weld inspection in butt joints
  • D. Hardness testing

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: The 60° shear wave is the most widely specified angle for inspecting butt weld fusion faces in carbon steel between 10 and 40 mm thickness. 45° and 70° are also used to provide complete coverage of different fusion face orientations.

Question 7: DAC stands for:

  • A. Decibel Adjustment Curve
  • B. Distance Amplitude Correction
  • C. Defect Acceptance Criteria
  • D. Dynamic Angle Calibration

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: DAC = Distance Amplitude Correction. The curve compensates for the natural attenuation and beam spread of the ultrasonic signal as it travels through material, allowing consistent sizing of reflectors at different depths.

Question 8: TCG stands for:

  • A. Time Corrected Gain
  • B. Total Coverage Gain
  • C. Transverse Crack Gain
  • D. Transducer Calibration Gain

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: TCG = Time Corrected Gain. Unlike DAC which is a curve drawn on the screen, TCG electronically amplifies signals at increasing time/depth so reflectors of equal size produce equal screen height regardless of depth.

Question 9: The near field length N of a circular transducer is calculated as:

  • A. D² / (4λ)
  • B. D²f / (4V)
  • C. Both A and B are correct
  • D. λ / (4D)

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Near field length N = D²/(4λ) where D = diameter and λ = wavelength. Since λ = V/f, this is equivalent to D²f/(4V). The near field is the region of complex interference where flaw sizing is unreliable.

Question 10: Beam divergence in the far field is reduced by:

  • A. Lower frequency
  • B. Smaller transducer diameter
  • C. Higher frequency and larger diameter
  • D. Increasing pulse width

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: The half-angle of beam divergence γ = 1.22λ/D for the 0-amplitude edge. Higher frequency (smaller λ) and larger diameter both reduce divergence, producing a more focused beam.

Question 11: Per EN 12668-1, which component is the pulser-receiver?

  • A. Part 1: Instruments
  • B. Part 2: Probes
  • C. Part 3: Combined equipment
  • D. Part 4: Cables

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: EN 12668 has three parts: Part 1 covers instruments (pulser-receiver, flaw detector electronics); Part 2 covers probes; Part 3 covers combined equipment performance.

Question 12: The IIW V1 calibration block is primarily used for:

  • A. Sensitivity setting only
  • B. Range calibration and angle verification
  • C. DAC construction
  • D. Couplant qualification

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The IIW V1 block (International Institute of Welding) is the most common calibration block. It is used for range/sweep calibration, angle verification (using the 100 mm radius and the 1.5 mm hole), and basic sensitivity checks.

Question 13: A skip distance for a 60° probe inspecting a 20 mm thick plate is:

  • A. 17.3 mm
  • B. 34.6 mm
  • C. 69.3 mm
  • D. 20 mm

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Full skip distance = 2 × thickness × tan(angle). For 60° and 20 mm: 2 × 20 × tan(60°) = 2 × 20 × 1.732 = 69.3 mm.

Question 14: Couplant is required to:

  • A. Reduce wear on the probe
  • B. Eliminate the air gap and transmit sound
  • C. Calibrate the instrument
  • D. Mark indication locations

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Couplant (water, gel, glycerine, oil) displaces the air between the probe and the part surface. Air has an acoustic impedance so different from steel that nearly 100% of the sound would reflect at the interface without couplant.

Question 15: A signal that occurs after the backwall echo and at twice the path length is most likely:

  • A. A lamination
  • B. A second backwall (multiple)
  • C. A surface crack
  • D. Mode conversion

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Multiple backwall echoes are normal in straight beam testing of thin plate with low attenuation. They occur at integer multiples of the thickness path length and confirm good coupling.

Question 16: The 6 dB drop sizing technique is used for:

  • A. Reflectors larger than the beam
  • B. Reflectors smaller than the beam
  • C. Calibration only
  • D. Couplant evaluation

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The 6 dB drop technique sizes reflectors that are LARGER than the ultrasonic beam by scanning across the indication until the signal drops by 6 dB (half amplitude). For reflectors smaller than the beam, the 20 dB drop or maximum amplitude method is used.

Question 17: Per ASME V Article 4, system linearity verification should be performed:

  • A. Every shift
  • B. Every calibration
  • C. When cables, probes, or wedges are changed
  • D. Annually

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 T-461 requires verification of system linearity and sensitivity when cables, probes, or wedges are changed because these components affect the calibrated response. Daily and pre-job checks are also required.

Question 18: A tandem technique is most useful for detecting:

  • A. Surface-breaking cracks
  • B. Vertically oriented planar flaws
  • C. Porosity clusters
  • D. Slag inclusions

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The tandem technique uses two probes (one transmitting and one receiving) positioned to catch the corner-reflected signal from vertically oriented flaws (lack of side wall fusion) that single-probe pulse-echo would miss.

Question 19: Mode conversion refers to:

  • A. Switching between A-scan and B-scan
  • B. Conversion of a longitudinal wave to a shear wave at an interface
  • C. Changing test frequencies
  • D. Changing display gain

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: When an angled beam strikes an interface, part of the energy converts between longitudinal and shear wave modes. This is a normal physical phenomenon but can produce spurious indications if misinterpreted.

Question 20: The standard reference reflector specified in ASME V Article 4 for piping welds is:

  • A. Flat-bottomed hole
  • B. Side-drilled hole
  • C. Notch
  • D. V-notch

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 specifies side-drilled holes (SDH) at 1/4T, 1/2T, and 3/4T depths in the basic calibration block as the primary DAC reference reflectors for weld inspection.

Question 21: Total internal reflection in UT occurs at:

  • A. The first critical angle
  • B. The second critical angle
  • C. Either critical angle
  • D. Above the second critical angle

Correct Answer: D

Explanation: Above the second critical angle (where the refracted shear wave reaches 90°), total internal reflection occurs and a surface (Rayleigh) wave is produced. This is used in surface wave inspection.

Question 22: A frequency of 5 MHz in steel produces a longitudinal wavelength of approximately:

  • A. 0.59 mm
  • B. 1.18 mm
  • C. 5.92 mm
  • D. 0.32 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Wavelength = Velocity / Frequency = 5,920 / 5,000,000 = 0.001184 m = 1.18 mm. Smaller wavelengths detect smaller flaws but attenuate more in the material.

Question 23: Per ISO 17640, the typical scanning gain above evaluation level is:

  • A. +3 dB
  • B. +6 dB
  • C. +12 dB
  • D. +20 dB

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17640 specifies a scanning sensitivity typically +6 dB above the evaluation sensitivity to ensure detection. Evaluation is then performed at the reference level for sizing.

Question 24: The thickness of the dead zone in a contact transducer is most affected by:

  • A. Couplant viscosity
  • B. Pulse width and damping
  • C. Probe cable length
  • D. Material temperature

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The dead zone (the region near the surface where reflectors cannot be detected) is governed by the pulse duration. Heavily damped probes with short pulses have smaller dead zones but lower sensitivity.

Question 25: A twin-crystal (TR) probe is used primarily for:

  • A. Angle beam weld inspection
  • B. Thin material thickness gauging and near-surface flaws
  • C. Through-transmission testing
  • D. Long-range guided waves

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Twin-crystal (TR) probes separate the transmitter and receiver elements with an acoustic barrier. This eliminates the dead zone, making them ideal for thin-wall corrosion mapping and near-surface flaw detection in thin plate.

Question 26: Surface wave (Rayleigh wave) velocity in steel is approximately:

  • A. 2,720 m/s
  • B. 3,250 m/s
  • C. 5,920 m/s
  • D. 1,480 m/s

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Rayleigh surface waves travel at approximately 0.9 times the shear wave velocity. For steel that gives roughly 0.9 × 3,250 = 2,925 m/s, commonly approximated as 2,720–2,900 m/s.

Question 27: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the minimum recommended training hours for UT Level II total are:

  • A. 8 hours
  • B. 40 hours
  • C. 80 hours (40 Level I + 40 Level II)
  • D. 120 hours

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 40 hours of formal training at Level I plus 40 hours at Level II for ultrasonic testing, plus method-specific experience hours.

Question 28: A high amplitude signal that disappears when the probe is rotated 360° around the indication position suggests:

  • A. A spherical reflector (porosity)
  • B. A planar reflector (crack or LOF)
  • C. A volumetric reflector
  • D. Mode conversion

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Planar reflectors (cracks, lack of fusion) are highly directional and only reflect strongly when the beam strikes them near perpendicular. Rotating the probe drops the signal sharply, distinguishing them from volumetric or spherical reflectors.

Question 29: The transfer correction (transfer loss) accounts for:

  • A. Difference in attenuation between calibration block and test piece
  • B. Probe wear
  • C. Couplant temperature
  • D. Cable loss

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Transfer correction compensates for differences in surface condition, grain structure, and attenuation between the calibration block and the actual test piece. It is added to the gain before evaluation per ASME V and ISO 17640.

Question 30: For a UT Level II to certify a procedure, what additional approval is required?

  • A. Site safety officer
  • B. Level III review and approval
  • C. Customer signature
  • D. No further approval needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, only a Level III is authorized to write, approve, and audit NDT procedures. A Level II performs inspections and interprets results per approved procedures. See our Level II vs Level III article.

Study Tips for UT Level II

  • Master the formulas: Wavelength, near field, beam divergence, skip distance, Snell’s Law. Practice 20+ calculation problems per topic.
  • Know your codes: Read ASME V Article 4 cover to cover. Highlight T-432, T-434, and T-461. Practice with the actual code book you will use in the open-book specific exam.
  • Practical: Spend at least 40 hours scanning real welds. Calibrate from scratch every day until DAC, TCG, and angle verification become muscle memory.
  • Question bank: Aim to solve 500+ practice questions before exam day. Track which topics you miss and re-study them.
  • Time management: The general exam typically allows 90 minutes for 40 questions, less than 2.5 minutes per question. Pace yourself.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Recommended Practice SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition)
  • ASNT UT Classroom Training Book by Davis & Hagemaier
  • ASME BPVC Section V (current edition)
  • ISO 17640:2018 NDT of welds — Ultrasonic testing
  • EN 12668 Parts 1, 2, 3 — NDT — Characterization and verification of ultrasonic test equipment
  • Krautkrämer Ultrasonic Testing of Materials (Springer)
  • Atlantis NDT UT Level II training course (40-hour classroom + 40-hour practical)

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How many hours of experience do I need before I can take the UT Level II exam?

A: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, you need 400 hours of UT Level I experience before progressing to Level II training. Some employers require an additional 400 hours of Level II experience before certification.

Q: Can I skip Level I and go directly to Level II?

A: Direct-entry Level II is allowed under SNT-TC-1A only if the candidate completes the cumulative training and experience for both levels (typically 80 hours of training and 800 hours of experience). PCN allows direct-entry Level 2 only for candidates with documented prior experience.

Q: How long is the UT Level II certification valid?

A: ASNT employer-based certification under SNT-TC-1A is valid for up to 5 years with annual eye exams and continuous activity. ASNT Central Certification (ACCP) and PCN are valid for 5 years with renewal exam at 10 years.

Q: What is the pass rate for UT Level II?

A: First-attempt pass rates vary by training provider but typically range from 60 to 75 percent for the composite exam. Atlantis NDT students average 85 percent first-attempt pass rate with our 80-hour blended program.

Q: Is PAUT covered in standard UT Level II?

A: No. Phased Array UT (PAUT) is a separate certification under SNT-TC-1A. You must hold standard UT Level II first and then complete an additional PAUT-specific training and exam.

Q: Can a UT Level II inspector approve procedures?

A: No. Only a UT Level III may write, approve, and audit procedures. See our Level II vs Level III comparison for full authority scope.

Q: What is the difference between ASME V Article 4 and ISO 17640?

A: ASME V Article 4 is the US code for ultrasonic weld inspection in pressure vessels and piping. ISO 17640 is the international (European) equivalent. Both require similar calibration but differ in acceptance criteria reference and reporting format.

Q: Do I need to know AWS D1.1 for UT Level II?

A: AWS D1.1 is required if you will inspect structural welds. The exam code (ASME, AWS, API) is chosen at certification time. Many inspectors hold dual certifications for ASME and AWS coverage.

Q: What couplant is recommended for hot surfaces above 50°C?

A: High-temperature couplants such as Sonotech Ultratherm or Echotrace HT are rated to 540°C. Below 50°C, standard glycerine, water-based gel, or cellulose paste is adequate.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT prepare candidates for the UT Level II exam?

A: Our 80-hour blended program covers 40 hours of theory (general + specific code training), 40 hours of supervised practical, four proctored mock exams, and a personalized study plan. We also include a copy of ASME V and ISO 17640 in the course fee. Enroll here or call +1 (281) 840-8969.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

title: RT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 ASME V & ISO 17636 MCQs
snippet: 2026 RT Level II practice questions: 30 MCQs with answers, ASME V Article 2 references, ISO 17636 coverage, radiation safety, plus FAQ and study plan.
content:
Welcome to the 2026 Radiographic Testing (RT) Level II practice exam bank. The questions below mirror the format of the ASNT general examination, the employer-administered specific examination, and the practical demonstration required by SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7. All questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 2, ISO 17636 Parts 1 and 2, and ASTM E94 (Standard Guide for Radiographic Examination).

RT Level II Exam Format Overview

RT Level II under SNT-TC-1A consists of three examinations:

  • General: 40 closed-book questions on radiation physics, equipment, film, image quality, and radiation safety. Pass mark 70%.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on the employer's written practice, applicable codes (ASME V, AWS D1.1, API), and procedures. Pass mark 70%.
  • Practical: Setup, exposure, processing, and interpretation of at least one radiograph. Pass mark 70%.
  • Composite: Average of all three at or above 80%.

Note: Radiation safety training (often 32 hours) is mandatory in most jurisdictions before any RT exam. Many countries also require a separate Radiation Protection Officer (RPO) license. For the bigger picture see our ASNT vs PCN comparison.

RT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: The SI unit of absorbed dose is the:

  • A. Roentgen
  • B. Gray
  • C. Sievert
  • D. Becquerel

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Gray (Gy) is the SI unit of absorbed dose, equal to 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of material. The Roentgen measures exposure in air, the Sievert measures equivalent dose, and the Becquerel measures activity.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 2, the minimum source-to-film distance (SFD) is determined by:

  • A. Tube voltage
  • B. Geometric unsharpness (Ug) formula
  • C. Film type
  • D. Radiation type

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-274.2 limits geometric unsharpness Ug = f × t / d, where f = focal size, t = source-to-object distance, and d = object-to-film distance. The minimum SFD is calculated to keep Ug at or below the limit (typically 0.51 mm or less depending on thickness).

Question 3: A penetrameter (IQI) is used to:

  • A. Measure film density
  • B. Verify radiographic sensitivity
  • C. Calculate exposure time
  • D. Determine source decay

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Image Quality Indicator (IQI) — hole-type or wire-type — is placed on the source side of the part to demonstrate that the radiographic technique can detect a specified percentage of the test object thickness. ASME V uses 2-2T sensitivity (2% essential hole visible).

Question 4: The half-life of Ir-192 is approximately:

  • A. 30 years
  • B. 5.27 years
  • C. 74 days
  • D. 60 days

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Iridium-192 has a half-life of 73.83 days. Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. Selenium-75 has a half-life of 119.8 days. Half-life governs source replacement intervals and exposure time calculations.

Question 5: Per ASME V Article 2, the acceptable film density range for the area of interest is:

  • A. 1.0 to 2.0 H&D
  • B. 1.8 to 4.0 H&D (composite up to 4.0)
  • C. 0.5 to 1.5 H&D
  • D. 3.0 to 5.0 H&D

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-282 requires film density of 1.8 to 4.0 in the area of interest for single-film viewing. For composite (two films viewed together), the through-density limit may extend higher, with each film between 1.3 and 4.0.

Question 6: Geometric unsharpness Ug is reduced by:

  • A. Larger focal spot
  • B. Shorter SFD
  • C. Larger SFD and smaller focal spot
  • D. Higher kV

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Ug = f × t / d. Reducing focal spot size (f) and increasing source-to-object distance (so that d, object-to-film, is small relative to t) both reduce geometric unsharpness. This is why panoramic shots use long SFD when possible.

Question 7: The inverse square law states that radiation intensity:

  • A. Decreases linearly with distance
  • B. Decreases as 1/d
  • C. Decreases as 1/d²
  • D. Increases with distance

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Inverse square law: I1/I2 = (d2/d1)². Doubling the distance from a point source reduces intensity to one quarter. This is fundamental to time-distance-shielding radiation safety practice.

Question 8: A diffraction mottle pattern on a radiograph indicates:

  • A. Defective film
  • B. Coarse grain structure in the part
  • C. Light leak
  • D. Backscatter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Diffraction mottling appears as a swirly low-contrast pattern caused by large crystalline grains in cast or coarse-grained materials (some austenitic stainless steels). It can mask real defects and is typically addressed by changing kV or using a different technique.

Question 9: A lead letter B on the back of a film cassette is used to detect:

  • A. Film fogging
  • B. Backscatter radiation
  • C. Source decay
  • D. Density variation

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per ASME V T-223, a lead letter B (typically 13 mm high, 1.6 mm thick) is placed on the back of the cassette. If the B appears as a light image on the developed film, backscatter is present and the technique must be modified (typically by adding lead screens or backing).

Question 10: Per ISO 17636-1, the wire IQI is placed:

  • A. On the film side, perpendicular to the weld
  • B. On the source side, parallel to the weld with finest wire outward
  • C. In the weld center
  • D. Between the film and the screen

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17636-1 (and EN ISO 19232) require the wire IQI on the source side, placed parallel to the weld axis with the smallest wire furthest from the weld center. Sensitivity is determined by the smallest visible wire.

Question 11: Tube voltage (kV) primarily controls:

  • A. Radiation intensity
  • B. Beam penetrating power and contrast
  • C. Film density only
  • D. Focal spot size

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Higher kV produces higher-energy (more penetrating) photons but reduces subject contrast. Lower kV produces softer, more contrasty radiographs but cannot penetrate thick sections. kV selection balances penetration vs. contrast.

Question 12: Tube current (mA) primarily affects:

  • A. Penetrating power
  • B. Beam quality
  • C. Quantity of radiation (intensity)
  • D. Wavelength

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: mA controls the number of electrons hitting the target per second, which is directly proportional to X-ray photon output. mA × time (mAs) controls film density without changing contrast.

Question 13: The reciprocity law states that:

  • A. Density depends on mAs only
  • B. kV and mA are interchangeable
  • C. Film responds equally to long-low and short-high exposures
  • D. Distance and time are reciprocal

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Reciprocity law: film density depends on total exposure (intensity × time). Long exposures at low intensity should produce the same density as short exposures at high intensity. Some films show reciprocity failure at extreme times.

Question 14: A wire IQI with wires 0.10, 0.13, 0.16, 0.20, 0.25, 0.32 mm in an 8 mm part requires visible wire of:

  • A. 0.32 mm
  • B. 0.20 mm (closest to 2%)
  • C. 0.10 mm
  • D. 2.0 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: For 2% sensitivity (Class A typical), the required wire diameter is 2% of 8 mm = 0.16 mm. Since 0.16 mm is in the set, that is the minimum visible wire; the 0.20 mm wire would correspond to a slightly relaxed sensitivity if 0.16 mm cannot be resolved.

Question 15: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays primarily at:

  • A. 1.17 and 1.33 MeV
  • B. 0.30 to 0.61 MeV
  • C. 0.066 MeV
  • D. 0.27 MeV

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Co-60 emits two gamma rays at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV — high energy suitable for steel up to 200 mm thick. Ir-192 emits a spectrum 0.21–0.61 MeV (effective approximately 0.4 MeV). Se-75 emits 0.066–0.40 MeV.

Question 16: A lead intensifying screen does what for the film?

  • A. Reduces contrast
  • B. Reduces exposure time and enhances image
  • C. Filters radiation
  • D. Eliminates backscatter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Lead foil screens (typically 0.13 mm front, 0.25 mm back) emit secondary electrons when struck by gamma photons, increasing film exposure. They reduce required exposure time and improve image quality. They also filter low-energy scatter.

Question 17: A dark, fuzzy, narrow line in the root of a single-V butt weld radiograph is most likely:

  • A. Tungsten inclusion
  • B. Lack of root penetration (LOP)
  • C. Slag
  • D. Concavity

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Lack of root penetration appears as a dark, sharp, straight line in the root of a single-V butt weld where the original root face was not melted. Slag is irregular and dark; tungsten inclusion is a small bright (light) spot; concavity is a darker root contour.

Question 18: Per ASTM E94, “shooting through” multiple layers in a single exposure requires:

  • A. No special consideration
  • B. IQI on source side and verification of sensitivity at each layer
  • C. Always two separate exposures
  • D. A different film type

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: When a single exposure radiographs multiple thicknesses (e.g., DWDI — double wall double image), an IQI is placed on the source side and the technique must achieve required sensitivity at both layers. ASTM E94 provides guidance.

Question 19: The annual dose limit for a radiation worker per ICRP 103 (and US 10 CFR 20) is:

  • A. 1 mSv
  • B. 5 mSv
  • C. 50 mSv with a 5-year average of 20 mSv
  • D. 500 mSv

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ICRP 103 and US 10 CFR 20 set occupational limits at 50 mSv per year with a 5-year running average of 20 mSv/yr. Public limit is 1 mSv/yr. Lens of the eye limit was reduced to 20 mSv/yr by ICRP 118.

Question 20: A digital radiography system uses what to capture the image?

  • A. Silver halide film
  • B. Photostimulable phosphor plate (CR) or flat panel detector (DDA)
  • C. Lead screen
  • D. Penetrameter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Digital RT replaces film with either Computed Radiography (CR) phosphor plates that are scanned after exposure, or Direct Digital Arrays (DDA) such as flat-panel detectors that produce a live image. See our DR vs film comparison.

Question 21: Per ASME V Article 2 (2021), digital radiography (CR/DDA) is:

  • A. Not permitted
  • B. Permitted with qualification and Article 2 Mandatory Appendix III/IV/V
  • C. Permitted only on aluminum
  • D. Permitted only for tubular sections

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V Article 2 was expanded with Mandatory Appendices for CR (App. III), DDA (App. IV), and computed tomography (App. V). Each requires demonstration of equivalent or superior performance to film.

Question 22: The basic spatial resolution (SRb) of a CR system is determined by:

  • A. Pixel size only
  • B. Pixel size and detector unsharpness (typically 2× effective pixel size)
  • C. Source size
  • D. kV

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: For CR, SRb depends on the phosphor plate properties, laser scanning resolution, and pixel size, typically 2 times the effective pixel size. SRb is measured per EN 14784 / ISO 17636-2 using a duplex wire IQI.

Question 23: A typical Class B sensitivity per ISO 17636-1 corresponds to:

  • A. Lower sensitivity than Class A
  • B. Higher sensitivity than Class A
  • C. Same as Class A
  • D. No defined limit

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17636-1 defines Class A (basic) and Class B (improved). Class B requires longer SFD, finer-grained film, and demonstrates a smaller wire/hole IQI. Class B is typically required for safety-critical welds.

Question 24: A double-wall double-image (DWDI) technique is used for:

  • A. Pipe at or below 76 mm OD
  • B. Pipe greater than 76 mm OD
  • C. Flat plates only
  • D. Castings only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: DWDI is used on small-diameter pipe (typically at or below 76 mm or 3 in OD) where the source is offset to produce an elliptical projection showing two opposite weld regions simultaneously. For larger pipe, single-wall single-image is used.

Question 25: Per ASME V T-276, the IQI hole “2T” means:

  • A. Hole diameter equal to 2× IQI thickness
  • B. IQI is 2 mm thick
  • C. Hole at 2 inches from edge
  • D. Two thicknesses of test piece

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In ASME V hole-type IQI, the holes are designated 1T, 2T, and 4T, where T is the IQI thickness. A “2-2T” sensitivity means a 2% IQI (2% of part thickness) showing the 2T hole visible — standard Level 2 sensitivity.

Question 26: The ALARA principle stands for:

  • A. As Low As Reasonably Achievable
  • B. Always Lower Allowed Radiation Average
  • C. Acceptable Limit And Reasonable Action
  • D. Annual Limit And Required Approval

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable — is the foundational radiation safety principle. Even below regulatory limits, exposures should be minimized using time, distance, and shielding.

Question 27: The HVL (half value layer) of Ir-192 in steel is approximately:

  • A. 2 mm
  • B. 13 mm
  • C. 50 mm
  • D. 100 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The half value layer of Ir-192 in steel is approximately 13 mm (0.5 in). For Co-60 the HVL in steel is about 22 mm. HVL is used to calculate shielding for radiation safety and exposure time for thickness changes.

Question 28: A typical Ir-192 source for industrial RT has activity of:

  • A. 1 GBq
  • B. 10 MBq
  • C. 0.5–3.7 TBq (15–100 Ci)
  • D. 50 mCi

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Industrial Ir-192 source projectors typically carry 0.5–3.7 TBq (15–100 Curies). Higher activity reduces exposure time but increases handling hazard. License conditions limit maximum activity per device.

Question 29: Per ISO 17636-1, the minimum SFD for a class A technique is determined by:

  • A. A simple rule of 10×t
  • B. The nomogram in Annex B based on focal spot size and Ug limit
  • C. Always 1 m
  • D. Always 50 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: SFD is calculated from the nomogram in ISO 17636-1 Annex B based on focal spot size, geometric unsharpness limit, and part thickness. Generic answers like 10 times thickness are not correct; always use the nomogram.

Question 30: A Level II RT inspector’s responsibilities include:

  • A. Writing the procedure
  • B. Setting up exposures, processing, and interpreting radiographs per approved procedure
  • C. Approving new procedures
  • D. Training Level IIIs

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per SNT-TC-1A, Level II personnel may set up and calibrate equipment, perform the test per a procedure, interpret and evaluate results, and train Level I personnel. Procedure writing and approval is Level III only.

Study Tips for RT Level II

  • Radiation safety first: Many candidates fail because they underestimate the safety questions. Master ALARA, time-distance-shielding, HVL/TVL, dose limits, and source handling.
  • Practice film interpretation: Look at 200+ real radiographs before exam day. Recognize porosity (round dark), slag (irregular dark), tungsten (bright spot), LOF (straight dark), LOP (sharp dark line), and cracks (sharp dark zig-zag).
  • Calculate exposure: Practice the relationship between mAs, distance, density, and time. The exam often requires re-calculation when distance or kV changes.
  • Source decay: Memorize Ir-192 (74 days) and Co-60 (5.27 years). Practice calculating remaining activity after N half-lives.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Radiographic Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 2 + Mandatory Appendices III, IV, V
  • ISO 17636-1 (film) and 17636-2 (digital)
  • ASTM E94 Standard Guide for Radiographic Examination
  • ASTM E1742 / E2033 / E2698 for digital radiography
  • Atlantis NDT RT Level II training with radiation safety officer module

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Do I need a radiation safety license to take the RT Level II exam?

A: A radiation safety license is required to OPERATE radioactive sources or X-ray equipment, but not strictly to take the certification exam. However, most reputable training programs include the 32-hour radiation safety training as part of RT Level II.

Q: Can I use my phone calculator during the exam?

A: Most exam boards provide a basic calculator or allow only non-programmable scientific calculators. Phones, smart watches, and devices with internet access are prohibited.

Q: What is the difference between RT Level II for film and for digital?

A: Standard RT Level II covers film. Digital radiography (CR/DDA) requires additional method-specific training and an addendum exam. ASNT now offers DR endorsements.

Q: How long is the RT Level II exam?

A: General: 90 to 120 minutes for 40 questions. Specific: 60 to 90 minutes for 20 questions. Practical: 4 to 6 hours including setup, exposure, processing, and report writing.

Q: What is the most common reason for failing the RT specific exam?

A: Inability to navigate the code book quickly. The specific exam is open book, candidates fail when they have not tabbed and indexed their ASME V book. Atlantis NDT provides a pre-tabbed code in our course.

Q: Can I take RT Level II if I am colour blind?

A: RT does not rely on colour, only on grayscale density. Near vision and contrast sensitivity (Jaeger 2 at 12 in) are required. See SNT-TC-1A para 8 on physical requirements.

Q: Is digital RT replacing film?

A: Digital RT is rapidly growing in oil & gas, aerospace, and pipeline inspection. Film is still widely used in heavy fabrication and where archival regulatory submission requires hard copies. See our DR vs film article.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT prepare candidates for RT Level II?

A: We offer an 80-hour blended program with 40 hours classroom, 32 hours radiation safety, 8 hours mock exam, plus 40 hours practical with real sources at our Houston darkroom. Group rates available for corporate cohorts. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 to enroll.

Q: What is the salary difference between RT Level I and Level II?

A: In the US, RT Level I averages a modest cost to a modest cost; RT Level II averages a modest cost to a modest cost, with experienced offshore inspectors earning $130,000+. See also our Level II vs III salary comparison.
