title: MT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 ASME V Article 7 MCQs
snippet: Free 2026 MT Level II practice exam with 30 multiple-choice questions, full explanations, ASME V Article 7, ASTM E709/E1444 and ISO 9934 references.
content:
This 2026 question bank for Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) Level II certification follows the format of the ASNT general exam (40 closed-book questions), the specific code-and-procedure exam (20 open-book), and the practical demonstration. All questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 7, ASTM E709 (Standard Guide for MT), ASTM E1444 (Standard Practice for Wet Fluorescent MT), and ISO 9934 Parts 1, 2, 3.

MT Level II Exam Format Overview

  • General: 40 closed-book questions, 90 minutes, 70% pass mark.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on the employer's procedure and applicable code (ASME, AWS, API, ISO).
  • Practical: Demonstration on at least one item with both AC and DC techniques, dry and wet methods.
  • Composite: 80% average across the three.

MT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: MT can only detect flaws that are:

  • A. Internal to the part
  • B. At or near the surface of a ferromagnetic material
  • C. In any material
  • D. Subsurface in any material

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: MT detects surface and near-surface flaws (typically within 3 mm of the surface) in ferromagnetic materials. It cannot detect deep subsurface flaws and cannot be used on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper, or other non-ferrous materials.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 7, the minimum tangential magnetic field strength is:

  • A. 1–2 kA/m
  • B. 2.4 kA/m (30 Oe) measured with a gauss meter
  • C. 10 kA/m
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-754 requires a tangential field of at least 30 Oersted (2.4 kA/m or 24 Gauss) measured with a gauss meter on the part surface, or alternatively verified by a magnetic field indicator (pie gauge or shim).

Question 3: A longitudinal magnetic field is produced by:

  • A. A central conductor
  • B. A coil or solenoid wrapped around the part
  • C. Head shot (direct contact)
  • D. Yokes only at side

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: A longitudinal field, used to detect transverse cracks, is produced by a coil with the part inside or by encircling magnetizing cable. Yokes can also produce longitudinal fields along the axis between the two poles.

Question 4: A circular magnetic field is best for detecting:

  • A. Transverse cracks
  • B. Longitudinal cracks aligned with the current
  • C. Subsurface porosity
  • D. Laminations

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: A circular field, produced by passing current through the part (head shot) or through a central conductor, detects cracks oriented parallel to the current flow (i.e., perpendicular to the magnetic flux lines).

Question 5: The right-hand rule states:

  • A. Current direction determined by thumb, flux direction by fingers
  • B. Flux is perpendicular to current
  • C. AC produces no flux
  • D. Field strength is independent of current

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: When the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of current flow, the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic flux lines. This is fundamental to predicting field direction in MT.

Question 6: AC magnetization is best for detecting:

  • A. Subsurface flaws
  • B. Surface flaws (due to skin effect)
  • C. Internal porosity
  • D. Lack of fusion at root

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Due to the skin effect, AC concentrates the magnetic field near the surface (within roughly 1.5 mm depth in carbon steel at 50/60 Hz). This makes AC ideal for surface crack detection but unable to detect subsurface flaws.

Question 7: DC or full-wave rectified (FWDC) magnetization penetrates:

  • A. Only the surface
  • B. Several millimeters into the part
  • C. The entire cross-section uniformly only with HWDC
  • D. Only at high amperage

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: DC and FWDC produce fields that penetrate several millimeters into the part, allowing detection of slightly subsurface flaws. HWDC (half-wave) produces a pulsed field that is intermediate between AC and FWDC.

Question 8: Per ASTM E709, residual magnetism after MT is typically required to be:

  • A. Less than 3 G (240 A/m)
  • B. Less than 10 G
  • C. Less than 50 G
  • D. Not required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: After MT, residual magnetism must be removed for parts that will be welded, machined, or have moving magnetic components. ASTM E709 typically requires less than 3 Gauss (240 A/m) measured with a field indicator, though customer specs may be tighter.

Question 9: A pie gauge (octagonal pie-shaped indicator) is used to:

  • A. Calibrate the gauss meter
  • B. Verify field direction and approximate strength on the part surface
  • C. Replace the IQI
  • D. Measure couplant

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The pie gauge consists of eight pie-shaped pieces of steel brazed together with a copper plate on top. When placed on a magnetized part, the joints show indications, confirming both field strength and direction.

Question 10: For a longitudinal field by coil shot, an empirical formula for amp-turns is:

  • A. NI = 45,000 / (L/D) for L/D between 4 and 15
  • B. NI = 100
  • C. NI = 1000/D
  • D. Not calculable

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASTM E1444 and ASME V give empirical formulas based on the length-to-diameter (L/D) ratio of the part. For 4 at or below L/D at or below 15, NI = 45,000/(L/D). Different formulas apply for short parts (low L/D) or with end pieces.

Question 11: Wet fluorescent MT inspection is performed under:

  • A. White light
  • B. UV-A (black light) of at least 1000 μW/cm²
  • C. Red light
  • D. Daylight only

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Wet fluorescent MT particles fluoresce under UV-A (320–400 nm) light. ASTM E1444 and ASME V require at least 1000 μW/cm² of UV-A on the part surface, with ambient white light at or below 20 lux (2 ftc).

Question 12: A bath concentration for wet fluorescent MT is typically:

  • A. 0.1–0.4 mL/100 mL settled in pear tube
  • B. 5 mL/100 mL
  • C. 20 mL/100 mL
  • D. Not measured

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-732 requires bath concentration of 0.1–0.4 mL settled particles per 100 mL of bath for fluorescent particles, measured in a pear-shaped centrifuge tube after 30 minutes settling. Visible (non-fluorescent) particles use 1.2–2.4 mL/100 mL.

Question 13: A yoke (electromagnetic yoke) has lifting power requirements of:

  • A. 10 lb for any yoke
  • B. 40 lb for DC and 10 lb for AC at maximum pole spacing
  • C. 100 lb for any yoke
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-762 requires lifting power tests: AC yokes must lift 10 lb (4.5 kg), DC/permanent yokes must lift 40 lb (18 kg) at maximum pole spacing. Verified daily or per shift on a known steel weight.

Question 14: A common non-relevant indication on MT is caused by:

  • A. Sharp geometry changes (fillets), surface roughness, magnetic writing
  • B. Internal porosity
  • C. Hydrogen
  • D. High temperature

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Non-relevant indications include sharp geometry changes (where flux leakage occurs naturally), surface roughness and machining marks, magnetic writing (transferred field from contact with magnetized tools), and grain boundaries in cold-worked material.

Question 15: The continuous method of MT means:

  • A. Current is on while particles are being applied and during indication formation
  • B. Current is on continuously for hours
  • C. Method used only on continuous welds
  • D. Particles applied continuously after demag

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In the continuous method, magnetizing current is on while particles are applied (or just after, for the residual method). The continuous method gives better sensitivity for low-retentivity steels.

Question 16: The residual method requires:

  • A. High-retentivity steel
  • B. Low-retentivity steel
  • C. Aluminum parts
  • D. Non-magnetic material

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The residual method magnetizes the part, removes the current, then applies particles to the residual magnetic field. It works only on high-retentivity steels (typically tool steel, hardened steel, ferritic stainless) that hold a field after the current is removed.

Question 17: A central conductor through a hollow part produces:

  • A. Circular field in the wall
  • B. Longitudinal field
  • C. No field
  • D. Reversed field

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: A central conductor carries current through the bore of a tubular part. By the right-hand rule, the resulting circular field in the part wall detects longitudinal cracks on both inside and outside surfaces simultaneously.

Question 18: Per ISO 9934-1, magnetic particle suspension viscosity should be:

  • A. Low (kerosene-like, less than 5 mPa·s)
  • B. 50 mPa·s
  • C. 200 mPa·s
  • D. Not relevant

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9934-1 and ASTM E1444 require a thin, low-viscosity carrier (typically a refined kerosene-based oil less than 5 mPa·s at 38°C) so particles can mobilize to flaw locations. Water-based with surfactant is also common.

Question 19: A typical MT defect indication for a surface fatigue crack appears as:

  • A. A sharp, well-defined line of particles
  • B. A diffuse cloud
  • C. Round dots
  • D. Streaks following the current

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Fatigue cracks produce tight, sharp, often slightly raised particle build-ups along the crack edge. Subsurface flaws produce broader, fuzzier indications because the leakage field spreads.

Question 20: Demagnetization is performed by:

  • A. Cooling the part below Curie point
  • B. Slowly reducing the alternating field while moving away from a coil
  • C. Hitting the part
  • D. Adding a magnet

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Demagnetization is achieved by subjecting the part to a continuously reversing field of decreasing amplitude — either AC of decreasing amplitude, DC reversed and decreased, or moving the part away from an AC coil at low speed.

Question 21: Per ASME V Article 7, the white-light intensity for visible particle MT is:

  • A. At least 100 fc (1076 lx) at surface
  • B. At least 50 fc
  • C. At least 1000 μW/cm² UV
  • D. No requirement

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-777.1 requires at least 100 footcandles (1076 lux) for visible (dry or wet non-fluorescent) inspection, measured at the part surface. UV-A requirements apply only to fluorescent inspection.

Question 22: The Curie temperature of carbon steel (above which it loses magnetic properties) is approximately:

  • A. 100°C
  • B. 770°C
  • C. 1500°C
  • D. 50°C

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Curie point of iron and carbon steel is approximately 770°C. Above this, the material becomes paramagnetic and cannot be magnetized for MT. This is why hot welds (just out of the arc) cannot be MT-tested directly.

Question 23: A QQI (quantitative quality indicator) shim is used to:

  • A. Replace the pie gauge
  • B. Verify field direction and adequacy on the part itself
  • C. Calibrate amperage
  • D. Test particle concentration

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: QQI shims (thin flexible steel shims with EDM-machined crosses) are placed directly on the part. They verify both field strength and direction in the area of interest, which is more representative than a pie gauge placed nearby.

Question 24: A typical MT Level II training duration per SNT-TC-1A is:

  • A. 8 hours total
  • B. 12 hours Level I + 8 hours Level II = 20 hours total
  • C. 40 hours
  • D. 80 hours

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 12 hours formal training for MT Level I and 8 hours additional for Level II, totaling 20 hours. Many employers exceed these minimums.

Question 25: In the residual method, the application of particles should be:

  • A. While the current is on
  • B. After the magnetizing current has been removed
  • C. Before any magnetization
  • D. Only in a coil

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The residual method depends on the material retaining magnetism after the current is removed. Particles are applied AFTER the current is shut off, relying on the remaining residual field to develop indications.

Question 26: Prods are used to magnetize:

  • A. Castings and weldments by direct current passage
  • B. Only thin sheets
  • C. Only fluorescent applications
  • D. Tubes only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Prods are pointed contact electrodes pressed onto the part to pass current locally for a circular field around each prod tip. Common on castings and heavy weldments. Prod spacing typically 75–200 mm; amperage 100 A/inch (4 A/mm) of prod spacing.

Question 27: Burning of the part by prod contact is mitigated by:

  • A. Sharper prods
  • B. Clean copper tips, firm contact, and breaking contact only after current is off
  • C. Higher amperage
  • D. Using AC only

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Arc burns from prods can cause weld defects in critical components. Prevention: clean tips, firm pressure before current-on, current off before lift-off, and avoid prod use on finished machined surfaces.

Question 28: For a multidirectional MT setup, current vectors must be:

  • A. Perpendicular and applied alternately fast enough that particles see both directions
  • B. Always parallel
  • C. DC only
  • D. Not allowed by ASME

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Multidirectional magnetization applies two or three magnetization currents in rapid succession (within seconds) so that particles see effective fields in multiple directions, eliminating the need for two separate shots.

Question 29: ISO 9934-2 covers:

  • A. Magnetic particle products (detection media)
  • B. General principles
  • C. Equipment
  • D. Acceptance criteria

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9934 is structured: Part 1 General principles, Part 2 Detection media (particles), Part 3 Equipment. Acceptance criteria are typically in the product code (ISO 23278 for welds, etc.).

Question 30: A Level II inspector finding a borderline (3 mm) linear indication on a Class 1 weld should:

  • A. Reject immediately
  • B. Re-clean and re-inspect; if confirmed, evaluate against the applicable acceptance code; consult Level III if ambiguous
  • C. Ignore
  • D. Re-magnetize with higher current

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Best practice: clean the surface (to eliminate false indications), re-magnetize, re-inspect. If the indication is confirmed, compare to the applicable acceptance criteria (e.g., ASME VIII Div 1 Appendix 6, AWS D1.1, API). Consult Level III for ambiguous calls.

Study Tips for MT Level II

  • Understand the physics: Flux leakage, hysteresis, skin effect, Curie point. Many exam questions test underlying physics not just procedure.
  • Practice formulas: NI = 45,000/(L/D), prod amperage 4 A/mm of spacing, central conductor 12 A/mm of bore diameter. Know when each formula applies.
  • Indication identification: Study reference photographs of cracks vs. magnetic writing vs. surface roughness vs. fillets.
  • Code knowledge: Memorize ASME V Article 7 key tables (lifting power, dwell, concentration) and the applicable acceptance criteria of your industry code.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Magnetic Particle Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 7
  • ASTM E709 (Standard Guide), ASTM E1444 (Standard Practice for Wet Fluorescent)
  • ISO 9934 Parts 1, 2, 3
  • Atlantis NDT MT Level II training course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can MT be used on stainless steel?

A: Only on ferritic and martensitic stainless steels (400 series) that are ferromagnetic. Austenitic stainless (300 series, 304/316) is non-magnetic and cannot be tested by MT — use PT instead.

Q: What is the minimum surface preparation for MT?

A: Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of scale, paint, oil, grease, or loose particles. Maximum paint thickness allowed (when MT through paint is permitted) is typically 0.05 mm verified by a known-flaw shim test.

Q: Is MT faster than PT for production parts?

A: Yes, MT is significantly faster on ferromagnetic parts. A yoke shot takes seconds vs. 10 to 60 minutes for full PT sequence. See our MT vs PT comparison.

Q: Can MT detect cracks under paint or plating?

A: Up to about 0.05 mm coating thickness, MT can detect cracks if calibrated against a known shim flaw. Thicker coatings reduce sensitivity significantly. Always remove coatings for critical inspections.

Q: What is the difference between dry powder and wet method?

A: Dry powder is best for hot surfaces (up to 320°C with high-temperature particles) and rough surfaces (castings, weldments). Wet method gives higher sensitivity for fine cracks on smoother surfaces and is the standard for fluorescent inspection.

Q: How often must yokes be tested for lifting power?

A: ASME V requires lifting power verification at least once per day of use, or whenever the yoke is suspected of being damaged. AC yokes 10 lb, DC yokes 40 lb at max pole spacing.

Q: Is MT acceptable instead of PT for surface inspection per ASME?

A: ASME generally allows MT or PT for surface examination when the material is ferromagnetic. For non-ferromagnetic materials only PT is allowed. Always check the construction code (e.g., ASME VIII, B31.1, B31.3) for specific requirements.

Q: How long is MT certification valid?

A: Same as other methods: 5 years under SNT-TC-1A with annual eye exam, 5 years under PCN with renewal exam at 10 years, 5 years under ACCP. See our ASNT vs PCN comparison.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT train MT Level II students?

A: Our 24-hour MT Level II program covers all magnetization techniques (yoke, prod, coil, central conductor, head shot, multidirectional), both visible and fluorescent inspection, ASME V Article 7 and acceptance to ASME, AWS D1.1, API, and ISO 23278. Includes practical with real welds. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 to enroll.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: PT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 ASME V Article 6 MCQs
snippet: Free 2026 PT Level II practice exam: 30 multiple-choice questions, full explanations, ASME V Art. 6, ASTM E165 and ISO 3452 references, FAQ and study plan.
content:
This 2026 question bank for Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) Level II certification mirrors the ASNT general (40 closed-book), specific (20 open-book), and practical examination. Questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 6, ASTM E165 (Standard Practice for Liquid Penetrant Examination), and ISO 3452 Parts 1 to 6.

PT Level II Exam Format Overview

  • General: 40 closed-book questions on physics, materials, and procedure principles. 70% to pass.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on employer's procedure and applicable code.
  • Practical: Demonstration on at least one item using the candidate's chosen technique (Type I or II, Method A/B/C/D).
  • Composite: 80% average.

PT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: PT detects flaws that are:

  • A. Subsurface only
  • B. Open to the surface only
  • C. Any internal flaw
  • D. Only in welds

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Liquid penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are open to the surface of the test material. Subsurface flaws and surface flaws filled with foreign matter (paint, oxide) cannot be detected without proper surface preparation.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 6 and ISO 3452-1, Type I penetrant is:

  • A. Visible (color contrast)
  • B. Fluorescent
  • C. Post-emulsified
  • D. Solvent-removable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO/ASME classification: Type I = Fluorescent, Type II = Visible (color contrast, typically red). Methods are then A (water-washable), B (post-emulsifiable lipophilic), C (solvent-removable), D (post-emulsifiable hydrophilic).

Question 3: The action that draws penetrant into a flaw is:

  • A. Pressure
  • B. Capillary action
  • C. Gravity
  • D. Magnetism

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Capillary action results from the balance of surface tension and adhesive forces between liquid and solid. Penetrants are formulated with low surface tension and good wetting properties to maximize capillary draw-in.

Question 4: Per ASME V T-672, the minimum dwell time for penetrant is:

  • A. Always 30 minutes
  • B. Per manufacturer instructions, typically 5 to 60 minutes
  • C. 2 minutes
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-672 requires the penetrant dwell (penetration time) per the manufacturer's instructions, with typical industry minimums of 5 to 10 minutes for cracks in metals and longer (30+ minutes) for tight fatigue cracks or porous ceramics.

Question 5: Method A (water-washable) penetrant contains:

  • A. Built-in emulsifier so it washes off with water spray
  • B. Oil only
  • C. Solvent only
  • D. No emulsifier

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Method A penetrants contain a self-emulsifier so they can be removed by direct water spray. They are faster than post-emulsified methods but tend to over-wash and lose sensitivity if rinse is not controlled.

Question 6: Method C (solvent-removable) penetrant excess is removed by:

  • A. Water rinse
  • B. Wiping with dry cloth, then clean with lightly dampened solvent cloth
  • C. Air blast only
  • D. No removal needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-673 (Method C): wipe excess with a dry cloth, then a clean cloth lightly dampened with solvent. NEVER spray solvent directly on the part — this washes penetrant out of the flaw.

Question 7: Developer types include:

  • A. Form a (dry), Form b (water-soluble), Form c (water-suspendible), Form d (non-aqueous wet)
  • B. Only dry
  • C. Only wet
  • D. No types

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 3452-1 / ASME V developer forms: Form a = dry powder, Form b = water-soluble, Form c = water-suspendible, Form d = non-aqueous wet (solvent suspension, typically used for high-sensitivity Type I-D combinations).

Question 8: Fluorescent PT must be inspected under:

  • A. UV-A 320 to 400 nm at minimum 1000 μW/cm²
  • B. White light only
  • C. Red light
  • D. No special light

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-676 requires UV-A light intensity of at least 1000 μW/cm² at the part surface for fluorescent PT, with ambient white light at or below 20 lux (2 ftc). Operator must dark-adapt for at least 1 minute before evaluation.

Question 9: For visible (Type II) PT, white-light intensity must be:

  • A. At least 100 fc (1076 lux)
  • B. At least 50 fc
  • C. At least 10 fc
  • D. No requirement

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-676 requires minimum 100 footcandles (1076 lux) of white light at the part surface for visible inspection. Most workshop areas already meet this; outdoor work in good daylight greatly exceeds it.

Question 10: A row of bleed-out dots aligned in a line is most likely:

  • A. A crack
  • B. Porosity
  • C. A linear indication that may indicate a tight crack with intermittent surface opening
  • D. Lack of fusion

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: A row of dots can be either porosity (round) or a tight intermittent crack. Per ASME V/VIII Appendix 8, any aligned indications separated by less than 1.6 mm are evaluated as continuous and treated as a linear indication.

Question 11: Per ASTM E165, the standard surface temperature range for PT is:

  • A. Below freezing only
  • B. 10 to 52°C standard, with qualification outside this range
  • C. Only above 25°C
  • D. Only above 50°C

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Standard penetrants are formulated for 10 to 52°C (50 to 125°F). Use outside this range requires qualification per ASTM E165 Annex (using a reference comparator). Low-temperature penetrants extend the range down to about −5°C.

Question 12: The penetrant must be removed completely from the surface before:

  • A. Penetrant application
  • B. Developer application
  • C. Pre-cleaning
  • D. No removal needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: After dwell, excess surface penetrant must be removed (rinse or wipe) so the developer can pull only the penetrant that was drawn into discontinuities. Over-removal washes out flaw indications; under-removal causes high background that masks indications.

Question 13: Pre-cleaning purposes include:

  • A. Remove dirt, oil, paint, scale; open flaw entrances; ensure surface compatibility
  • B. Decoration
  • C. Marking the part
  • D. Heat treatment

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Pre-cleaning removes contaminants that could block flaw entrances or react with the penetrant. Methods include solvent wipe (most common), alkaline cleaning, vapor degreasing. Mechanical cleaning (grit blast) is avoided because it can close flaw openings.

Question 14: A typical Level 2 sensitivity Type I-A penetrant detects cracks as small as:

  • A. 100 μm
  • B. 10 to 20 μm
  • C. 1 mm
  • D. Not measurable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Modern fluorescent Type I-A penetrants achieve Level 3 high sensitivity, detecting cracks 5 to 10 μm wide. Solvent-removable Level 2 typically detects 10 to 20 μm. Sensitivity is qualified by reference panels per ISO 3452-2.

Question 15: Per ISO 3452-3, reference test panels are:

  • A. Aluminum with thermal cracks of known width
  • B. Painted plywood
  • C. Magnetized steel
  • D. No reference panels exist

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 3452-3 specifies aluminum reference blocks with controlled crack widths produced by quenching. Type 2 panels have five panels with cracks of progressively smaller size, used to qualify penetrant system sensitivity.

Question 16: A relevant indication on a forging is one that:

  • A. Is more than 1.6 mm in any dimension and is from an actual discontinuity
  • B. Has any size
  • C. Only fluorescent indications
  • D. Only linear indications

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V/VIII Appendix 8 generally considers any indication with major dimension greater than 1.6 mm as relevant. Non-relevant indications include those from surface roughness, fillets, or part configuration.

Question 17: After developer application, the part should be evaluated:

  • A. Immediately
  • B. After 10 to 60 minutes per manufacturer
  • C. After 24 hours
  • D. Without developer

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-674 specifies developer dwell of 10 minutes minimum, with most procedures using 15 to 30 minutes. After dwell, bleed-out indications reach their maximum visibility before fading.

Question 18: Re-testing the same part with PT requires:

  • A. Just re-applying penetrant
  • B. Thorough cleaning to remove all previous penetrant from flaws
  • C. Heating only
  • D. Not allowed by code

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Re-test requires removing all residual penetrant from prior application, typically by vapor degrease, ultrasonic cleaning, or thorough solvent wash. Residual penetrant in flaws gives muted, unreliable indications on re-test.

Question 19: Per ASME V Article 6, typical acceptance criteria for class 1 weld surfaces are:

  • A. No relevant linear indications greater than 1.6 mm
  • B. No relevant linear indications; rounded indications limited per construction code
  • C. All indications allowed
  • D. Determined by Level II

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Typical ASME VIII Div 1 Appendix 8 acceptance: no relevant linear indications (3 times width); rounded indications limited (e.g., at or below 5 mm acceptable per spacing rules). Exact criteria vary by class.

Question 20: Penetrant testing on titanium and high-nickel alloys requires:

  • A. Low halogen and low sulfur content penetrants
  • B. Standard penetrants
  • C. No special considerations
  • D. Magnetic penetrant

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Halogens (chlorine, fluorine) and sulfur can cause stress corrosion cracking in nickel alloys and titanium at elevated service temperature. Penetrants for these materials are certified low-halogen and low-sulfur (less than 1% by weight typically).

Question 21: A flat indication on a casting that follows a grain or shrinkage pattern is most likely:

  • A. Crack
  • B. Porosity
  • C. Shrinkage or non-metallic inclusion stringer
  • D. Lack of fusion

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Casting defects include shrinkage cavities, gas porosity (round), cold shuts (smooth linear), and inclusion stringers (irregular linear). PT can detect all surface-breaking versions but cannot distinguish them without metallurgical knowledge.

Question 22: An indication that bleeds out and grows during developer dwell suggests:

  • A. A small flaw
  • B. A large flaw with substantial penetrant volume
  • C. Surface roughness
  • D. Developer error

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Indications that bleed out and grow during developer dwell indicate larger volume cavities or wider/deeper cracks. Tight, small flaws produce small static dots; large or deep flaws bleed broadly.

Question 23: PT cannot be used effectively on:

  • A. Porous materials (unfired ceramics, sintered metals)
  • B. Smooth steel
  • C. Aluminum
  • D. Stainless steel

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Highly porous materials absorb penetrant into the bulk, producing high background that masks real surface flaws. PT is also problematic on parts with surface coatings, oil contamination, or extreme roughness.

Question 24: Per SNT-TC-1A, the recommended training for PT Level II totals:

  • A. 12 hours (4 hours Level I + 8 hours Level II)
  • B. 40 hours
  • C. 80 hours
  • D. 160 hours

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 4 hours formal training at PT Level I and 8 hours additional at Level II, total 12 hours. Method-specific experience hours are also required (typically 70 hours Level I + 140 hours Level II).

Question 25: PT is sometimes preferred over MT because:

  • A. Higher sensitivity to subsurface flaws
  • B. Works on all materials (ferrous and non-ferrous)
  • C. Lower cost
  • D. Faster than MT on castings

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: PT works on virtually all non-porous materials — stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, ceramics, polymers. MT is restricted to ferromagnetic materials. See our MT vs PT comparison.

Question 26: A reference panel comparator block (TAM panel) is used to:

  • A. Demonstrate procedure suitability
  • B. Verify penetrant system sensitivity each work day
  • C. Calibrate the lamp
  • D. Test surface roughness

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The TAM/CRC panel has controlled cracks of known size. Per ASME V and ISO 3452, verification of system performance on the comparator is required at intervals (e.g., daily, before re-use, or whenever consumables change).

Question 27: Excessive developer thickness:

  • A. Improves sensitivity
  • B. Masks fine indications
  • C. Has no effect
  • D. Required by code

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Developer must form a thin, uniform white coating. Excessive developer (especially aqueous) covers small bleed-out indications and reduces visibility of fine cracks. Apply developer in short bursts to a dry surface.

Question 28: Maximum hold time after pre-cleaning before applying penetrant should be:

  • A. Per procedure, but typically minimized to prevent re-contamination and oxidation
  • B. No limit
  • C. 24 hours
  • D. Always 1 hour

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Industry good practice: apply penetrant as soon as the part is dry after pre-cleaning. Long delays risk dust, fingerprints, or oxidation re-contaminating the surface and blocking flaw entrances.

Question 29: A Level II inspector witnesses an indication that does not bleed back after a developer wipe-test. The indication is likely:

  • A. Real
  • B. Non-relevant (surface contamination or pre-existing dye)
  • C. Subsurface
  • D. Always rejectable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The wipe-and-redevelop test: gently wipe the indication; if it reappears as developer pulls more penetrant, it is real. If it does not, it was likely surface contamination or pre-existing dye from another source.

Question 30: Per ASTM E165 and ISO 3452, periodic system contamination tests include:

  • A. Water content for water-based, contamination by oil/grease/other penetrant type
  • B. Color only
  • C. Viscosity only
  • D. No testing

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Periodic system contamination tests: water content (water-based emulsifiers), fluorescence brightness (Type I), color (Type II), removability, and absence of cross-contamination between Type I and Type II materials.

Study Tips for PT Level II

  • Know the classifications: Type I vs II, Methods A/B/C/D, Forms a/b/c/d. Combinations like Type II Method C Form d are very common exam questions.
  • Process steps: Pre-clean, apply penetrant, dwell, remove excess, developer, evaluate, post-clean. Memorize minimum times for each step.
  • Recognize indications: Look at 100+ real PT photographs to distinguish cracks, porosity, fillet bleed-back, and non-relevant indications.
  • Code knowledge: ASME V Article 6, ASTM E165, ISO 3452-1. Tab your code books before the specific exam.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Liquid Penetrant Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 6
  • ASTM E165 (Standard Practice for Liquid Penetrant Examination)
  • ISO 3452 Parts 1 to 6
  • Atlantis NDT PT Level II training course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can PT be performed on hot surfaces?

A: Standard penetrants are limited to about 52°C (125°F). High-temperature penetrants extend operation up to 150 to 175°C with qualification. Above this, the penetrant evaporates from the flaw before developer can pull it out.

Q: Is PT acceptable instead of MT for ferromagnetic steel?

A: Yes, PT can be used on any non-porous material, including carbon steel and ferritic stainless steel. However, MT is usually faster and more sensitive for surface-breaking flaws in ferromagnetic materials. See MT vs PT.

Q: How long after a weld can PT be performed?

A: Allow the weld to cool below the maximum penetrant temperature (52°C standard, 150°C high-temp). Some weld defects develop only after cool-down (delayed hydrogen cracking), so PT 24 to 48 hours after welding is often specified.

Q: What is the difference between water-washable and post-emulsified penetrant?

A: Water-washable has built-in emulsifier; faster process but lower sensitivity due to over-wash risk. Post-emulsified (Methods B/D) applies a separate emulsifier before water rinse, giving better sensitivity but more processing steps.

Q: Can PT detect cracks under paint?

A: No. Paint must be removed in the inspection area. The exception is some thin MT-through-paint applications, which do not apply to PT.

Q: Why do some PT procedures specify a separate dwell time for developer?

A: Developer dwell allows the developer to absorb and amplify the bleed-out from flaws. Minimum 10 minutes per ASME V; typical 15 to 30. Inspect during dwell, not after fading begins.

Q: How are PT consumables certified?

A: PT material families are certified together as a system per ISO 3452-2 (sensitivity classification 1 to 4) and tested on reference panels. Mixing materials from different families is generally not allowed without re-qualification.

Q: How long is PT certification valid?

A: 5 years under SNT-TC-1A with annual eye exam, 5 years under PCN with renewal exam at 10 years. See our ASNT vs PCN article.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT include code books in PT Level II training?

A: Yes — our PT Level II course includes pre-tabbed copies of ASME V Article 6 and ASTM E165. Students also receive practice with TAM reference panels and real production hardware. Enroll here or call +1 (281) 840-8969.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: API 510 Practice Questions 2026: 30 MCQs with Answers & Code References
snippet: 2026 API 510 exam prep: 30 practice MCQs with full explanations, ASME VIII Div 1 and API 510/571/572/580 references, exam tips, study plan and FAQ.
content:
This 2026 practice question bank prepares candidates for the API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector certification exam administered by the American Petroleum Institute (API). The questions below are referenced to the API 510 Body of Knowledge (BOK), with primary code references to API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspection Code (In-service Inspection, Rating, Repair, and Alteration), API RP 572 (Inspection Practices for Pressure Vessels), API RP 576 (Inspection of Pressure-Relieving Devices), API RP 577 (Welding Inspection and Metallurgy), API RP 580 (Risk-Based Inspection), API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 (Fitness-for-Service), and ASME BPVC Sections V, VIII Div 1, and IX.

API 510 Exam Format Overview

The API 510 exam is administered as a computer-based test (CBT) at Prometric centers in two parts:

  • Closed-book: 50 multiple-choice questions in 2 hours and 45 minutes. Covers general knowledge of vessel inspection, basic metallurgy, NDT, welding, corrosion, and code requirements that can be answered without reference materials.
  • Open-book: 60 to 80 multiple-choice questions in 4 hours and 45 minutes. Candidates use the full set of API 510 reference publications (downloaded as searchable PDFs at the test center).
  • Pass mark: 70% (combined or per section depending on cycle).
  • Recertification: Every 3 years (with reduced exam) and 6 years (full exam).

API 510 Practice Questions

Question 1: Per API 510, the maximum interval between external inspections of a pressure vessel is:

  • A. 1 year
  • B. 3 years
  • C. 5 years
  • D. 10 years

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Per API 510 Section 6.4, external inspection intervals shall not exceed 5 years or the required internal/on-stream inspection interval, whichever is less. Insulated vessels follow the same rule with CUI considerations.

Question 2: The maximum internal inspection interval for a pressure vessel is:

  • A. The lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years
  • B. 5 years
  • C. 20 years
  • D. Never required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 510 Section 6.5.1 limits the internal (or on-stream) inspection interval to the lesser of one-half the remaining corrosion life or 10 years. RBI-based intervals can extend this with proper justification under API 580.

Question 3: Long-term corrosion rate is calculated by:

  • A. Initial thickness minus current thickness divided by time since installation
  • B. Current thickness divided by years in service
  • C. Wall loss in the last year
  • D. Not calculated

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Long-term corrosion rate (LTCR) = (t-initial − t-actual) / (years between t-initial and t-actual). Short-term rate (STCR) uses the period between the previous and current inspection. The greater rate is generally used for remaining life calculations.

Question 4: Per API 510, a pressure vessel weld repair requires:

  • A. No special procedure
  • B. Written repair plan approved by the inspector and engineer, qualified WPS, qualified welders, NDT, and post-weld treatment as required
  • C. Only welder qualification
  • D. Only NDT after repair

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: API 510 Section 8 requires a documented repair plan, qualified WPS/PQR per ASME IX, qualified welder/welding operator, applicable NDT, and post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) where required by original construction code or alteration analysis.

Question 5: A vessel’s MAWP is governed by:

  • A. Hydrostatic test pressure
  • B. The weakest component, calculated using current thickness less FCA
  • C. Operator preference
  • D. Nameplate pressure regardless of corrosion

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: MAWP is the maximum pressure at which the weakest component will safely operate, calculated using current measured thickness minus the future corrosion allowance (FCA). MAWP is updated when corrosion or alterations change the rating.

Question 6: Per API 580, RBI (Risk-Based Inspection) uses:

  • A. Probability of failure (PoF) × Consequence of failure (CoF) = Risk
  • B. Only corrosion rate
  • C. Only vessel age
  • D. Random selection

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Risk = PoF × CoF. PoF accounts for damage mechanisms, inspection effectiveness, and remaining life; CoF accounts for safety, environmental, and business impact. The risk matrix drives inspection planning per API 580/581.

Question 7: Pressure relief valve (PRV) inspection per API 510 and API 576 must occur:

  • A. At the same interval as the vessel internal inspection, not to exceed 5 years (clean service) or 10 years for RBI
  • B. Every 20 years
  • C. Never
  • D. Only when leaking

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 510 Section 6.6 and API 576 typically require PRV testing/inspection every 5 years (clean services) or 10 years (RBI-justified). PRVs in severe or fouling service may require more frequent inspection.

Question 8: Per ASME VIII Div 1 Appendix 3, the minimum thickness for a cylindrical shell under internal pressure is:

  • A. t = PR / (SE − 0.6P)
  • B. t = PD / 2S
  • C. t = PR / (SE + 0.4P)
  • D. Determined by test only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME VIII Div 1 UG-27: t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) for circumferential stress (governs thin-walled cylinders). The alternate formula t = PR / (2SE + 0.4P) for longitudinal stress is rarely governing. Joint efficiency E depends on RT.

Question 9: An on-stream inspection differs from internal inspection in that:

  • A. It is performed while the vessel is in service using NDT from outside
  • B. It requires shutdown
  • C. It is illegal
  • D. Only used for tanks

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: On-stream inspection uses external NDT (UT, RT, profile RT, guided wave UT, PEC) to assess vessel condition without entry. Per API 510, on-stream may substitute for internal inspection if the inspector and engineer can determine vessel integrity to the same degree.

Question 10: Per API 510, an authorized pressure vessel inspector must:

  • A. Hold a current API 510 certification and the experience requirements of API 510 Section 4
  • B. Hold ASNT Level III in all methods
  • C. Be a licensed PE
  • D. Be the vessel owner

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Authorized inspectors must hold current API 510 certification with required experience (4-year degree + 1 yr, or 2-year degree + 2 yrs, or HS + 3 yrs, etc.) and operate under a quality system. PE is required only when API 510 specifies engineer involvement.

Question 11: When a vessel has a corrosion rate of 0.1 mm/yr, FCA of 1.6 mm, current thickness of 12 mm, minimum required thickness of 10 mm, the remaining life is:

  • A. 4 years
  • B. 20 years
  • C. 100 years
  • D. 2 years

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Remaining life = (t-actual − t-min) / corrosion rate = (12 − 10) / 0.1 = 20 years (without FCA) or (12 − 10 − 1.6) / 0.1 = 4 years if FCA must be retained. API 510 uses the more conservative number for inspection planning.

Question 12: Per API 510 alteration vs repair definition, an alteration is:

  • A. Any physical change that changes the design conditions, vessel rating, or geometry
  • B. Any weld repair
  • C. Replacement of a gasket
  • D. External painting

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Per API 510, an alteration changes the design conditions (T, P, MAWP), vessel rating, or geometry (e.g., adding a nozzle). A repair restores the vessel to a condition suitable for safe operation without changing the rating. Alterations require engineering review.

Question 13: Hot tapping refers to:

  • A. Welding on equipment in service while contents are flowing
  • B. Cleaning the vessel with steam
  • C. Heat treatment
  • D. Hydrostatic test

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Hot tapping is welding (typically a nozzle) onto a pressurized line or vessel and then drilling through. API RP 2201 governs hot tap procedures including burn-through prevention, hazard analysis, and procedure qualification.

Question 14: Per API 510, weld overlay used as a repair must:

  • A. Be classified as a temporary repair only
  • B. Use a qualified WPS, NDT after welding, and PWHT if required
  • C. Not be permitted
  • D. Use bolted patches

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Weld overlay (build-up) repairs are permitted as permanent repairs under API 510 Section 8, requiring qualified WPS, qualified welders, NDT, and PWHT if mandated by base metal P-number or carbon equivalent rules.

Question 15: A fillet weld patch (lap patch) is:

  • A. A permanent repair
  • B. A temporary repair limited by API 510 Section 8.1.5
  • C. Always prohibited
  • D. A nozzle attachment

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Fillet welded patches are permitted as temporary repairs per API 510 Section 8.1.5 with limits on size, design analysis, NDT, and a defined service period until a permanent repair can be made.

Question 16: Per ASME VIII Div 1 UCS-79, post-weld heat treatment is required when:

  • A. Always
  • B. Based on P-number, thickness, and service per UCS-56 tables
  • C. Only stainless
  • D. Never required

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME VIII Div 1 UCS-56 specifies PWHT requirements based on material P-number and nominal thickness. Common rule: P-No. 1 carbon steel typically needs PWHT above 19 mm (3/4 in) thickness; lower-alloy steels at lesser thickness.

Question 17: API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 Level 1 assessment is for:

  • A. Conservative screening calculations using look-up tables and simple formulas
  • B. Finite element analysis only
  • C. Material replacement
  • D. Never used

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 579 organizes Fitness-for-Service assessments in three levels: Level 1 (conservative tables/formulas), Level 2 (more detailed calculations with material properties), Level 3 (advanced FEA / probabilistic). The inspector typically performs Level 1; engineers Level 2 and 3.

Question 18: Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in stainless steel is typically caused by:

  • A. Chloride ion exposure at elevated temperature
  • B. Carbon dioxide
  • C. Sulfur
  • D. Inert gas

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Chloride stress corrosion cracking (Cl-SCC) of austenitic stainless steel (304/316) occurs typically above 60°C in chloride-bearing solutions. Insulation chlorides leaching with water is a common source. API RP 581 lists SCC mechanisms.

Question 19: Per API RP 577, hydrogen damage in welds includes:

  • A. Hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC), sulfide stress cracking (SSC), HTHA
  • B. Only fatigue
  • C. Only creep
  • D. Only erosion

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API RP 577 and API 571 cover hydrogen damage: HIC (blistering and crack networks in wet H2S), SSC (sulfide stress cracking in hard welds and HAZ), HSC (hydrogen stress cracking), and HTHA (high-temperature hydrogen attack — Nelson curves).

Question 20: Per API 510, a vessel that has had a major repair must be:

  • A. Hydro-tested at 1.3 × MAWP or otherwise verified
  • B. Hydrotested at MAWP only
  • C. Vented
  • D. Replaced

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Hydrostatic test pressure after major repair/alteration is typically 1.3 × MAWP × (Sa/Sd) per ASME VIII Div 1 UG-99, where Sa/Sd is the stress ratio at test/design temperatures. Alternative NDT and engineering analysis may substitute.

Question 21: The most common NDT method for verifying vessel wall thickness from outside is:

  • A. Ultrasonic thickness gauging (UT)
  • B. Liquid penetrant
  • C. Magnetic particle
  • D. Visual only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: UT thickness is the workhorse NDT for vessel wall measurement. Spot UT at TML (thickness measurement locations) and scanning UT (corrosion mapping) are both used. Profile RT, PAUT corrosion mapping, and PEC for through-insulation are also acceptable.

Question 22: A vessel’s thickness measurement location (TML) is selected based on:

  • A. Damage mechanism, geometry (heads, shells, nozzles), and historical thinning
  • B. Random
  • C. Only the manway
  • D. Anywhere convenient

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: TMLs are placed at expected damage locations based on the dominant damage mechanism, geometry (shells, heads, knuckle radii, nozzles, manways), inlet/outlet, level lines, and historical thinning. API RP 572 provides guidance on TML selection.

Question 23: Per API 510, the inspector’s authority includes:

  • A. Approving repair plans, accepting NDT results, and verifying conformance to code
  • B. Designing new vessels
  • C. Setting operating pressure
  • D. Hiring welders without qualification

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The authorized inspector is responsible for verifying inspection, repair, and alteration activities meet API 510 and applicable code. Design and reratings involve the engineer (PE or qualified equivalent).

Question 24: Joint efficiency E in ASME VIII Div 1 depends on:

  • A. Type of joint and extent of radiography
  • B. Only the welder
  • C. Pressure
  • D. Material density

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME VIII Div 1 Table UW-12 gives joint efficiencies based on joint type (Type 1 butt weld, Type 2 single-V, etc.) and radiography category (Full, Spot, None). Typical values: E=1.0 for Type 1 with full RT; E=0.85 with spot; E=0.70 with no RT.

Question 25: A nameplate on a pressure vessel must include:

  • A. Manufacturer, MAWP, design temperature, year built, serial number, code stamp
  • B. Only serial number
  • C. Only manufacturer
  • D. No requirement

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME VIII Div 1 UG-119 requires the nameplate to include manufacturer, MAWP, design temperature, MDMT, year of construction, manufacturer’s serial number, and the appropriate ASME code stamp (U, UM, etc.).

Question 26: Per API 571, sulfidation corrosion typically occurs:

  • A. At elevated temperatures in sulfur-containing hydrocarbon streams (e.g., crude unit, FCC)
  • B. At ambient temperature
  • C. Only in stainless
  • D. Only with water

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Sulfidation is high-temperature corrosion of iron-based alloys by sulfur compounds, typically above 260°C. The McConomy curves and modified McConomy provide thinning rate vs. temperature, sulfur content, and material. Common in crude distillation and FCC units.

Question 27: A pressure vessel under cyclic service may be subject to:

  • A. Fatigue damage
  • B. Only creep
  • C. No damage
  • D. Only corrosion

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Pressure cycles, thermal cycles, and vibration can initiate and propagate fatigue cracks, particularly at stress concentrations (nozzles, weld toes). API RP 579-1 Part 14 provides fatigue assessment procedures.

Question 28: The minimum design metal temperature (MDMT) of a vessel is:

  • A. The lowest metal temperature at which the vessel can safely contain pressure
  • B. Ambient temperature
  • C. Operating temperature
  • D. Hydrotest temperature

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: MDMT is the lowest expected metal temperature considering operation, startup, shutdown, and upsets. Material toughness must be sufficient at MDMT per UCS-66 charts. Brittle fracture risk increases as temperature drops below MDMT.

Question 29: Per API 510, a temporary repair must be replaced with a permanent repair:

  • A. By the next scheduled turnaround, or as specified in the repair plan
  • B. Never — temporary repairs are permanent
  • C. Within 1 hour
  • D. Only if leaking

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Temporary repairs are limited in scope and time. API 510 Section 8.1.5 requires them to be replaced with a permanent repair by the next scheduled turnaround or as documented in the engineering and inspector-approved repair plan.

Question 30: Welder qualification per ASME IX requires:

  • A. Successful welder performance qualification (WPQ) test record
  • B. Only a written test
  • C. Visual inspection only
  • D. No qualification needed

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME IX requires a welder performance qualification (WPQ) including production of a test coupon and acceptable NDT (RT or bend testing). The WPQ has essential variables that, if changed, may require requalification. Welders must maintain continuity (typically welding within the 6 months prior).

Study Tips for API 510

  • Master the BOK: Download the API 510 Body of Knowledge from the API Individual Certification Programs (ICP) page. Every question on the exam maps to a BOK item.
  • Use the right edition: The exam references specific editions of API 510, RP 572, RP 576, RP 577, RP 580, ASME V, VIII Div 1, IX, and API 571. Check the API ICP body of knowledge document for the current exam cycle.
  • Tab your books: Open-book is open-book in name only — if you cannot find the answer in 90 seconds, you will not finish. Tab key sections in every reference: API 510 Sections 5-8, ASME VIII UG-22 to UG-37 and UG-99, ASME IX QW-200 to QW-300.
  • Practice calculations: MAWP from t-min, remaining life, corrosion rates, joint efficiency, hydrotest pressure. Plan on 200+ calculation problems before the exam.
  • Read API 571: Damage mechanisms appear on every exam. Memorize the 30+ mechanisms in API 571 with morphology and typical NDT.

Recommended Study Materials

  • API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspection Code (current edition)
  • API RP 572 Inspection Practices for Pressure Vessels
  • API RP 576 Inspection of Pressure-Relieving Devices
  • API RP 577 Welding Inspection and Metallurgy
  • API RP 580 Risk-Based Inspection
  • API 571 Damage Mechanisms Affecting Fixed Equipment
  • ASME BPVC Sections V, VIII Div 1, and IX
  • Atlantis NDT API 510 exam preparation course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What experience do I need to sit the API 510 exam?

A: API 510 requires combinations like: BS in engineering plus 1 year, or 2-year engineering degree plus 2 years, or high school plus 3 years of NDT/inspection-related experience. Verify the current API ICP requirements.

Q: How long does API 510 certification last?

A: 3 years to a reduced recertification exam (open-book only), then 6 years for the full recertification exam. Continuous practice as an inspector is also required.

Q: Are API 510 and ASNT certifications the same?

A: No. API 510 certifies you as a vessel inspector (a code-driven role); ASNT certifies you in NDT methods (UT, RT, MT, PT, etc.). Many inspectors hold both. See our ASNT vs PCN comparison for NDT body certifications and our ASNT certification page for ASNT routes.

Q: Is API 510 recognized internationally?

A: Yes. API 510 is widely recognized globally, especially in oil & gas. In Europe, PED-driven Notified Body assessments may also apply. In Saudi Aramco SAES requirements explicitly reference API 510 inspectors.

Q: What is the difference between API 510 and API 570?

A: API 510 covers pressure vessels; API 570 covers in-service piping. See our API 510 vs API 570 comparison.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer API 510 review courses?

A: No. Atlantis NDT does not run API 510 exam-preparation courses. Our API 510 pressure vessel inspection support is ASNT Level III technical work on vessel programmes — RBI, FFS and data review — not exam coaching.

Q: Can I take the API 510 exam online?

A: API exams are administered through Prometric test centers worldwide (computer-based test). Online proctoring options have been piloted; verify the latest with API ICP at the time of registration.

Q: What is the API 510 exam pass rate?

A: Industry averages range from 50 to 65% first attempt. Candidates from structured prep courses typically report 80%+ first try.

Q: How much does an API 510 certified inspector earn?

A: In the US, $90,000 to $140,000/year base, plus offshore/turnaround premiums. In the Middle East, $7,000 to a modest cost/month tax-free for experienced inspectors. Salary scales with API 570 + 653 stacking.

Q: Does the API 510 exam include ASME IX?

A: Yes — welding procedure and welder performance qualification under ASME IX is a major open-book topic. Tab QW-200 (WPS/PQR), QW-300 (welder performance), and QW-400 (essential variables tables).

About Atlantis NDT

We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

title: API 570 Practice Questions 2026: 30 Piping Inspector MCQs & Answers
snippet: 2026 API 570 piping inspector practice exam: 30 multiple-choice questions, code references (ASME B31.3, API 570/571/574/577), study tips and FAQ.
content:
This 2026 practice exam bank prepares candidates for the API 570 Piping Inspector certification. The questions reflect the API 570 Body of Knowledge (BOK) and reference API 570 Piping Inspection Code (In-service Inspection, Rating, Repair, and Alteration), API RP 574 (Inspection Practices for Piping System Components), API RP 577 (Welding Inspection and Metallurgy), API RP 578 (Material Verification Program), API RP 580 (Risk-Based Inspection), API 571 (Damage Mechanisms), ASME B31.3 (Process Piping), and ASME B16.5, BPVC V and IX.

API 570 Exam Format Overview

  • Closed-book: ~50 questions on basic principles, NDT, welding, corrosion, code requirements that should be remembered.
  • Open-book: ~80 questions referencing the full API 570 publications package.
  • Total time: 7.5 hours (closed + open).
  • Pass mark: 70%.
  • Recertification: 3-year reduced and 6-year full cycle.

API 570 Practice Questions

Question 1: Per API 570, the maximum interval for visual external inspection of Class 1 piping is:

  • A. 5 years
  • B. 10 years
  • C. 1 year
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 Table 6.1 gives Class 1 piping maximum external inspection interval of 5 years (or 1/2 remaining life). Class 2 is 5 years, Class 3 is 10 years, Class 4 is optional. Class definitions depend on consequence (toxic/flammable/etc.).

Question 2: Class 1 piping per API 570 is:

  • A. Highest consequence (e.g., flammable services that vaporize, anhydrous HF, H2S above 3%)
  • B. Lowest consequence
  • C. Tanks
  • D. Vessels only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 classifies piping by consequence: Class 1 highest (flashing flammables, HF, H2S above 3%, anhydrous HCl), Class 2 (most flammables, on-site steam, acids/caustics), Class 3 (flammables that do not vaporize, non-toxic), Class 4 (water, plant air).

Question 3: Per ASME B31.3, the minimum required thickness of straight pipe under internal pressure is:

  • A. t = PD / (2(SE + PY))
  • B. t = PR / 2S
  • C. t = D / 10
  • D. Determined experimentally

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME B31.3 Eq. 3a: t = PD / (2(SE + PY)) where P = pressure, D = OD, S = allowable stress, E = quality factor, Y = coefficient from Table 304.1.1. Add mill tolerance (typically 12.5%) and corrosion allowance for required nominal thickness.

Question 4: A thickness measurement location (TML) for piping is typically:

  • A. At elbows, tees, reducers, and high-velocity/turbulent zones where erosion/corrosion is expected
  • B. Anywhere convenient
  • C. Only on straight runs
  • D. Never on fittings

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Per API 570 and RP 574, TMLs concentrate at locations of expected damage: elbows (extrados & intrados), tees, reducers, dead legs, injection points, mixing points, vents/drains, and at known damage mechanism locations.

Question 5: Injection points per API 570 require:

  • A. Special inspection circuits with dedicated TMLs upstream, downstream, and at the injection point
  • B. No special inspection
  • C. Removal at every turnaround
  • D. Visual only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Injection points (e.g., corrosion inhibitor, water, antifoulant injection) experience accelerated localized corrosion downstream. API 570 Section 6.2.2.5 requires dedicated inspection circuits with TMLs from 12 in upstream to 25 ft (or 3 pipe diameters) downstream.

Question 6: Corrosion under insulation (CUI) is most likely on piping in service between:

  • A. −12 to 175°C (10 to 350°F), with peak risk near dew point
  • B. Above 500°C only
  • C. Cryogenic only
  • D. Not real

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: CUI is most aggressive in the temperature range where moisture can be present beneath the insulation: −12 to 175°C (carbon steel). API 570 and API RP 583 give CUI risk-based inspection guidance. Stainless can suffer chloride SCC in this same range.

Question 7: Dead legs in piping are concerning because:

  • A. Stagnant fluid concentrates corrosion attack
  • B. They reduce pressure drop
  • C. They are required by code
  • D. They prevent corrosion

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Dead legs (block valves, vent lines, dead-end caps) accumulate stagnant fluid, water, sediment, or vapor that drive localized corrosion, MIC, and freeze damage. API 570 requires identification and special inspection of dead legs.

Question 8: Per API 570, online (on-stream) inspection may be used in lieu of internal inspection when:

  • A. External NDT can determine the integrity of the piping with equivalent confidence
  • B. The owner waives the inspection
  • C. Pressure is below 50 psi
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Most piping cannot be entered for internal inspection. API 570 requires external NDT (UT, RT, guided wave UT, PEC, PAUT corrosion mapping) at intervals that establish integrity. Internal inspection at openings is performed where access allows.

Question 9: A piping system suffering high temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA) per API 941 (Nelson curves) typically has:

  • A. Service above hydrogen partial pressure / temperature limits for the alloy
  • B. Service in air only
  • C. Cold service
  • D. Vacuum service

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: HTHA per API 941 occurs in carbon and low-alloy steels exposed to hydrogen partial pressure and elevated temperature combinations that exceed Nelson curve limits. AUBT (Advanced Ultrasonic Backscatter Technique), TOFD, and metallographic replication are used to detect HTHA.

Question 10: Per API RP 578, a material verification program (PMI) is required to:

  • A. Verify alloy components are the specified material grade
  • B. Measure thickness
  • C. Detect cracks
  • D. Test welds only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Positive Material Identification (PMI) uses portable XRF or OES to verify alloy composition during construction, repair, and in-service. API RP 578 prevents catastrophic failures from material mix-ups (e.g., carbon steel instead of 5Cr-1/2Mo in a hot piping system).

Question 11: Per API 570, the maximum thickness measurement interval for Class 1 piping is:

  • A. 5 years or 1/2 remaining life, whichever is less
  • B. 10 years
  • C. 20 years
  • D. Never required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 Table 6.1 limits Class 1 thickness measurement to 5 years (or 1/2 remaining life). Class 2 also 5 years, Class 3 is 10 years, Class 4 optional. RBI may modify these intervals.

Question 12: An authorized piping inspector per API 570 must:

  • A. Hold current API 570 certification and meet experience requirements
  • B. Hold ASNT Level III
  • C. Be a PE
  • D. Be the owner

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 Section 4 requires the inspector to hold current API 570 certification, experience per the API ICP requirements, and operate under the owner/user’s inspection management system.

Question 13: A repair to in-service piping per API 570 requires:

  • A. Written repair plan approved by inspector and engineer, qualified WPS, qualified welders, NDT, and post-weld treatment as required
  • B. Just the welder’s name
  • C. Only the engineer
  • D. No documentation

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 Section 8 requires documented repair plans, qualified WPS/PQR per ASME IX or B31.3 Chapter V, qualified welders, applicable NDT, and PWHT as required by base metal and service.

Question 14: A bolted clamp on a leaking pipe is:

  • A. A temporary repair allowed under specific API 570 limits
  • B. Always prohibited
  • C. A permanent solution
  • D. Required at every flange

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Bolted clamps and enclosures (e.g., engineered leak repair) are temporary repairs that must be designed, documented, and replaced with a permanent repair by the next planned turnaround per API 570 Section 8.

Question 15: ASME B31.3 sets the allowable stress S based on:

  • A. The lower of UTS/3, YS/1.5, creep, or rupture data at temperature
  • B. Only UTS
  • C. Only YS
  • D. Manufacturer choice

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME B31.3 Table A-1 allowable stress S is the lowest of (UTS at T)/3, (UTS at 38°C)/3, (YS at T)/1.5, (YS at 38°C)/1.5, and creep/rupture rules. Different ratios apply for high-pressure piping (Chapter IX).

Question 16: A flange rating per ASME B16.5 (e.g., Class 150, 300, 600) refers to:

  • A. Pressure-temperature rating tables for various materials
  • B. Outside diameter
  • C. Bolt count
  • D. Manufacturer code

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: B16.5 Class is a pressure rating that varies with material group and temperature. For example, Class 300 carbon steel (Group 1.1) rates 740 psig at 100°F and drops to 290 psig at 850°F. Each class has a full temperature-pressure curve.

Question 17: A test pressure for piping per ASME B31.3 is typically:

  • A. 1.5 × design pressure (hydrostatic) or 1.1 × (pneumatic)
  • B. 1.0 × design
  • C. 5 × design
  • D. No test required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: B31.3 paragraph 345 specifies hydrostatic test at 1.5 × design pressure adjusted for temperature ratio, or pneumatic at 1.1 × design with hazard considerations. Sensitive leak testing is allowed under specific conditions.

Question 18: Per API 571, naphthenic acid corrosion (NAC) typically affects:

  • A. Crude unit vacuum tower and side draws at 220 to 400°C, high TAN crudes
  • B. Sour water piping
  • C. Refrigerated services
  • D. Steam lines

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: NAC affects crude distillation and vacuum unit piping when TAN exceeds 0.5 mg KOH/g, in the 220 to 400°C window, with high velocity/turbulence. 316/317 stainless or 5Cr-1/2Mo with selective upgrade are typical remedies.

Question 19: A pipe support that is missing or damaged may cause:

  • A. Excessive thermal stress, sag, fatigue, and accelerated wear at adjacent supports
  • B. No issue
  • C. Improved flow
  • D. Heat loss only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Inspectors should record damaged or missing pipe supports during external inspection. Loss of support shifts loads to remaining supports, creates fatigue, and may cause excessive stress in nozzles and flanges.

Question 20: Per API 570, soil-to-air interface inspection on buried piping is critical because:

  • A. Accelerated corrosion occurs at the transition due to moisture, coatings damage, and aeration
  • B. Decoration
  • C. Maintenance access only
  • D. Not required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The soil-to-air interface (typically 6 in below grade to 12 in above) experiences accelerated external corrosion. API 570 Section 9.2.1 requires inspection of these zones including coating removal where indicated.

Question 21: A piping system with intermittent service that allows water accumulation may suffer:

  • A. Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC)
  • B. No damage
  • C. Only creep
  • D. Only fatigue

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: MIC by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) and other microbes accelerates pitting and weld metal corrosion. Common in firewater piping, intermittent service lines, and hydrotest water left in pipe. API 571 documents MIC mechanisms and inspection.

Question 22: A guided wave UT (GWUT) survey on piping is best for:

  • A. Screening long lengths of pipe for significant cross-section reductions
  • B. Crack sizing
  • C. Surface flaw detection
  • D. Hardness

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: GWUT sends low-frequency (20 to 100 kHz) torsional/longitudinal waves along the pipe wall. It detects cross-sectional area changes (typically >5%) up to 30 to 50 m on insulated, buried, or elevated pipe. It is a screening tool, not a sizing tool.

Question 23: Pulsed eddy current (PEC) inspection of insulated piping detects:

  • A. Average wall thickness loss through insulation without removal
  • B. Surface cracks
  • C. Painted welds
  • D. Internal liquid

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PEC pulses a magnetic field through insulation/weather jacket and measures the decay to estimate average wall thickness. It is a screening tool for CUI — not absolute thickness. Spot UT after PEC indications is standard practice.

Question 24: A piping circuit per API 570 is:

  • A. A grouping of piping with similar service, material, and damage potential for inspection planning
  • B. Only one pipe
  • C. Tank only
  • D. Vessels

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Piping is grouped into inspection circuits by service, material, expected damage mechanism, and operating conditions. Each circuit has a defined set of TMLs and inspection records. API RP 574 provides circuit definition guidance.

Question 25: Per ASME B31.3, branch reinforcement is required when:

  • A. The header is weakened by the branch opening beyond the limits in para 304.3
  • B. Always
  • C. Only for vacuum
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME B31.3 paragraph 304.3 requires branch reinforcement calculation. If header thickness in excess of pressure-design accounts for the removed material, no extra reinforcement is needed; otherwise, pads, weldolets, or wall thickness must compensate.

Question 26: A flange leak path most commonly occurs at:

  • A. The gasket seating surface due to inadequate bolt torque, gasket damage, or thermal cycling
  • B. The pipe wall
  • C. The nut threads
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Most flange leaks are gasket seating issues. Proper bolt torque (per ASME PCC-1), gasket selection (compatible with service), and avoiding flange face damage are key. Hot-bolting (re-tightening at operating temperature) is sometimes needed.

Question 27: A pipe wall thickness reading of 9.5 mm on a 10.0 mm nominal pipe with 12.5% mill tolerance is:

  • A. Acceptable within mill tolerance (minimum 8.75 mm)
  • B. Unacceptable
  • C. Indicates massive corrosion
  • D. Always rejected

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Mill tolerance on seamless pipe is 12.5% under nominal. A 10 mm nominal pipe could be as thin as 8.75 mm new. 9.5 mm is normal new-pipe variation; corrosion is not implied unless previous baseline was higher.

Question 28: Per API 570 owner/user responsibilities include:

  • A. Establishing the inspection program, classifying piping, supervising the inspector
  • B. Performing the inspection personally
  • C. Designing the piping
  • D. Only welding

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: API 570 places the program responsibility with the owner/user, who classifies piping, sets inspection intervals, employs authorized inspectors and engineers, and maintains records. The inspector verifies code compliance.

Question 29: A piping system below MDMT during a startup may be at risk of:

  • A. Brittle fracture
  • B. Creep
  • C. Sulfidation
  • D. Erosion

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Carbon steel below MDMT (often around −29°C for non-impact-tested A106) loses toughness and may fail brittlely when pressurized. Cold blowdowns and autorefrigeration upsets must be analyzed and limited.

Question 30: NDT methods commonly used by an API 570 inspector include:

  • A. VT, UT thickness, UT shear wave, RT (profile), PT, MT, PAUT, GWUT, PEC, MFL
  • B. Only VT
  • C. Only RT
  • D. Hardness

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: An API 570 inspector commands a broad NDT toolbox: visual, thickness UT, shear wave UT (for cracks), profile RT, PT, MT, PAUT, TOFD, GWUT, PEC, MFL, eddy current array. The inspector selects techniques based on the damage mechanism — not the other way around.

Study Tips for API 570

  • Master ASME B31.3: Especially para 304 (design), Chapter V (fabrication and inspection), and the allowable stress tables in Appendix A. B31.3 is heavily referenced on open-book questions.
  • Know the damage mechanisms: API 571 is essential. Memorize CUI, MIC, NAC, sulfidation, HTHA, chloride SCC, caustic embrittlement, and their typical NDT.
  • Practice TML and remaining life calculations: Long-term and short-term corrosion rates, remaining life with and without FCA, MAWP for a piping circuit.
  • Tab your code books: API 570 sections 5 to 9, ASME B31.3 para 304/Chapter V/Appendix A, ASME IX QW-200 essential variables, API RP 574 inspection methods.
  • Practice 300+ MCQs: Work through several hundred practice questions across all eight reference codes before exam day.

Recommended Study Materials

  • API 570 Piping Inspection Code (current edition)
  • API RP 574 Inspection Practices for Piping System Components
  • API RP 577 Welding Inspection and Metallurgy
  • API RP 578 Material Verification Program
  • API RP 580 Risk-Based Inspection
  • API 571 Damage Mechanisms
  • ASME B31.3 Process Piping
  • ASME BPVC Sections V and IX
  • Atlantis NDT API 570 exam preparation course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the difference between API 570 and API 510?

A: API 570 covers in-service piping inspection; API 510 covers in-service pressure vessels. See our API 510 vs 570 comparison.

Q: Can I take API 570 before API 510?

A: Yes — the API ICP certifications are independent. Many inspectors take API 510 first (more vessel work) but API 570 first is fine.

Q: How long does API 570 certification last?

A: 3 years to the reduced recertification, 6 years to the full exam recertification.

Q: What is API 570 Class 1 piping?

A: The highest consequence category — toxic, flammable that vaporizes on release, HF acid, H2S above 3%. Class 1 has the shortest inspection intervals.

Q: Is hot tapping covered in API 570?

A: API 570 references API RP 2201 for hot tapping procedures. Pre-tap NDT, qualified hot tap WPS, and burn-through prevention are required.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer corporate group API 570 training?

A: No. Atlantis NDT does not run API 570 exam-preparation courses. Our API 570 piping inspection support is ASNT Level III technical work on piping programmes, not exam coaching.

Q: Is API 570 recognized in the Middle East and India?

A: Yes — widely recognized by Aramco, ADNOC, KOC, QatarEnergy, Reliance, Indian Oil, BPCL, and most major refineries.

Q: What is the API 570 exam pass rate?

A: Industry averages 50 to 65% first try. Structured prep typically lifts this to 80%+.

Q: How much does an API 570 inspector earn?

A: US base $90,000 to $135,000/year; Middle East a modest cost to a modest cost/month tax-free. Adding API 510 + 653 stacks significantly (a 510+570+653 inspector commonly earns $150,000+ in the US).

Q: How does API 570 relate to CSWIP 3.1?

A: CSWIP 3.1 is a welding inspection certification commonly used in welding fabrication QC. API 570 is in-service piping inspection. Many inspectors hold both for complete fabrication-to-service coverage.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.
