title: Odoo vs SAP for NDT Companies: Why Enterprise ERP Overkills a 50-Person Inspection Firm
snippet: SAP is built for multinational manufacturers, not a 50-person inspection firm. A direct comparison of implementation cost, timeline, and actual fit.
content:
The Wrong-Sized ERP Problem

Somewhere between a 15-person inspection shop running QuickBooks and email, and a 500-person multinational testing conglomerate, there's a size where the owner or CFO of an NDT company starts hearing "you need real ERP" from every accountant, consultant, and LinkedIn ad in their feed — and "real ERP" very often gets translated, in that conversation, to mean SAP. It's the name every finance professional recognizes, the safe-sounding choice, the one nobody gets blamed for recommending. It is also, for the overwhelming majority of independent and regional NDT inspection firms in the 20-to-100-employee range, a genuine mismatch between the tool and the job — not because SAP is bad software, but because it was designed to solve a different, larger, more structurally complex problem than the one a mid-size inspection company actually has.

This is a direct, practical comparison for owners and operations leaders evaluating Odoo-based platforms against SAP for a 50-person-scale NDT inspection or calibration services business — where the real differences show up, and where each system genuinely fits.

What a 50-Person NDT Firm Actually Needs From an ERP

Strip away the buzzwords and a mid-size inspection company's core operational needs are fairly consistent: job and project management tied to specific clients and assets, technician scheduling that respects current certification levels (ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualification records, method-specific competency), equipment calibration tracking with due-date enforcement, document control for procedures and reports under an ISO 9001 quality system, inventory management for consumables and calibration standards, invoicing tied to completed and approved work, and reasonably standard financial reporting. That's a real, non-trivial list — but it's a bounded one. It doesn't require multi-entity consolidated financials across dozens of legal entities, complex intercompany transfer pricing, deep manufacturing MRP with multi-level bills of materials, or the kind of global trade compliance modules that justify SAP's architecture for a Fortune 500 manufacturer running plants on five continents.

SAP's Design Center of Gravity: Built for a Different Scale of Problem

SAP S/4HANA — and its predecessor ECC before it — was architected for large, complex, often multinational enterprises: deep manufacturing resource planning, multi-currency and multi-entity consolidation, elaborate approval hierarchies, and integration across dozens of business units. That architecture is genuinely valuable if you have that problem. If you don't, you inherit its complexity anyway, because SAP's configuration model, data structures, and implementation methodology are built around the assumption that this complexity exists somewhere in the organization, even when a 50-person inspection company's actual requirements are a fraction of what the platform is designed to handle. The practical result is a system that takes specialized SAP consultants to configure even for simple workflows, a steep learning curve for office staff who need to run day-to-day operations, and an ongoing dependency on expensive, scarce SAP expertise just to make routine changes — a change to an invoice template or an approval workflow that would be a same-day configuration change in a lighter platform can become a multi-week SAP consulting engagement.

Implementation Timelines and Resource Requirements Compared

SAP implementations, even scaled-down mid-market offerings like SAP Business ByDesign, commonly run six months to well over a year for a company implementing core financials, procurement, and operations modules, typically requiring a dedicated internal project team plus external implementation consultants for the duration. Odoo-based implementations for a comparably sized service business — particularly when built on a pre-configured industry template rather than a ground-up build — commonly run weeks to a few months for core modules, because the platform's modular, app-based architecture lets a firm implement project management, calibration tracking, and invoicing without first building out modules the company will never use. For a 50-person firm, the difference between a 3-month and a 10-month implementation isn't just calendar time — it's months of an operations manager's attention diverted from running the business into managing an implementation project sized for a much larger organization.

Total Cost of Ownership Over a Realistic Planning Horizon

Cost comparisons here need to separate two very different pricing philosophies rather than pretend they're the same kind of purchase. SAP's licensing model — whether traditional on-premise ECC-style licensing or S/4HANA Cloud subscriptions — is built around enterprise-scale user counts and module bundles, and independent ERP benchmarking research, including the annual reports published by implementation consultancies like Panorama Consulting, has for years shown average SAP implementations landing well into six and seven figures in total first-year cost once license fees, implementation services, and internal resource time are all counted, with substantial ongoing annual maintenance and support fees after go-live regardless of company size. Odoo's open-core, per-application licensing architecture is structurally different: a company licenses the specific applications it uses rather than an enterprise-wide platform fee, which is a large part of why Odoo-based implementations tend to scale their cost with actual usage rather than with a flat enterprise assumption. Atlantis NDT's Odoo-based ERP platform follows that same philosophy — configured specifically for NDT and inspection workflows, with pricing quoted based on your firm's actual scope rather than a generic enterprise tier. The right way to evaluate this for your firm isn't to compare a published SAP list price against a vague Odoo estimate; it's to request a scoped quote from each vendor against the exact same requirements list and compare like for like.

Customization Philosophy: Configuration vs. Custom Development

SAP's customization model traditionally leans on custom development (historically ABAP code, increasingly extension frameworks in S/4HANA) performed by certified SAP developers — powerful, but slow and expensive to iterate on, and prone to creating a tangle of custom code that complicates future upgrades. Odoo's architecture favors configuration and modular app development in a more accessible technology stack (Python, with a well-documented API), which is a meaningful practical difference for a mid-size firm that doesn't have — and doesn't want to build — an internal SAP development team. When an NDT company's workflow needs a genuinely custom feature, such as a specific ASNT competency-tracking rule or a client-specific report format, the speed and cost of building that customization differs enormously between the two ecosystems, and that difference compounds every time the business needs to adapt the system to a new client requirement or a new service line.

Where SAP Actually Makes Sense (And Why It's Probably Not You)

SAP is the right answer for organizations that genuinely have SAP-scale problems: multinational inspection conglomerates with dozens of legal entities and complex intercompany billing, companies with heavy manufacturing operations requiring deep MRP alongside their service business, or firms already standardized on SAP across a parent company and needing a subsidiary to integrate into that existing landscape. If your firm is a 30-to-100-person independent or regional NDT inspection company without those structural complexities, the honest evaluation question isn't "can SAP do what we need" — it almost certainly can, eventually, at a price — it's "does the complexity SAP requires you to manage actually map to complexity your business has," and for most firms at this scale, the answer is no.

Industry-Specific Functionality Neither Vendor Ships Out of the Box

Neither SAP nor stock Odoo ships with NDT-specific functionality out of the box — technician certification-level enforcement against ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice requirements, method-specific competency tracking, calibration-linked equipment checkout, or inspection report generation tied to job records. Both require configuration or custom development to get there. The practical question is which platform gets you to that industry-specific functionality faster and more affordably. A pre-built, NDT-specific configuration layer on top of a flexible core — which is the approach Atlantis NDT takes with its Odoo-based platform — starts a firm much closer to a finished, industry-fit system than either a stock SAP implementation or a stock Odoo installation, because the NDT-specific workflow logic doesn't have to be designed and built from a blank slate.

A Concrete Scenario: Calibration Due-Date Enforcement in Each System

Abstract platform comparisons are easy to nod along with and hard to actually act on, so walk through one specific, everyday workflow: preventing a technician from being scheduled with an ultrasonic thickness gauge that's a week overdue for calibration. In a well-configured Odoo-based system built for NDT workflows, this is a rules-based check baked into the scheduling and equipment-checkout module — the scheduler tries to assign the gauge to a job, the system checks its calibration due date against today's date, and blocks or flags the assignment automatically, because the underlying data model was built from the start around the idea that equipment, personnel, and jobs are linked records with enforceable rules between them. In a standard SAP implementation, this same requirement usually has to be custom-built as an extension or a workaround inside the plant maintenance or quality management modules — modules designed around manufacturing equipment maintenance schedules, not field-deployed inspection instrument calibration — which means real development time, a certified SAP consultant, and ongoing maintenance of a custom object every time the business logic needs to change. The requirement is identical in both cases. The cost and speed of meeting it are not.

The Hidden Cost of Modules You'll Never Use

One of the least-discussed costs of an oversized ERP platform is the ongoing burden of modules a company licenses, implements, or at minimum navigates around, but never actually uses for its business. SAP's bundled module structure, even in scaled-down mid-market offerings, tends to bring along functionality — advanced production planning, complex procurement workflows, multi-warehouse logistics optimization — that a 50-person inspection firm has no use for but still has to account for in training, in system navigation, and often in licensing cost, because SAP's pricing tiers are rarely granular enough to strip out everything irrelevant to a service-only business. This isn't just wasted spend; it's wasted cognitive overhead for every employee who has to learn a system more complicated than the job actually requires, and it's a recurring source of user error when staff navigate a bloated interface built for a different kind of company.

A Practical Comparison Checklist

Before committing either direction, run both vendors through the same specific checklist rather than a generic feature comparison:

  • Can the system enforce technician scheduling against current ASNT certification level and method-specific competency without custom development?
  • Can equipment calibration due dates block job assignment automatically, out of the box or with light configuration?
  • How long, realistically, from contract signature to a live, usable system for core operations — not a pilot, a production system your team actually runs the business on?
  • Who makes routine configuration changes after go-live — an internal admin with basic training, or a specialized, billable consultant?
  • What does the vendor's own reference base look like for companies your actual size, not their largest logo customers?
  • What's the realistic all-in cost over a five-year horizon, including implementation, licensing, support, and the internal staff time each option will consume?

Migration and Exit Risk

It's worth thinking about exit risk before you're locked into either platform. SAP's data structures and customization layers can make migrating away expensive and technically complex years down the line, which is part of why so many organizations stay on SAP even when it no longer fits well — the switching cost itself becomes the reason to stay. Odoo's more open architecture and standard PostgreSQL database backend generally make data extraction and migration more straightforward if a firm's needs change dramatically in the future. For a growing but still mid-size firm, keeping that future flexibility is a real, if underappreciated, part of the total cost equation.

Making the Decision

The clearest signal for a 50-person NDT firm is this: if your finance team is asking for SAP because it's the name they know, rather than because you've identified a specific structural requirement — multi-entity consolidation, deep manufacturing MRP, an existing corporate SAP mandate — that only SAP can meet, you're very likely about to buy far more platform than your business needs, at a cost and implementation timeline to match. Get a scoped requirements list together first, request quotes against that exact list from both ends of the market, and let the comparison be about fit, not brand recognition. The firms that regret an ERP decision two years later are almost never the ones that chose too small a platform and had to upgrade sooner than expected — that's a manageable, incremental problem. They're the ones that chose too large a platform, sank a year and a significant budget into an implementation sized for a company they aren't, and are now stuck deciding whether to absorb the sunk cost or go through a second painful migration to something that actually fits.

title: Odoo vs NetSuite for NDT Companies: Total Cost of Ownership Compared
snippet: Two cloud ERP platforms, two different cost structures. Here's how to model five-year total cost of ownership for an NDT firm before you sign either contract.
content:
Two Cloud-Native Platforms, Two Different Cost Models

NetSuite and Odoo get compared more often than SAP and Odoo do, and for good reason — both are genuinely cloud-native, both target growing mid-market companies rather than Fortune 500 conglomerates, and both show up on the shortlist when a 30-to-150-person NDT inspection or calibration services firm outgrows QuickBooks plus spreadsheets. The comparison is legitimate in a way the SAP comparison usually isn't. But the two platforms carry structurally different cost models, and an NDT company owner comparing them on sticker price alone — or worse, on a sales rep's verbal ballpark — is going to miss real cost differences that only show up once you model total cost of ownership properly across a multi-year horizon.

What "Total Cost of Ownership" Actually Includes

A proper TCO comparison has to include more than the monthly subscription line a sales rep quotes first. It needs: base platform licensing, per-user costs at your actual and projected headcount, the specific modules your NDT workflow requires (project/job management, inventory, procurement, CRM, and whatever handles equipment calibration and personnel certification tracking), implementation services to configure and deploy the system, data migration from your current tools, training time for staff, ongoing support and maintenance, and the cost of any custom development needed to fill NDT-specific gaps neither platform ships with out of the box. Skipping any one of these categories — and implementation and custom development are the two most commonly underestimated — produces a TCO comparison that looks favorable on paper and turns out wrong within the first year.

NetSuite's Pricing Architecture: Base Platform Plus Per-User, Plus Modules

NetSuite's commercial model, as commonly published by NetSuite solution partners and resellers (Oracle NetSuite itself generally quotes directly rather than publishing a public price list), is built around a base platform subscription fee plus a per-user licensing fee, with additional modules — advanced inventory, fixed asset management, SuitePeople HR, and others relevant to a service business — priced as add-ons on top of that base. Partner-published figures have commonly cited base platform fees in the range of roughly $999 per month, with per-user costs commonly cited somewhere between $99 and $129 per user per month depending on user role and negotiated terms, though actual contracted pricing varies by deal size, term length, and which modules a specific company needs. The practical implication for a 50-person NDT firm is that your all-in NetSuite cost scales substantially with headcount and with how many specialized modules you need to cover NDT-specific requirements NetSuite doesn't handle natively — and because most of your staff (field technicians, not just back-office admin) may need at least some system access for scheduling and reporting, per-user costs can climb faster than firms initially budget for.

Odoo's Pricing Architecture: Per-Application, Configured for What You Use

Odoo's open-core, per-application licensing model works differently: rather than a flat enterprise platform fee plus per-user costs across every module, a company licenses the specific applications it actually runs — project management, inventory, accounting, and so on — with pricing that scales more directly with actual usage than with a fixed enterprise assumption. For an NDT-specific deployment like Atlantis NDT's ERP platform, pricing is quoted against your firm's actual scope — headcount, modules needed, and the specific NDT workflows (calibration tracking, technician certification enforcement, ISO 9001 document control) you require — rather than a generic per-seat enterprise tier. The honest way to compare this against NetSuite isn't to compare a public partner-published NetSuite estimate against an abstract Odoo number; it's to get a scoped quote from each vendor against your firm's exact requirements list and compare the two real numbers side by side.

Implementation Cost and Timeline Compared

NetSuite implementations for a mid-size service company commonly run two to six months depending on scope and how many modules are being configured simultaneously, typically requiring a NetSuite-certified implementation partner rather than being realistically self-service for a company without dedicated in-house NetSuite expertise. Odoo-based implementations, particularly when built on a pre-configured industry template rather than a blank installation, often run faster for a comparably scoped project, because the modular app architecture allows a phased rollout — core project management and invoicing live first, with calibration tracking, document control, and reporting integration added in subsequent phases — without requiring the entire platform to be configured before any part of it goes live. Implementation cost tracks timeline closely in both cases: longer implementations mean more consultant hours, and consultant hours are typically the single largest line item in either platform's true first-year cost, frequently exceeding the software licensing cost itself.

SuiteSuccess vs Industry-Specific Configuration

NetSuite offers industry-specific "SuiteSuccess" editions with pre-built configurations for certain verticals — but NDT and inspection services is a narrow enough niche that no SuiteSuccess edition targets it directly, meaning an NDT firm implementing NetSuite is typically starting from a general services or field-service-adjacent template and building NDT-specific functionality (certification-linked scheduling, calibration-linked equipment checkout, method-specific competency tracking) as custom development on top, using NetSuite's SuiteScript and SuiteFlow customization tools, which require specialized (and billable) NetSuite development expertise to build and maintain. This is the same category of gap Odoo starts with in its unconfigured, generic form — but because Atlantis NDT's Odoo-based platform is purpose-built and pre-configured for NDT workflows specifically, a firm starts meaningfully further along the path to an NDT-fit system than beginning from either platform's generic starting point.

Year-Two-and-Beyond Costs: The Part Most Comparisons Skip

Sales conversations focus heavily on first-year cost, but a five-year TCO comparison usually tells a different story, because subscription-based platforms like NetSuite carry ongoing per-user and module fees every year indefinitely, and those costs grow as a firm adds headcount or adds modules to cover new service lines. A firm that starts NetSuite at 40 users and grows to 65 over three years is paying materially more in year four than year one, on top of whatever module expansion happens along the way. Odoo's per-application model can grow similarly as a firm adds modules, but because the base architecture doesn't carry the same flat enterprise-wide platform fee structure, firms typically find the marginal cost of adding a user or a lightly-used module more predictable and proportionate to actual usage. Model this out for your own firm's realistic three-and five-year headcount and module growth before comparing sticker prices — a platform that looks cheaper in year one can be the more expensive choice by year four.

Where NetSuite Has a Real Edge

NetSuite genuinely wins for companies with complex multi-subsidiary, multi-currency operations — an NDT firm with legal entities in multiple countries, or one doing substantial international invoicing and needing sophisticated consolidated financial reporting across currencies, will find NetSuite's built-in multi-subsidiary architecture more mature out of the box than most alternatives. It also has a large, established partner ecosystem and a long track record with finance and accounting teams who may already have NetSuite experience from a previous employer, which can shorten the learning curve for a newly hired controller or CFO.

Where Odoo Has a Real Edge for NDT-Specific Workflows

For a domestically focused or single-entity NDT firm without heavy multi-subsidiary complexity, Odoo's advantages are speed to an NDT-fit system, lower ongoing per-user cost pressure as headcount grows, and — specifically with a pre-configured NDT platform like Atlantis's — a shorter distance between "system goes live" and "system actually enforces our industry-specific rules" like certification-gated scheduling and calibration-linked equipment checkout. The open, PostgreSQL-based data architecture also tends to make future data portability and integration with other tools (a digital twin platform, a dedicated reporting tool, a client portal) more straightforward than working within NetSuite's more closed ecosystem.

A Concrete Scenario: Adding a New Service Line Mid-Contract

Consider a realistic situation: your firm has been running UT and MT inspection services for five years, and you're adding phased array services with a new equipment fleet and two newly certified technicians. In a well-configured Odoo-based platform, adding a new service line typically means configuring a new project type, adding the new equipment to the calibration-tracked asset register, and updating the technician competency records to reflect the new certification — changes an internal administrator with basic system training can usually make directly, often within days. In NetSuite, depending on how deeply the original implementation was customized, a meaningful workflow change like this may require re-engaging your implementation partner to modify SuiteScript customizations or SuiteFlow logic, adding both cost and calendar time to what should be a routine business expansion. Ask both vendors directly, during evaluation, to walk through exactly this scenario — adding a new service line six months after go-live — and pay close attention to whether the answer involves your own staff or a billable consulting engagement.

Integration Ecosystem: Connecting to NDT-Specific Tools

Neither NetSuite nor stock Odoo natively handles NDT-specific functions like radiographic film/digital image management, phased array data file storage, or integration with a dedicated inspection reporting tool — both platforms need to integrate with or be extended to cover this ground. NetSuite's integration approach typically runs through its SuiteTalk API and a marketplace of third-party connectors (SuiteApps), which work well but often carry their own licensing costs and implementation effort per integration. Odoo's more open architecture and large open-source module ecosystem generally make custom integrations — connecting to a dedicated NDT reporting platform or a digital twin platform for asset visualization — more straightforward to build and maintain without per-connector licensing fees stacking on top of the core platform cost. For a firm planning to connect its ERP to inspection-specific tools rather than trying to force all NDT data into a generic ERP data model, this integration flexibility is a real and recurring cost factor worth weighing alongside the base platform TCO.

A Practical Comparison Checklist

Run both vendors through the same specific test scenarios rather than a generic feature checklist:

  • Request a scoped quote against your actual headcount, modules needed, and NDT-specific requirements from both vendors — not a generic per-seat estimate.
  • Ask each vendor to demonstrate adding a new service line or equipment type as a live configuration exercise, and note whether it requires your staff or a billable consultant.
  • Confirm how each platform handles technician certification-level enforcement in scheduling, and whether that's native functionality or custom-built.
  • Model total cost across a five-year horizon at your realistic projected headcount, not just year-one pricing.
  • Check integration cost and complexity for connecting to any dedicated NDT reporting, digital asset, or field data capture tools your operation already uses or plans to adopt.
  • Ask each vendor for references from companies genuinely close to your size and industry, not their largest flagship accounts.

A Five-Year TCO Framework You Can Run Yourself

Build a simple model before deciding: list your current headcount and a realistic 3-and-5-year growth projection, list the specific modules each platform requires to meet your NDT workflow needs (not generic modules — the specific ones), request implementation cost quotes from both vendors against that exact scope, add estimated annual licensing at your projected headcount for each year, and add a reasonable estimate for custom development needed to close NDT-specific functionality gaps. Total each platform across five years, not one. This exercise alone — done honestly, with real vendor quotes rather than sales-rep ballparks — resolves more Odoo-versus-NetSuite decisions than any amount of feature-list comparison, because it forces the actual cost structure differences between the two platforms into a number you can compare directly.

Making the Decision

If your NDT firm is a single U.S. entity without complex multi-currency or multi-subsidiary requirements, and NDT-specific workflow fit — certification tracking, calibration enforcement, inspection report integration — matters more to your daily operations than deep multi-entity financial consolidation, a purpose-built Odoo-based platform is very likely to win both the implementation-speed and the five-year TCO comparison. If your firm genuinely has multi-subsidiary, multi-currency complexity today, that's the specific factor worth weighing seriously against NetSuite's real strength — not brand reputation, but that one structural capability. Either way, insist on scoped quotes against your actual requirements before deciding, not a generic per-seat price from either vendor's website. And whichever direction you lean, run the new-service-line scenario above with each finalist vendor before signing — it's a small test that reveals more about real ongoing cost and operational agility than any feature comparison sheet either sales team will hand you.

title: Field Service Management Software for NDT Technicians: GPS Dispatch and Mobile Reporting
snippet: Generic field service apps break down on NDT jobs. Here's what GPS dispatch and mobile reporting actually need to handle for certified inspection crews.
content:
Why NDT Field Service Doesn't Fit Generic Dispatch Software

Most field service management (FSM) platforms were built for HVAC techs, plumbers, and electricians — trades where the job is "diagnose and fix" and the paperwork is an invoice. Non-destructive testing is a different animal. A UT technician showing up to a refinery turnaround isn't just a body with a truck; they're a certified individual whose qualification level, current recertification date, and vision test currency all have to match the scope of work before they're even allowed on site. The output of the visit isn't a repaired unit — it's a report that becomes part of the client's fitness-for-service record under API 510, API 570, or API 653, and that report has to trace back to a calibrated instrument, a specific calibration block, and in the case of radiography, a licensed source with a documented chain of custody. Dispatch a plumber to the wrong address and you lose an hour. Dispatch an NDT technician whose Level II UT certification expired eleven days ago to a pressure vessel inspection, and you've created a nonconformance that can follow the client's asset file for years.

This is why field service management for NDT companies has to be purpose-built, not adapted. It needs to know what "qualified" means for a given job, track equipment calibration status alongside technician certification status, and produce a mobile reporting workflow that survives a radiography bay with zero cell signal. Generic dispatch software can move a technician from point A to point B. It can't tell you the technician's MT wet fluorescent qualification lapsed last month, or that the crawler-mounted UT unit assigned to the job is three days overdue for its annual calibration.

What GPS Dispatch Actually Solves in Inspection Work

Turnaround and Shutdown Scheduling

Refinery and petrochemical turnarounds compress months of inspection work into a two-to-six-week window, often running three shifts a day across a site the size of a small town. Getting the right technician — RT Level II with current film interpretation sign-off, or PAUT operator qualified on the specific procedure — to the right unit at the right hour is a live logistics problem, not a spreadsheet exercise. GPS-aware dispatch lets a scheduler see which crews are on-site, which are en route, and which are sitting idle waiting on a permit, then re-route in real time when a vessel entry gets pushed back four hours because confined-space monitoring hasn't cleared. Without that visibility, companies default to over-staffing turnarounds "just in case," which is the single biggest avoidable labor cost in outage work.

On-Call Rotations and Emergency Callouts

Pipeline operators and refineries don't schedule leaks and unplanned shutdowns. A field service system with GPS and availability tracking lets a dispatcher find the nearest qualified UT or MT technician to an emergency callout instead of calling down a paper phone tree — which matters when a client's outage clock is running at a documented cost per hour and the nearest qualified tech might be forty minutes closer than the one who happens to answer first.

Radiography Source Tracking and RSO Compliance

Companies running industrial radiography under an NRC or Agreement State license have a Radiation Safety Officer who is personally accountable for knowing, at all times, where every licensed source is and who is transporting it. GPS-tagged dispatch that logs source movement alongside job assignment gives the RSO a real-time answer instead of a phone call to the field, and it builds the utilization log the license inspector will ask for at the next audit — device serial number, source serial number, curie content on the date of use, and the technician who signed for it under 10 CFR 34.

What Mobile Reporting Actually Needs to Handle in the Field

Offline-First, Not Offline-Sometimes

A lot of "mobile-enabled" reporting software is really a web form that happens to render on a phone — and it breaks the moment the technician steps into a radiography vault, a tank interior, or a pipeline right-of-way forty miles from the nearest tower. Field reporting for NDT has to capture a complete UT thickness map, an MT indication sketch, or a PT bleedout photo set fully offline, then sync cleanly when connectivity returns, without creating duplicate records or silently dropping data. This is one of the most common failure points companies hit when they pilot consumer-grade field service apps against real turnaround conditions.

Digital Technique Sheets and Calibration Traceability

Every UT reading should carry the calibration block ID and calibration date used that shift, not just a technician's signature attesting it happened. Every MT and PT report should reference the specific batch number of the magnetic particle ink or dye penetrant used, with expiration date checked automatically against the job date. Digitizing this at the point of capture — rather than reconstructing it from memory back at the office — is what turns a field report into a defensible quality record instead of a liability.

Photo Documentation and Geotagging

Indication photos with embedded GPS coordinates and timestamps matter more than most companies realize until a client disputes a reported wall-loss location on a 40-foot column six months later. A mobile reporting tool that geotags photos and links them directly to the corresponding indication entry in the report removes the ambiguity before it becomes a dispute.

Digital Signatures and Chain of Custody

For work governed by API or ASME code, the report needs a clean, timestamped signature chain — technician, and where required, a Level III review — captured at the point of origin, not re-typed into a template two days later from field notes. That re-typing step is where transcription errors creep into reports, and it's exactly the step mobile-first capture is meant to eliminate.

Generic FSM vs NDT-Built Dispatch: A Side-by-Side

  • Technician-job matching: Generic FSM matches by skill tag or zip code. NDT-specific dispatch matches by certification method, level, current recertification date, and vision test currency against the actual procedure called for on the job.
  • Equipment assignment: Generic FSM tracks a truck's tool inventory. NDT dispatch tracks which specific UT flaw detector, probe set, or radiography camera is assigned, its calibration due date, and whether it's already committed to a conflicting job that day.
  • Compliance artifacts: Generic FSM produces a work order and invoice. NDT dispatch needs to produce (or feed) a report tied to a code reference, a calibration record, and — for RT — a source utilization log.
  • Offline resilience: Generic FSM assumes intermittent 4G. NDT field reporting has to assume zero signal for hours at a stretch inside vessels, vaults, and remote rights-of-way.
  • Regulatory license tracking: Generic FSM has no concept of an NRC or Agreement State radioactive materials license. NDT dispatch has to track licensed source inventory and radiography device serials as first-class data, not an attachment.

Connecting Dispatch to the Back Office

A dispatch calendar that lives on its own, disconnected from job costing and invoicing, creates double entry and reconciliation headaches that eat the labor savings dispatch was supposed to deliver. The stronger pattern is dispatch as a module inside a broader NDT inspection management platform, where a completed field visit automatically becomes a billable line item, technician hours flow into payroll and per diem tracking, and the report itself — built in dedicated NDT reporting software — is cross-referenced to the job record instead of living in a separate silo. Companies that run dispatch, reporting, and invoicing as three disconnected tools tend to discover the gap at month-end close, when someone has to manually match field tickets to invoices to timesheets.

Rollout Considerations for US Inspection Companies

A few practical issues come up repeatedly when US-based NDT companies roll out field service and mobile reporting software:

  • Multi-state DOT hours-of-service exposure for crews driving between job sites across state lines — dispatch software that tracks drive time can flag a schedule that would push a technician into a hours-of-service violation before it happens, not after a roadside inspection catches it.
  • Client-specific insurance and certificate-of-insurance requirements — many refineries and pipeline operators won't badge in a technician without a current COI on file; dispatch systems that gate scheduling on document currency prevent a crew showing up to a gate they can't get through.
  • Site-specific access and TWIC/OSHA 30 requirements — maritime and marine terminal work often requires a current Transportation Worker Identification Credential; tracking this alongside NDT certification avoids a wasted trip.
  • Integration with existing accounting — most small-to-mid NDT shops run QuickBooks or a similar system already; a dispatch and reporting platform that exports cleanly into existing accounting avoids a painful forced migration.

A Practical Evaluation Checklist

Before committing to a field service and mobile reporting platform, walk it through these questions with a live demo, not a slide deck:

  • Can it block dispatch of a technician whose certification for the required method has lapsed, automatically, without a human catching it manually?
  • Does the mobile app fully function with zero connectivity, including photo capture, sketch tools, and multi-page technique sheets, and sync without data loss when signal returns?
  • Can it track calibration due dates on instruments and flag a conflict if an overdue unit gets assigned to a job?
  • Does GPS tracking integrate with source/device utilization logging for radiography work, or is that a separate manual log?
  • How does a completed field visit flow into invoicing — automatically, or does someone re-key it?
  • What happens during a multi-day outage with no connectivity at all — does the whole crew's data queue safely, or does someone need to physically return to a signal area to sync?

The answers separate software that was built for NDT from software that was adapted for it after the fact. Companies evaluating a switch often benefit from a structured ASNT Level III consulting review of their current field workflow before selecting a platform — it's much cheaper to fix a workflow gap on paper than to discover it mid-turnaround with a client watching.

Data Security and Access Control on Sensitive Client Sites

Role-Based Access Matters More Than It Looks Like It Does

A field service platform holding job photos, thickness readings, and asset condition data from a refinery or a defense-adjacent fabrication shop is holding information many clients consider sensitive — sometimes contractually, under a mutual non-disclosure agreement, and sometimes because a wall-loss map of a specific vessel is exactly the kind of detail a competitor or a plaintiff's attorney would want in a future dispute. Role-based access control needs to be granular enough that a technician can see their own assigned jobs and the historical record they personally need, a dispatcher can see the full schedule without necessarily seeing every historical report's technical detail, and a client-facing portal (where one exists) exposes only that specific client's data — never a cross-client view that a careless permission setup could accidentally create.

Photo and Document Storage Under NDA Terms

Many refinery and petrochemical clients require inspection contractors to sign site-specific confidentiality terms before badge-in, and those terms often extend to where and how inspection photos and data can be stored — some clients explicitly prohibit certain cloud storage configurations or require data residency within specific jurisdictions. A field service platform's data storage and encryption practices need to be something a company can actually describe accurately to a client's security team during onboarding, not a vague assurance. Encryption at rest and in transit, clear data retention and deletion policies, and the ability to segregate a specific client's data on request are all reasonable questions a security-conscious client will ask, and a company should be able to answer them before, not during, a contract negotiation.

Gate List and Badge System Integration

Larger industrial sites often run their own contractor access management systems, syncing an approved technician gate list against the site's own badge system. Field service software that can export a clean, current technician roster — certification status, background check currency, site-specific training completion — directly into a client's access management workflow removes a recurring manual task that otherwise falls on someone in the office re-typing the same roster information into a client portal every time it changes.

Common Mistakes When Rolling Out Field Service Software

Company-Wide Rollout Instead of a Pilot Crew

Switching an entire technician roster and every dispatcher over to a new system on the same day, without a pilot period, magnifies every workflow gap at once and makes it hard to tell whether a problem is a software limitation or a training gap. A stronger pattern is piloting with a single crew or a single service line — say, the UT crew serving one regional client — for several weeks, working out the rough edges in scheduling rules, offline sync behavior, and report handoff before extending to the full operation.

No Clear Protocol for Dispatch Overrides

Every certification-aware dispatch system will eventually hit a scenario where a dispatcher believes an override is justified — a technician's recertification exam is scheduled for the next morning and the current job doesn't start until then, for instance. Without a clear, documented override protocol — who can approve one, what justification gets logged, how it's reviewed afterward — dispatchers either freeze up waiting for someone else to decide, or start overriding routinely without real scrutiny, which defeats the purpose of certification-aware dispatch in the first place.

Underestimating Offline Sync Conflict Handling

When two technicians on the same job both enter data offline and sync at different times, or when a technician's device loses a sync mid-transfer, the software needs a clear, predictable conflict resolution behavior — and the company needs to understand what that behavior is before it happens in the field, not discover it during an actual data conflict on an active turnaround. Ask any vendor directly how simultaneous offline edits and partial syncs are handled, and test it deliberately during the pilot period rather than assuming it will simply work.

What to Track After Go-Live

Once field service and mobile reporting software is live, a handful of operational metrics reveal whether it's actually delivering value rather than just feeling modern: average time between job completion and report delivery to the client, the frequency of dispatch conflicts caught by certification or calibration gating (each one is a near-miss the old process would likely have missed), technician time spent on administrative data entry versus billable inspection work, and how often office staff still need to manually re-enter or reconcile data that should have flowed through automatically. Tracking these consistently for the first two quarters after rollout gives a company a real, company-specific picture of return on the switch, rather than relying on a vendor's general claims about what the software should deliver.

title: NDT ERP Migration Guide: Moving Off Spreadsheets Without Losing Historical Data
snippet: A step-by-step guide for NDT companies migrating calibration, certification, and job history off spreadsheets into an ERP without breaking audit traceability.
content:
Why NDT Companies Wait Too Long to Leave Spreadsheets

Almost every NDT company that has been operating for more than five years is running some part of its business on a spreadsheet, and there's a good reason it happened: spreadsheets are free, flexible, and nobody had to ask permission to build one. A scheduling tab turns into a certification tracker, which turns into a calibration due-date log, which turns into a jerry-rigged job costing sheet with macros only one person understands. The system works — until that person goes on vacation during a turnaround, or a client audit asks for a complete calibration traceability chain going back three years and the answer is scattered across fourteen versions of "Calibration Log FINAL v3 (2).xlsx" on three different laptops.

The trigger for migration is rarely "we want new software." It's usually a near-miss: a technician dispatched with an expired certification because the tracker wasn't updated, a client audit that took two weeks of manual reconciliation instead of two hours, or a growth spurt that outpaced what one overworked office manager can keep current by hand. By the time the decision gets made, the spreadsheets often hold years of calibration records, certification histories, and job data that the company legally and contractually needs to keep — which is exactly what makes migration feel risky. This guide walks through how to move that data into a proper NDT ERP system without losing the audit trail that took years to build.

Step One: Audit What You Actually Have

Inventory Every Source of Truth

Before touching a migration tool, list every spreadsheet, shared drive folder, and paper binder that currently holds operational data: technician certification records, equipment calibration logs, job history, client contact and contract terms, source inventory logs for radiography, and inventory of consumables. Most companies are surprised to find the "real" data is split across six files with three different formats for the same field — one calibration log uses MM/DD/YYYY, another uses DD-MMM-YY, and a third just has "last week" typed into a date column.

Identify the Non-Negotiable Records

Not all data is equally important to migrate cleanly. Calibration records tied to open or recently closed jobs, technician certification histories going back through the current recertification cycle, and any data referenced in an active client contract or ongoing litigation hold are non-negotiable — they need to move with full fidelity, not a summary. Older job history from a decade ago, by contrast, can often be archived as read-only PDF exports rather than fully re-keyed into the new system's live database.

Step Two: Clean Before You Migrate, Not After

A rule that saves companies weeks of pain: never migrate dirty data and plan to clean it up "later" in the new system. Later never comes, and now the mess lives inside a system that's supposed to be the trusted source of truth. Before migration:

  • Standardize date formats and technician name spellings across every source file (the same tech listed as "Bob Smith," "R. Smith," and "Robert Smith Jr." in three sheets will become three different technician records unless you fix it first).
  • Reconcile duplicate client and equipment records — merge the four rows for "Valero Port Arthur" and "Valero — Port Arthur Refinery" into one canonical client entry.
  • Flag and resolve any calibration or certification records with missing dates rather than guessing on import; a wrong recertification date in the new system is worse than a gap that's flagged for follow-up.
  • Decide on unit consistency (mils vs. thousandths of an inch, metric vs. imperial thickness readings) before data crosses into a system that will treat every number as authoritative.

Step Three: Map Fields, Don't Assume They Match

Spreadsheets tend to have ad hoc columns that grew organically — "Notes," "Status," "Misc" — that don't map cleanly onto a structured ERP schema. Before import, build an explicit field map: which spreadsheet column becomes which ERP field, and what happens to the columns that don't have an obvious home. A common mistake is letting free-text "Notes" columns simply vanish during import because nobody assigned them a destination — and six months later someone needs the context that was quietly dropped. Better to migrate anything ambiguous into a general notes field on the record than to lose it.

Step Four: Run a Parallel Period Before Full Cutover

Never flip a switch on a Friday and expect Monday to work. The safer pattern is a defined parallel-run period — typically two to four weeks — where technicians and office staff enter new jobs and calibration events into both the old spreadsheet system and the new ERP simultaneously. This does two things: it surfaces workflow gaps in the new system while the old system is still the safety net, and it gives you a clean way to validate that historical data imported correctly by cross-checking a sample of records against the source spreadsheets. Pick jobs and technicians from different service lines — UT, RT, MT, PT — for the validation sample, since import mapping errors often show up in only one data type.

What Companies Get Wrong: Common Migration Pitfalls

Losing Calibration Traceability

The single most damaging migration mistake is breaking the link between a historical job report and the calibration record that supported it. If a client asks for the calibration certificate behind a UT reading from fourteen months ago and the new system can't produce it because the migration only carried over "calibration due dates" going forward, not historical calibration events, you have a quality system gap that can surface in an ISO 9001 or client audit at the worst possible time.

Treating Certification Records as a Snapshot Instead of a History

Spreadsheets often only show a technician's current certification level and expiration date. A proper migration needs to preserve the full certification history — prior levels, recertification dates, method-by-method qualification — because that history is what proves continuous qualification if a client or code authority ever questions whether a technician was properly certified on the date a specific job was performed.

Underestimating Training Time

The technical migration is often easier than the human one. Office staff and field technicians who have used the same spreadsheet workflow for years will route around a new system if it's not clearly faster for their specific daily tasks. Budget real training time — not a one-hour webinar — and identify an internal champion on both the office and field sides who can answer day-to-day questions during the first month.

No Rollback Plan

Even a well-planned migration can hit a blocking issue mid-cutover. Keep the old spreadsheet system fully intact and accessible (not deleted, not archived to a drive nobody can find) for at least one full quarter after cutover, so there's a clean fallback if a critical gap surfaces after go-live.

What a Modern NDT ERP Should Do With That Data Once It's In

Migration isn't the finish line — it's what unlocks the reason companies migrate in the first place. Once historical data lives in a structured system, calibration due dates can trigger automatic alerts before equipment goes out of tolerance, technician certification expirations can block dispatch automatically rather than relying on someone remembering, and job costing can roll up in real time instead of at month-end. Reporting that used to require manually pulling and combining three spreadsheets — say, "show me every UT job for this client in the last two years with the technician and calibration record attached" — becomes a query that runs in seconds. That's the difference between data that exists and data that's actually usable, and it's the return on the migration effort.

A Practical Migration Timeline

  • Weeks 1-2: Full data audit and inventory of every spreadsheet, log, and record source.
  • Weeks 3-4: Data cleaning — standardize formats, merge duplicates, flag gaps.
  • Week 5: Field mapping between spreadsheet columns and ERP schema, with explicit decisions on every ambiguous column.
  • Weeks 6-7: Test import into a staging environment, validate against source data sample by service line.
  • Weeks 8-11: Parallel run — both systems live, staff trained, discrepancies logged and resolved.
  • Week 12: Full cutover, old system retained read-only as fallback.

Companies migrating from spreadsheets into a purpose-built inspection management ERP don't need to do this alone — a structured onboarding process, paired with ASNT Level III consulting on how the new system should encode your specific quality procedures, turns a risky data migration into a controlled upgrade. And once the historical record lives in a structured system, it becomes the foundation for far more — including feeding asset history into a digital twin platform for clients who want inspection data visualized against the physical asset over time.

Handling Special Cases: Radiography Source Logs and Client-Owned Data

Migrating Source Utilization and License Records

Companies running radiography under an NRC or Agreement State materials license carry a separate category of historical data that needs particularly careful handling during migration: source utilization logs, leak test records, and device inventory history tied to license conditions. These records often exist in a format dictated by the license itself rather than by the company's own preference, and a migration that reformats them without preserving the exact fields a license inspector expects to see can create a compliance gap that has nothing to do with the ERP system's general capability and everything to do with how the migration was executed. Treat these as a distinct migration workstream with its own validation pass, ideally reviewed by whoever holds Radiation Safety Officer responsibility before the old logs are retired from active use.

Client-Owned Historical Reports

Some client contracts specify that inspection records and reports are considered client property, with the contractor obligated to retain and produce them on request for a defined retention period — sometimes seven years, sometimes the life of the asset. When migrating historical job data, flag which records fall under this kind of contractual retention obligation, since losing or degrading fidelity on those specific records carries contractual risk beyond general operational inconvenience. It's worth cross-referencing active contracts against the migration plan before finalizing what gets fully migrated versus archived as a read-only export.

Choosing Between a Big-Bang Migration and a Phased Approach

Not every company needs the full twelve-week phased timeline described above — the right pace depends on company size and data complexity. A small shop with a handful of technicians and a few years of relatively clean spreadsheet history might reasonably compress this into four to six weeks. A larger multi-crew operation with a decade of mixed-format records, multiple service lines, and several active client contracts with specific retention terms should expect the fuller timeline, and attempting to compress it usually just moves the cleanup work from before go-live to after — which is a worse place for it to happen, because by then the bad data is already inside the system people are relying on daily.

Signs a Company Is Rushing the Migration

  • Data cleaning is happening simultaneously with import rather than before it, because "we'll fix it once it's in the new system."
  • No one has actually opened and reviewed a sample of migrated calibration records against the original source to confirm they match.
  • The parallel-run period is being skipped or compressed to "just a few days" because staff are eager to stop maintaining two systems.
  • Field technicians weren't consulted on the new mobile workflow before go-live and are encountering it live on a job for the first time.

Any one of these is a signal to slow down. A migration that takes an extra month but preserves clean, traceable historical data is a far better outcome than a fast migration that quietly breaks the audit trail a company spent years building.

Working With a Vendor or Consultant During Migration

Most ERP vendors offer some level of migration support, but the depth varies enormously — some provide a generic import template and leave data cleaning entirely to the customer, while others offer hands-on data mapping and validation support as part of onboarding. Before committing to a vendor, get specific about what migration support is actually included: will the vendor's team review a sample of migrated calibration and certification records for accuracy, or is that entirely the customer's responsibility? Companies without in-house expertise in structuring quality records for migration often benefit from outside ASNT Level III consulting support specifically for the data validation phase — someone who knows what a complete, audit-ready calibration record actually needs to contain can catch gaps that a general IT migration specialist, unfamiliar with NDT-specific compliance requirements, would likely miss entirely.

title: RFP Checklist for NDT Company ERP Software: 40 Questions to Ask Every Vendor
snippet: 40 specific RFP questions across certification tracking, calibration, dispatch, mobile reporting, financials, migration, and vendor viability for NDT ERP buyers.
content:
Why NDT Companies Need a Different Kind of RFP

Most ERP request-for-proposal templates in circulation were written for distribution warehouses or general field service contractors, and they ask the wrong questions for an inspection company. They'll ask a vendor about inventory management and invoicing, which matter, but they won't ask whether the system can block a job dispatch when a technician's Level II UT certification has lapsed, or whether it can produce a calibration traceability chain for a report a client is disputing from eighteen months ago. Running a generic RFP process against NDT-specific software vendors produces vague, hard-to-compare answers, because the questions don't touch the parts of the system that actually determine whether it will work for inspection operations.

This checklist is built specifically for companies evaluating ERP software for NDT, calibration, or technical inspection services. It's organized into eight categories with forty concrete questions — send it to every vendor on your shortlist verbatim, and score the answers side by side rather than relying on a sales deck. A vendor who can answer these specifically, with a live demo, is a very different proposition from one who answers "yes, the platform is fully configurable" to everything.

Category 1: Personnel Certification Management

  • Can the system track certification by individual NDT method (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, PAUT, TOFD) and qualification level separately, not as a single blanket "certified" flag?
  • Does it track recertification cycles and automatically flag technicians approaching expiration, with configurable lead time (30/60/90 days)?
  • Can it track vision test currency (near and color vision per SNT-TC-1A recommended practice) as a distinct data point from certification level?
  • Does the system store the full certification history for each technician, not just current status, so past qualification on a given job date can be proven later?
  • Can it block or flag dispatch of a technician to a job requiring a method or level they aren't currently qualified for?

Category 2: Equipment and Calibration Management

  • Can the system track calibration due dates by individual instrument serial number, with automatic alerts before a unit goes out of tolerance?
  • Does it store calibration certificates and traceability documentation (NIST-traceable standards) attached to each calibration event?
  • Can it flag a scheduling conflict if an instrument due for calibration is assigned to a job before that calibration is completed?
  • Does it support tracking of consumables with expiration dates — penetrant, developer, magnetic particle ink batches — separately from capital equipment?
  • For companies running radiography, can it track licensed source inventory, device serial numbers, and source utilization logs as required for NRC or Agreement State license compliance?

Category 3: Job Scheduling and Dispatch

  • Does the scheduling module cross-reference technician certification and equipment calibration status automatically before confirming an assignment?
  • Can it handle multi-day turnaround/outage scheduling with shift-based crew rotation, not just single-visit service calls?
  • Is there GPS or location tracking for field crews, and does it integrate with the dispatch calendar?
  • Can dispatchers see real-time crew status (en route, on-site, delayed) without a phone call?
  • Does the system support on-call rotation management for emergency callout work?

Category 4: Mobile Field Reporting

  • Does the mobile app function fully offline, including data entry, sketch/diagram tools, and photo capture, with reliable sync once connectivity returns?
  • Can field technicians complete a full method-specific technique sheet (UT thickness map, MT/PT indication log, RT exposure record) on a phone or tablet in the field?
  • Does the app support digital signatures with a timestamped audit trail, including Level III review sign-off where required?
  • Can photos be geotagged and linked directly to specific indications or readings within the report?
  • How is data loss prevented if a device is dropped, damaged, or loses battery mid-shift?

Category 5: Reporting and Compliance

  • Can the system generate reports formatted to specific code requirements (API 510/570/653, ASME Section V, AWS D1.1) without manual reformatting?
  • Is there an audit trail showing every edit to a report after initial submission, with who made the change and when?
  • Can it produce a complete calibration and certification traceability package for a specific historical report on demand, for a client or code-authority audit?
  • Does it support customer-specific report templates for clients who require their own format?
  • How does the reporting module relate to dedicated NDT reporting software — is it built in, or does it require a separate integrated product?

Category 6: Financials and Job Costing

  • Can the system track job costing in real time (labor, equipment, consumables, per diem) rather than only at month-end reconciliation?
  • Does it support both day-rate and footage/unit-rate billing models, common in pipeline and turnaround work?
  • Can it integrate with existing accounting software (QuickBooks, Sage, Xero) without requiring a full accounting migration?
  • Does it handle multi-entity billing for companies operating under more than one brand or subsidiary?
  • Can it track per-client contract terms (rates, payment terms, insurance requirements) and flag violations before a job is scheduled?

Category 7: Data Migration and Implementation

  • What is the vendor's process for migrating existing spreadsheet or legacy-system data, and who does the data cleaning — the vendor or your team?
  • Is there a parallel-run period supported, where old and new systems operate simultaneously before full cutover?
  • What is the realistic implementation timeline for a company of your size and service mix, based on comparable past implementations?
  • Who owns the data if the relationship ends — can you export a complete, usable copy of your historical records?
  • What training is included, and is it role-specific (dispatcher, field technician, office admin, Level III reviewer) or generic?

Category 8: Vendor Viability and Support

  • How long has the vendor specifically served NDT or inspection-industry clients, versus adapting a generic ERP?
  • What is the support model — dedicated account contact, ticket queue, phone support — and what are realistic response times during an active outage?
  • How often is the platform updated, and how are updates tested against existing customizations before deployment?
  • Can the vendor provide references from companies of comparable size and service mix (not just their largest client)?
  • What happens to system access and support continuity if the vendor is acquired or changes ownership?

How to Score the Responses

Resist the temptation to score every question equally. Weight Categories 1, 2, and 5 — certification tracking, calibration management, and compliance reporting — most heavily, because these are the categories where a gap creates real regulatory and contractual risk, not just operational friction. A vendor that's weak on job costing dashboards but airtight on certification and calibration traceability is a safer bet for an NDT company than the reverse. Build a simple scoring matrix — 1 to 5 per question, organized by category — and have more than one person score each vendor's demo independently before comparing notes; a single evaluator tends to be swayed by whichever feature was demoed most smoothly, which isn't always the feature that matters most day to day.

Red Flags to Watch For During Demos

  • A vendor who can't answer a specific certification-tracking or calibration-traceability question without "checking with engineering" during a sales call — this usually means the feature exists on paper but hasn't been built out for real-world use.
  • Mobile offline capability that's demoed only with wifi on, or with a caveat about "most areas having signal" — insist on a demo with airplane mode enabled.
  • No clear answer on data ownership and export rights — this is a contract term to nail down in writing before signing, not something to take on faith.
  • Reference clients who are all significantly larger or smaller than your company, or none in the same service mix (RT/UT-heavy vs. visual/MT-heavy operations have different real-world needs).

Beyond the RFP: What Happens After Selection

An RFP process that surfaces the right vendor is only the first half of the decision — the second half is a realistic implementation plan, ideally with outside ASNT Level III consulting input on how your specific quality procedures and code requirements should be encoded into the new system's workflows, since that's the part generic implementation teams tend to get wrong. Companies that skip this step often end up with software that's technically installed but doesn't actually reflect how a Level III would structure the qualification and traceability rules that keep the operation audit-ready.

How to Structure the RFP Process Itself

Set a Realistic Vendor Shortlist

Sending this checklist to a dozen vendors dilutes evaluation effort across too many options and usually results in a shallow review of each. A shortlist of three to five vendors — narrowed by an initial screening call confirming they have genuine NDT-industry experience, not just a generic ERP platform with an inspection module bolted on — lets an evaluation team go deep on the questions that matter most rather than spreading thin across many.

Require a Live Demo Against Your Own Scenarios

A canned vendor demo is built to show the platform's best features in the best light. A far more revealing exercise is handing the vendor two or three of your company's actual, real job scenarios in advance — a turnaround scheduling conflict, a technician certification edge case, a multi-currency invoice if relevant — and asking them to demo how the system handles those specific situations live. Vendors who can do this fluently know their product deeply; vendors who struggle or need to "follow up separately" are revealing something important about how well the platform actually fits inspection-industry workflows versus how well it was positioned in the sales pitch.

Involve the People Who Will Actually Use It

RFP evaluation run entirely by ownership or office management, without input from the dispatchers, field technicians, and accounting staff who will use the system daily, tends to weight the wrong factors — a system that looks impressive in a boardroom demo can be genuinely frustrating for a technician trying to complete a report one-handed in a tank. Include at least one field technician and one dispatcher in the demo review process, and weight their feedback seriously; they'll catch usability problems that a purely management-level evaluation will miss entirely.

What a Strong Vendor Proposal Actually Looks Like

Beyond the forty questions above, a genuinely strong proposal from an NDT-experienced vendor will typically include: specific examples of how the certification and calibration gating logic has been configured for other inspection companies (without naming confidential client details, but with enough specificity to show real prior implementation, not theoretical capability); a realistic, phased implementation timeline rather than a vague promise of "quick onboarding"; a clear, written data ownership and export policy included in the contract terms, not just a verbal assurance during the sales process; and named, specific support contacts rather than a generic ticket-queue email address as the only point of contact during initial rollout.

After the RFP: Turning the Winning Proposal Into a Contract

Once a vendor is selected, make sure the specific commitments made during the RFP process — response times, data export rights, included training scope, implementation timeline — are written into the actual contract or statement of work, not left as things "the sales rep said." Verbal assurances during a competitive sales process have a way of softening once the contract is signed and the account moves to a different team. A brief internal review of the final contract against the RFP responses, comparing what was promised to what's actually written down, catches this gap before signature rather than after a company discovers a promised feature was never contractually guaranteed.

Companies without in-house procurement expertise for specialized inspection software sometimes bring in outside ASNT Level III consulting support specifically for this contract review stage — someone who understands both the technical requirements of NDT operations and the practical realities of software implementation can catch gaps between what was demoed and what's actually contractually committed, which is exactly the kind of detail that's expensive to discover after the fact.

Why This Checklist Skews Toward Compliance Over Convenience Features

Readers evaluating multiple ERP vendors will notice this checklist devotes far more of its forty questions to certification tracking, calibration management, and compliance reporting than to features like dashboard aesthetics, third-party integrations, or general usability polish. That weighting is deliberate. A beautifully designed interface with a weak certification-gating engine still lets an under-qualified technician get dispatched to a job — the software just makes the mistake look modern while it happens. An NDT company's software failure modes are fundamentally different from a typical small-business software failure mode: a scheduling glitch at a landscaping company costs a missed appointment, while a certification-tracking gap at an inspection company can cost a client's confidence in years of prior reports, or worse, contribute to a missed flaw on an asset still in service. Evaluators who keep this asymmetry in mind during vendor demos tend to ask sharper follow-up questions and are less likely to be swayed by a polished interface built around a weaker compliance core.
