title: Corporate NDT Training vs Sending Techs to a Public Course: Which Wins?
snippet: In-house cohort training or public courses? A Level III breaks down the headcount threshold, logistics, scheduling, and written-practice fit that actually decide it.
content:
A QA manager on the Houston Ship Channel has six technicians who need UT Level II renewal before a scheduled turnaround at a Deer Park unit. Two hundred miles east, a small fabrication shop in Beaumont-Port Arthur has one welder-turned-inspector who needs PT Level I for the first time, with no other tech on staff needing anything similar this year. Both companies are asking the same question — corporate training or a public course — and the honest answer is that they should land on different sides of it. The mistake most companies make isn't picking the "wrong" option — it's applying one company's logic to a different set of circumstances.

The Real Question Isn't "Which Is Better" — It's "Which Fits Your Crew"

In-house or corporate cohort training — bringing an instructor and a curriculum on-site, or running training internally through a qualified Level III — and sending techs one at a time to open-enrollment public courses are both legitimate, widely used paths to building an ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualified workforce. Neither is a shortcut and neither is inherently more rigorous; SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based scheme either way, which means your written practice, not the delivery format, ultimately governs qualification. What changes between the two paths is logistics, cost structure, scheduling control, and how tightly the training maps to your actual equipment and procedures. A QA manager weighing this is really weighing five factors: how many people need training and how similar their needs are, travel and downtime cost versus instructor mobilization, how training interacts with the production calendar, how closely the material needs to match your written practice, and whether your procedures belong in a shared classroom at all. Walk through those factors honestly and the right answer for your operation usually becomes obvious.

The Headcount Threshold: When In-House Starts to Make Sense

The single biggest variable in this decision is how many technicians need the same method in roughly the same window. One or two people needing PT or MT renewal this quarter is a very different math problem than six UT techs who all need to be current before a turnaround.

In practice, the threshold shows up somewhere around four to six technicians needing the same method at the same time. Below that, the per-person overhead of arranging an on-site instructor, classroom space, and equipment rarely pencils out better than sending people individually to a public course — you're paying for infrastructure that only one or two people will use. Above that threshold, the math flips: an instructor traveling to you and training six people in one week is training six people for one mobilization, while sending those same six people to a public course means six sets of travel, six sets of lodging, and six people pulled off the floor at different times if the course doesn't have six open seats in the same session.

There's a second dimension that matters just as much: how similar the group's needs are. If your six techs all need the same method at the same level, in-house training is efficient because one curriculum session serves everyone. If they need six different things — one needs RT Level II, one needs a PT refresher, one needs eddy current for the first time — a single in-house session doesn't cover the group as cleanly, and a public course calendar with rolling sessions across methods may serve a scattered crew better than forcing a custom on-site week to cover everything at once. Companies staffing up a program from scratch, or standing up a new method they've never run before, often find it useful to get outside guidance on where that threshold sits for their own crew mix — this is one of the more common questions we field through ASNT Level III consulting engagements, because the right answer depends on turnaround cycles and method mix specific to the company.

Logistics: What You're Actually Paying to Avoid

Every company running technicians through certification pays for logistics somewhere — the question is just where that cost shows up. Sending techs to a public course means covering travel, lodging, meals, and the wage or opportunity cost of days away from the job site, on top of the course fee itself. For a company with crews scattered across Baytown, Freeport, and the Baton Rouge-to-New Orleans corridor, that can mean techs from three job sites converging on one training location, multiplying the travel bill by however many people are sent.

Bringing training on-site flips that cost structure. Now you're covering an instructor's travel and, depending on the method, transporting equipment to your facility instead of moving people to it. For methods like UT or PAUT that require calibrated instruments and reference blocks, that can mean shipping or hand-carrying sensitive equipment. For MT or PT, where equipment needs are lighter, on-site delivery is usually simpler.

The trade isn't automatically a win for on-site training — it's a trade, and the crossover point tracks closely with the headcount threshold above. One instructor's travel and setup time, spread across six techs trained the same week, is usually a better deal than six sets of individual travel and lodging. Spread across one or two techs, that same mobilization cost carries far less weight, and a public course's per-seat pricing starts to look more efficient. Neither path is "cheaper" as a blanket rule — it depends on how many people are sharing the fixed cost of getting an instructor and equipment to one place at one time.

Scheduling Around Turnarounds, Outages, and Production Windows

This is where in-house training earns its keep for companies running to a turnaround calendar. Public courses run on their own published schedule — fixed dates, fixed locations, fixed enrollment windows. If a session lands during your outage window, or two weeks before a planned turnaround when every hand is needed on the floor, that's simply the schedule you get: pull a tech off critical work, or wait for the next offering and hope it lines up better.

Corporate or in-house training can be scheduled around your production calendar instead of the other way around — the week after a turnaround wraps, or in the gap between outages when the shop floor is quieter — rather than eating into billable capacity at the exact moment a company can least afford it. For operations along the Gulf Coast refining and petrochemical corridor, where turnaround season creates predictable crunch periods, this scheduling control is often the deciding factor even when headcount is borderline. A company with five techs who'd normally sit right at the in-house/public-course threshold may still choose in-house training simply to avoid it colliding with the turnaround itself.

The flip side is real too: in-house training requires you to have — or bring in — a qualified instructor and, for SNT-TC-1A purposes, someone with the Level III authority to structure and sign off on the program. If your internal Level III is already stretched thin managing the turnaround, adding "run a training cohort" to their plate during the same window can create its own bottleneck. Some companies solve this by using contracted Level III support for the training push specifically, keeping their internal Level III focused on turnaround-critical work.

Written Practice Alignment: Generic Course vs. Your Own Procedures

SNT-TC-1A is explicit that the employer, not ASNT, certifies personnel — using a written practice the employer establishes, following ASNT's recommended guidelines on training hours, experience, and exam content. That structure creates a real gap between "generic training that satisfies the recommended hour minimums" and "training that's actually built around your written practice."

A public course is, by design, generic. It's built to serve technicians from dozens of employers, so it teaches the method broadly — the physics, the general procedure, the classic hour minimums the industry commonly cites (UT and RT typically run around 40 classroom hours each for Level I and Level II, MT lighter at roughly 12 hours for Level I and 8 for Level II, PT around 4 hours each level, ET around 40 each, VT around 8 each — typical industry practice, not a fixed rule every employer must follow). What a public course generally can't do is teach your specific acceptance criteria, reporting format, or the code edition your written practice invokes for a given job. An in-house program built around your own written practice closes that gap directly. The written practice exam component, the practical demonstrations, and the classroom material can all be built to mirror exactly what a tech will be doing on your floor — not a generalized version of the method. For companies working to ASME Section V, Section VIII, or B31.3 requirements that reference SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, that alignment matters at audit time: an assessor reviewing your qualification records wants to see that training maps cleanly to what your written practice actually requires, not just that a tech attended a course somewhere.

None of this means public courses produce non-compliant technicians — plenty of companies successfully take a public course certificate and layer their own written-practice-specific qualification exam on top, which is a perfectly valid way to close the gap without building a full in-house program. It just means the alignment work has to happen somewhere, and in-house training front-loads it into the curriculum instead of bolting it on afterward.

Training on Your Actual Equipment, Not a Classroom Demo Unit

A technician who trains on a classroom's shared UT flaw detector and a set of generic reference blocks learns the method. A technician who trains on your actual flaw detector model, calibrated against your actual reference blocks and configured the way your procedures specify, learns the method and the job. That distinction matters more for some methods than others — PT and VT are relatively equipment-agnostic, while UT, PAUT, and TOFD are heavily dependent on instrument-specific settings, probe selection, and calibration routines that vary between manufacturers and even between firmware versions.

Public courses train on whatever equipment the provider owns, which is rarely the exact model your crew runs in the field. That's not a disqualifying flaw — the underlying physics and interpretation skills transfer — but it does mean there's a second, shorter learning curve after the course, when the tech gets back and has to map what they learned onto your actual instrumentation. For a straightforward method like PT, that gap closes in an afternoon. For PAUT on an unfamiliar instrument, it can take meaningfully longer, and that shows up as reduced field productivity in the weeks right after training — which cuts against the whole point of getting the tech qualified quickly.

In-house training removes that second learning curve by design. Techs calibrate and scan on the instrument they'll actually use, with the reference blocks and defect standards your written practice specifies. Companies tracking equipment inventories and calibration records through a system like Atlantis NDT ERP often find this alignment easier to plan around, since the same equipment records that drive calibration due-dates can inform what instrumentation a training cohort should be built around in the first place.

Confidentiality and Proprietary Procedures

Public courses put your techs in a classroom with technicians from other companies — sometimes competitors, sometimes clients, sometimes both. For most companies that's a non-issue; the method itself isn't proprietary and there's real value in comparing notes with peers from other shops. But for companies with proprietary inspection procedures, unusual acceptance criteria negotiated with a specific client, or in-house techniques that represent a competitive advantage, an open classroom is the wrong place to walk through those details. An in-house session keeps that material inside the building. This consideration doesn't usually override the headcount or logistics math on its own — a company with two techs and no proprietary procedures still generally comes out ahead sending people to a public course. But when a company is already sitting near the in-house threshold on headcount and scheduling, confidentiality is often the factor that tips the decision the rest of the way.

The Case for Public Courses — and a Decision Framework

It's worth stating plainly what public courses are genuinely good at, because the case for in-house training can start to sound like the default answer if you only read the sections above. Public courses have real advantages that matter for a large share of companies:

  • Low coordination overhead. No need to source an instructor, arrange a classroom, or manage equipment logistics — you register a seat and send a tech.
  • No dependency on having a Level III on staff. Smaller shops without an internal Level III, and without an ongoing consulting relationship, can still get techs certified without first solving that staffing question.
  • Better fit for rare or one-off method needs. A company that needs eddy current qualification once every few years for a single tech has no reason to build or contract an in-house program around it.
  • Exposure to a broader peer network. Techs training alongside people from other companies pick up field perspective and troubleshooting approaches an in-house session, taught entirely by one instructor to one company's crew, can't replicate.
  • Fixed, published scheduling. For companies without hard turnaround-driven deadlines, a known course calendar is simpler to plan around than coordinating an instructor's availability against internal production windows.

A one- or two-tech shop in Beaumont-Port Arthur with no recurring need for a given method, no proprietary procedures to protect, and no internal Level III is very often better served by a public course — full stop. The in-house case only starts to win as headcount, schedule sensitivity, procedure specificity, or confidentiality needs climb. That leaves a practical way to decide: run your situation through the following questions in order. The first one or two usually settle it.

  • How many techs need the same method in the same window? Roughly four or more pointing at in-house; one or two point at a public course.
  • Does the training window collide with a turnaround, outage, or peak production period? A hard collision favors in-house, where you control the calendar.
  • Do you have — or can you contract — Level III authority to structure and sign off on an in-house program? No available Level III support tips toward public courses, or toward a consulting engagement to establish that authority first.
  • Does the method depend heavily on specific instrumentation (UT, PAUT, TOFD)? Equipment-dependent methods gain more from on-site, equipment-matched training than equipment-agnostic ones like PT or VT.
  • Do you have proprietary procedures or client-specific criteria that shouldn't be discussed in an open classroom? A yes here pushes toward in-house even at lower headcounts.
  • Is this a recurring need or a one-off? Recurring core methods justify building repeatable in-house infrastructure; rare or specialty methods rarely do.

The Mixed Approach Most Companies Actually Use

Few companies pick one path exclusively, and that's the right instinct. The common pattern among operations with recurring, high-headcount needs is to build in-house training around the core methods their crew uses constantly — UT and MT for a typical mechanical integrity program — where headcount, equipment specificity, and turnaround scheduling all point the same direction. Those same companies route techs to public courses for methods that come up rarely: a single tech needing eddy current for a specialty job, or PAUT for a one-time project outside normal scope. That mix captures the efficiency of in-house training where volume justifies it, without carrying the overhead of a full program for methods that see occasional use. Building that kind of program — sizing it correctly, structuring the written practice so it holds up under code review, and deciding which methods justify in-house delivery versus public courses — is worth working through with a Level III who's set this up before rather than guessing at the threshold. NDT training programs built around a company's actual crew size, method mix, and turnaround calendar tend to outperform a one-size-fits-all approach, and pairing that with the equipment-tracking discipline of tools like NDT reporting software makes the resulting qualification records easier to defend at audit time.

There's no universal winner between corporate training and public courses — the right call comes down to your crew size, your schedule, and how tightly your written practice needs to map to the training itself.

title: How to Pick an ASNT Level III to Sign Off Your Written Practice
snippet: A practical vetting framework for choosing the ASNT Level III who develops or approves your SNT-TC-1A written practice — credentials, code fluency, and audit-readiness.
content:
What a Written Practice Actually Is, and Why It Matters Who Signs It

Every NDT department along the Gulf Coast petrochemical corridor — whether it's a fabrication shop feeding pressure vessels into Baytown, a service provider running UT crews through the Houston Ship Channel, or an in-house inspection group at a Beaumont-Port Arthur refinery — operates its NDT personnel qualification program off one governing document: the written practice. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the written practice is the internal document an employer establishes to define how it trains, examines, certifies, and re-certifies its own NDT personnel in each method it uses: ultrasonic (UT), radiographic (RT), magnetic particle (MT), liquid penetrant (PT), visual (VT), eddy current (ET), and increasingly TOFD and phased array UT (PAUT). It spells out minimum training hours by level and method, required work experience, vision testing frequency, examination content and passing scores, and the procedure for granting, renewing, and revoking certification.

The written practice is not paperwork for paperwork's sake. It is the document an auditor, a client's quality group, or an ASME/API code inspector will ask to see the moment they want to know whether the technician who just performed a UT scan on a girth weld — or the RT tech who shot film on a tank floor plate — is actually qualified to have done so. If the written practice is thin, outdated, or internally inconsistent with the procedures it's supposed to support, every certification issued under it is exposed to challenge.

That's why SNT-TC-1A recommends — and nearly every serious NDT organization requires — that the written practice be developed and/or approved by an ASNT NDT Level III, the person in the qualification chain expected to understand code requirements, examination design, and the breadth of methods and materials well enough to build a document that will actually hold up. Picking the right Level III for this job is a decision that affects every certification your company issues until the next revision. It deserves more scrutiny than most companies give it.

Two Very Different Things Called "ASNT Level III"

The single biggest point of confusion buyers run into — and the first thing to get straight before you vet anyone — is that "ASNT Level III" describes two different credentialing paths, and they are not interchangeable.

The first is employer-based Level III certification under SNT-TC-1A. SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a consensus standard: the employer certifies its own personnel, following ASNT's guidelines on training hours, experience, and exams, through its own written practice. A Level III certified this way was qualified by an employer — their own, a client company, or a consulting Level III's own written practice — not by ASNT directly. This is completely legitimate and is how most Level IIIs in industrial NDT are credentialed. But the title alone tells you nothing about which employer's written practice, which exam, and which scope of methods that person was actually qualified against.

The second path is ASNT's own central certification, issued through ASNT's ACCP (ASNT Central Certification Program) via direct examination administered by ASNT itself. An ACCP-certified Level III holds a credential issued directly by the certifying body, not by an employer's internal process. It's a different kind of proof — closer in spirit to a licensing exam than an internal qualification.

There's a third reference point worth knowing: ANSI/ASNT CP-189, a true consensus standard (unlike SNT-TC-1A's "recommended practice" status) that some clients — particularly in nuclear and federal contracting — specify instead of or alongside SNT-TC-1A. A written practice built to satisfy CP-189 differs from one built purely to SNT-TC-1A, and a Level III who has only worked under one may need to adjust for the other.

None of these paths is inherently "better" in the abstract — they answer different questions. What matters is that you, as the buyer, know which one you're getting and ask the candidate to show supporting documentation: the certificate itself, the scope of methods and levels it covers, the date of issue and expiration or renewal cycle, and — for employer-based certification — the written practice and examinations it was issued under. A Level III consultant who can't produce this paper trail on request is not someone you want developing your own company's qualification records.

Match Experience to Your Methods and Your Industry

A Level III credential establishes a floor of competence across methods and a demonstrated ability to interpret codes and write procedures. It does not establish that the person understands your industry's failure mechanisms, inspection intervals, or the practical realities of your inspection environment. This is where a lot of written practices quietly go wrong: a technically valid document gets built by someone whose real-world depth is in a different domain entirely.

Consider two Level IIIs, both properly credentialed. One spent fifteen years doing UT and MT on refinery pressure vessels and storage tanks along the Baton Rouge-to-New Orleans chemical corridor, fluent in API 653 in-service tank inspection context, and has written qualification procedures for crews doing shell and floor scanning during turnarounds. The other built a career in aerospace composite inspection — eddy current and advanced UT on airframe structures, working to entirely different acceptance criteria. Both are legitimate Level IIIs. Neither is automatically the right fit for your fabrication shop, pipeline integrity program, or storage tank inspection crew.

Before you engage anyone, ask directly: which methods have you personally practiced at Level II or higher, in which industries, and for how long? If your work is process piping and pressure vessel fabrication feeding facilities around Deer Park or Freeport, you want a Level III whose UT, RT, and PT background is grounded in that world — someone who has sat through a code inspector's audit of a fabrication shop's NDT records, not just studied the code in the abstract. If your scope includes tank floor and shell inspection or turnaround work, API in-service inspection context (API 510, 570, 653) should be part of their working vocabulary — though those API credentials are separate inspector certifications, not something bundled into an SNT-TC-1A written practice.

The practical test: ask the candidate to walk you through how they'd structure the training-hour and experience requirements for your specific method-and-industry combination, and see whether their answer reflects real operational judgment or a generic template pulled from a boilerplate document.

Code Fluency: Know the Documents Your Level III Needs to Actually Use

A written practice doesn't exist in isolation — it has to align with the codes and specifications that govern the actual inspection work your company performs. A Level III who is going to develop or approve your written practice needs working fluency in the documents your technicians will be tested against and your customers will audit you to.

At minimum, that includes ASME Section V (the article-by-article source for NDE methods and acceptance requirements referenced by most construction codes), ASME BPVC Section VIII (pressure vessel design and fabrication, which invokes Section V), and ASME B31.3 (process piping — the code most fabrication and inspection work along the Gulf Coast petrochemical corridor is built around). If your scope touches in-service inspection, your Level III also needs to understand how API 510 (pressure vessels), API 570 (piping), and API 653 (storage tanks) interact with NDT personnel qualification — even though those are separate API inspector certifications, not part of what an SNT-TC-1A written practice certifies.

It's also worth knowing that ISO 9712 is the international personnel certification scheme common outside the US and on multinational EPC projects, and that PCN (administered by BINDT) is the equivalent scheme used heavily in the UK and Europe. If your company bids international work, a Level III who understands how these schemes differ from SNT-TC-1A can flag scope gaps before they become a contract problem — though your written practice itself has no need to cover ISO 9712 or PCN, which are separate certification bodies with their own qualification pathways entirely outside SNT-TC-1A.

Ask candidates directly which editions of Section V, Section VIII, and B31.3 they've worked from most recently, and ask for an example of how they've resolved a conflict between a client specification and a base code requirement. The answer tells you more about real fluency than any certificate will.

Availability and Responsiveness: The Overlooked Deal-Breaker

A written practice is not a document you write once and file away. It needs revision when you add a method, change equipment, update to a newer code edition, or respond to an audit finding. Certification exams need to be administered on your schedule, not whenever a consultant has an opening three months out. A new hire who needs Level II certification before they can be deployed to a turnaround doesn't help you if your Level III takes six weeks to return an email.

Before you engage a Level III — in-house or outside consultant — get a straight answer on turnaround expectations. How quickly can they administer an exam when a technician is ready? What's their process for approving a written practice revision? Is there a retainer arrangement, or a one-time project with no defined path back to them six months from now? A consultant who treats the relationship as a one-time transaction and then goes dark is a liability the first time you need a fast turnaround before a project mobilizes.

Will They Actually Write It, or Just Sign It?

There's a meaningful difference between a Level III who sits down with your operations and quality leadership, understands your equipment, your methods, your workforce, and builds a written practice that genuinely reflects how your company operates — versus one who takes a document you drafted internally (or worse, a template pulled off the internet) and signs off on it with minimal review.

The second scenario is more common than it should be, and it's the one that falls apart during an audit. A code inspector or client auditor reviewing your NDT qualification program will ask questions a rubber-stamped document can't answer: why does this training-hour requirement exist, how was this exam question bank validated, why does this procedure diverge from the base SNT-TC-1A recommendation? If your Level III can't explain the reasoning because they didn't build it, you have a document with a signature but no substance behind it.

When vetting a candidate, ask them to describe their process for developing a written practice from scratch: do they conduct an on-site review of your current procedures and equipment, interview your Level II staff, review your existing certification records, and then build the document — or do they primarily review and approve something you hand them? Either can be legitimate depending on your starting point, but you should know which you're buying, and the price of a genuine development engagement should reflect real involvement, not a signature fee.

Documentation and Audit-Readiness

The real test of a written practice — and of the Level III behind it — comes when a customer's quality team, a third-party auditor, or an ASME/API code inspector shows up and asks to see the records. Can your program produce, for any currently certified technician, a complete file: initial qualification exam results, vision test records at the required interval, experience logs, training hour documentation, and a clear chain showing how each certification traces back to the current written practice?

A Level III worth engaging should be able to tell you, before you sign anything, how they structure records to survive that kind of scrutiny — and ideally should help you build or clean up your recordkeeping, not just the written practice document. Software matters here as much as the paper: a qualification program tracked in scattered spreadsheets is harder to audit cleanly than one managed through a system built for it, which is why NDT organizations increasingly pair written practice work with a platform like Atlantis NDT ERP, keeping technician certification records, training hours, and calibration data in one auditable system rather than reconstructed under pressure the week before a client audit.

Ask a candidate Level III directly: if a client audited our program next month, what would you expect them to ask for, and how would you help us be ready? A consultant with real audit experience will have a specific, detailed answer. One without it will speak in generalities.

Independence and Conflict of Interest

There's a structural tension worth naming plainly: a Level III who both writes your written practice and certifies the technicians under it, without any independent check, is grading their own work. That's not automatically a problem — plenty of legitimate, well-run programs operate exactly this way, especially at smaller companies where a single in-house Level III reasonably wears both hats. But it's worth being deliberate about, particularly if your certifications feed into contracts with clients who run their own vendor NDT audits.

For higher-stakes environments — nuclear-adjacent work, programs governed by CP-189, or strict vendor qualification audits — some companies bring in an outside Level III to independently review a written practice developed internally, or to administer exams independently of the person who trained the candidate. This isn't about distrust; it's about withstanding a skeptical auditor's question of "who checks the checker?" If your client base has this kind of scrutiny, ask a prospective Level III how they'd structure independence into the process, and whether they're comfortable being the independent reviewer rather than the sole author.

Questions to Ask Before You Engage a Level III

Use this as a working checklist when you're screening candidates, whether you're hiring in-house or bringing in outside ASNT Level III consulting:

  • Are you certified under SNT-TC-1A (employer-based), ACCP (ASNT central certification), CP-189, or some combination — and can you provide documentation of scope, methods, and levels covered?
  • Which methods (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, PAUT) have you personally practiced at Level II or higher, in which industries, and for how long?
  • Which editions of ASME Section V, Section VIII, and B31.3 have you worked from most recently, and can you give an example of resolving a code-versus-client-specification conflict?
  • What is your process for developing a written practice — on-site review and interviews, or primarily reviewing a draft we provide?
  • What is your typical turnaround for exam administration and for written practice revisions once we request them?
  • Do you offer an ongoing retainer relationship, or is this a single, one-time engagement?
  • Can you walk through how you'd structure documentation so it holds up under a client or code-inspector audit?
  • If our client base requires independent review, are you willing to serve as an independent reviewer of an internally drafted practice rather than the sole author?
  • Can you provide references from companies in a similar industry and method mix to ours?

A candidate who answers these questions specifically and without hesitation is showing you they've actually done this work before, in environments like yours. A candidate who gets vague on specifics is telling you something too.

Getting the written practice right is foundational, but it's one piece of a larger quality system. The training your Level II and Level III candidates receive needs to actually produce the competence the written practice assumes — which is why the same rigor you apply to vetting a Level III consultant should apply to your NDT training provider. And once technicians are certified, the records and inspection data they generate need a home that keeps everything traceable, whether that's NDT reporting software for day-to-day documentation or a digital twin platform for tying inspection history to specific asset locations over a facility's life.

A written practice built by someone who genuinely understands your methods, your codes, and your industry — and who stays engaged as your program evolves — is worth more than a signature on a template. Take the time to vet it properly; the certifications your company issues for years afterward depend on it.

Whether you handle this in-house or bring in outside expertise, Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting is built around the vetting criteria above — real method and industry experience, direct involvement in drafting and maintaining your written practice, and documentation that holds up when it's audited.

title: ASNT Recertification: What Changes Every 3 (or 5) Years
snippet: Recert intervals aren't set by ASNT but by your employer's written practice. Here's what actually gets checked, what a lapse costs you, and how to track it across a crew.
content:
Every NDT technician has had this moment: you pull your wallet card to check the expiration date, or your QA manager forwards a spreadsheet with a highlighted cell next to your name, and you realize your certification is closer to lapsing than you thought. For a workforce that spends its career interpreting indications against acceptance criteria, it's a strange irony that so much confusion still surrounds a question that should be simple — when does my certification actually expire, and what happens between now and then?

The honest answer is that recertification isn't a single fixed rule handed down from ASNT headquarters. It's a decision made, within guidelines, by your employer, documented in a written practice, and shaped by which method you hold, which fabrication or inspection code governs the work, and how your company chose to interpret ASNT's recommendations. That flexibility is exactly why recert dates get lost on multi-method crews, why techs working a turnaround along the Houston Ship Channel end up scrambling the week before a shutdown, and why "every 3 or 5 years" doesn't mean the same thing at every shop in Baytown, Beaumont-Port Arthur, or Deer Park.

Who Actually Sets Your Recertification Clock

ASNT's Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A is, by design, an employer-based certification scheme. ASNT does not issue your Level I or Level II certification and does not set a single, universal recertification interval that applies to every technician in the country. Instead, SNT-TC-1A gives employers a framework — recommended minimum training hours, experience hours, examination content, and general guidance on recertification intervals — and the employer builds its own written practice around that framework. Your employer's Level III signs off on that written practice, and your employer's Level III (or a qualified designee) is the one who actually certifies you.

This is the detail that trips people up most often: your certification card says "Atlantis Inspection Services" or "XYZ NDT Corp," not "ASNT," because your employer certified you under its own written practice, using ASNT's guidelines as the reference standard. That's also why the same technician can end up with different recertification intervals at different jobs. A refinery turnaround contractor running a tight schedule of shutdowns along the Baton Rouge-to-New Orleans chemical corridor might set a 3-year cycle for UT and PAUT personnel because of how frequently those crews rotate through Section V and B31.3 work. A fabrication shop building pressure vessels to ASME Section VIII might run MT and PT techs on a longer cycle because the work is more repetitive and the risk profile, in the employer's judgment, supports it.

Industry practice commonly lands somewhere in a 3-to-5-year range, and you'll hear both numbers thrown around at toolbox talks and in training classes. But neither number is a law — what matters is what your specific employer's written practice says, method by method. If you've moved between employers, or your company was acquired and merged its written practice with another, don't assume your old interval still applies. Check the current document, not your memory of the last place you worked.

The codes that most Gulf Coast fabrication and inspection work references — ASME Section V, ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section VIII, and ASME B31.3 for process piping — all point back to SNT-TC-1A (or its companion document, ASNT CP-189, which some employers use instead) as the basis for personnel qualification. None of these codes dictate a specific recertification interval either; they defer to the employer's written practice, provided that practice follows the recommended guidelines. API 510, API 570, and API 653 inspector certifications are a separate matter entirely — those are individual credentials issued and renewed directly by API, with their own renewal cycles and continuing education requirements, and they run on a completely different track from your SNT-TC-1A method certifications. The same goes for ISO 9712, which is a personnel certification scheme administered by accredited certification bodies outside the ASNT employer-based system. If your facility requires ISO 9712 credentials for certain contracts, that renewal is managed through the certifying body you're credentialed under, not through your employer's SNT-TC-1A written practice.

What Actually Gets Reassessed at Recertification

When your recert date does arrive, what happens isn't usually a repeat of your original certification exam from scratch — though it can be, depending on how your employer's written practice is structured. More often, recertification is a bundle of smaller checks, some of which happen every year regardless of where you are in the multi-year cycle.

Vision Screening Happens Annually — Not Just at Recert

This is the single most common point of confusion on a crew. SNT-TC-1A guidelines call for annual near-vision acuity screening, independent of the 3-to-5-year recertification cycle. That typically means demonstrating near-vision acuity equivalent to Jaeger J1 or J2, or Snellen 20/25 or better (natural or corrected), plus periodic color-contrast screening for methods where distinguishing color or contrast matters. If you're the tech who assumes vision testing is bundled into your big recert exam every few years, you're the one most likely to show up on an audit finding for a missing annual screening. It's a separate, standing requirement that runs on its own calendar, and it applies to every certified technician every year, not just in a recert year.

A Knowledge Refresh — Not Always a Full Exam

Depending on the employer's written practice, recertification can involve anything from an abbreviated review exam covering procedure and code changes, to a full reexamination equivalent to initial certification. Some companies use a shortened, open-book or closed-book review focused on what's changed since the last cycle — new code editions, revised procedures, updated acceptance criteria. Others, particularly for higher-consequence methods like RT or PAUT, require a more comprehensive retest. Neither approach is wrong; it's a risk-based decision the employer's Level III makes and documents in the written practice.

Documentation Review: Continued Satisfactory Performance and OJT

Recertification also typically involves a documentation review — has the technician maintained continued satisfactory job performance in the method, and is there a record of it? This is where a lot of shops quietly struggle, because "continued satisfactory performance" has to be evidenced somehow: job records, report sign-offs, supervisor observations, or a documented trail of on-the-job training (OJT) hours if the technician has been building experience toward a higher level. Companies running paper-based systems, or juggling scattered spreadsheets and folders of scanned reports, often find this is the slowest part of the recert process precisely because pulling together a clean performance record for one technician across several years takes real digging. This is one of the areas where NDT reporting software earns its keep — when every report a technician has signed off on lives in a searchable, structured system rather than a shared drive of PDFs, a Level III can pull a clean performance history in minutes instead of days.

Supervisor or Level III Evaluation

Finally, most written practices call for some form of direct evaluation — a supervisor's assessment of the technician's field performance, or a Level III's review and sign-off on the whole recertification package. For methods where interpretation carries real consequence — a missed crack indication in a pressure boundary weld, a misclassified porosity cluster — that Level III judgment call is the last line of defense before a certification gets renewed. It's also where a company's overall NDT qualification program either holds up under audit or doesn't, because auditors want to see that this evaluation happened and was documented, not just asserted.

Level III Certification Runs on a Different Clock Entirely

Everything above describes the employer-based Level I and Level II system under SNT-TC-1A. ASNT NDT Level III certification is a different animal, and conflating the two is a common mistake. ASNT operates its own central certification program for Level III — the ASNT Certified Programs (ACCP) — and Level III certificates issued through ACCP are administered, issued, and renewed directly by ASNT itself, not by an employer's written practice. Because ACCP renewal is governed by ASNT's own current program requirements — which can include continuing education or professional development points, renewal application procedures, or other criteria ASNT sets and periodically updates — this article won't state a specific ACCP renewal cycle length as fixed fact. Those rules can and do change, and an unverified number here would do a working Level III a disservice. If you hold or are pursuing an ACCP Level III certification, check ASNT's current renewal requirements directly through ASNT rather than relying on secondhand information from a training class or a former employer's practice.

This distinction matters operationally too. A company's own Level III — who writes and approves the written practice, qualifies Level I and II personnel, and signs off on procedures — may hold that role through ASNT's ACCP central certification or through an employer-based SNT-TC-1A Level III qualification, depending on how the company structured its program. Either path is legitimate, but they run on separate renewal tracks, and a company auditing its qualification program needs to know which track its Level III is actually on. If you're building or reviewing your facility's Level III structure, that's exactly the kind of gap where outside ASNT Level III consulting is useful — someone who's set up and defended these programs across multiple facilities can tell you quickly whether your written practice and your Level III's actual credentialing basis are aligned, before an auditor finds the mismatch for you.

What Happens If You Let It Lapse

There's a meaningful practical difference between a recertification completed on time and a certification that's allowed to lapse. A timely recert, even a thorough one with a full reexamination, is a continuation — your written practice's process runs, the documentation gets reviewed, the vision screening gets logged, and your certification date rolls forward without a gap in your qualified status. A lapse is different. If a certification expires and nobody catches it before the date passes, the written practice may require treating that technician as no longer certified in that method — which can mean going back to something closer to initial certification requirements: retraining hours, a full exam, and a fresh qualification period, rather than the lighter-weight recertification review. Exactly how a lapse is handled depends on the employer's written practice, but the safe assumption on any well-run program is that a lapse costs more time and paperwork than staying ahead of the date ever would.

The immediate operational consequence is straightforward: a technician whose certification has lapsed generally cannot sign off inspection reports, release NDT results, or perform safety-related sign-offs tied to that method until recertified or requalified. On an active job — a shutdown at a Freeport TX facility, a piping inspection tied to a turnaround schedule — that's not abstract. It's a technician who can't work the method they were scheduled for, a report that can't be finalized, or a Level II stepping in to redo interpretation work that should have already been signed off. It also becomes a finding. When a customer audits a contractor's NDT qualification program, or a code-compliance audit reviews personnel records against the written practice, a lapsed certification with work performed during the gap — or even one sitting undetected in the files — is exactly what auditors are trained to catch. It reads as a gap in program control, not just an administrative slip, and it tends to trigger a broader look at how the whole qualification program is tracked.

Tracking Recert Dates Across a Crew Working Multiple Methods

Here's where the theory runs into the reality of running an NDT department. A single senior technician might hold UT, MT, and PT certifications, each certified on a different date, each potentially on a different recert interval depending on how the written practice treats that method, plus an annual vision screening date that's separate from all three. Multiply that across a crew of fifteen or twenty technicians working a mix of UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, and PAUT, and you've got a matrix of dates that's easy to build once and painfully easy to let go stale. This is exactly where spreadsheets fail quietly. A spreadsheet doesn't flag a date six weeks out unless someone remembers to open it. It doesn't tie a technician's OJT hours or performance records to their upcoming recert, and it doesn't stop someone from scheduling a technician onto a job in a method where their certification expired last month. Nobody notices until an audit, a near-miss, or the technician themselves catches it — the wrong order of discovery for a compliance-driven program.

This is precisely the kind of operational tracking a purpose-built system solves better than a spreadsheet ever will. Atlantis NDT ERP is built around exactly this problem — certification and recert dates, per technician, per method, tied to vision screening schedules, OJT logs, and job performance history, with automatic flags before a date arrives rather than after. For companies running multiple crews across several Gulf Coast sites, or a mixed roster of directly employed and contracted technicians, having certification tracking live in the same system as job assignments and inspection reports means a scheduler can't book someone onto a method they're not currently certified for — the system catches it before the crew truck leaves the yard. Some facilities are also tying that certification and inspection history into a digital twin platform, so an asset's inspection record — which technician, which method, which date — stays attached to the physical equipment itself, not scattered across systems reconciled by hand during an audit.

Practical Prep for Your Own Recert

If your own recertification date is approaching, a few habits separate technicians who sail through the process from those who scramble:

  • Start early, not at the deadline. Pull your written practice's recertification requirements at least a few months out, not the week your card expires. If a full reexamination is required for your method, cramming a week before doesn't hold up the way spaced review does, and it leaves no runway if you need to redo the vision screening or track down missing OJT documentation.
  • Check for code edition changes since your last cycle. ASME Section V, Section VIII, and B31.3 all get revised on their own publication cycles, and acceptance criteria, procedure requirements, or referenced standards can shift between your last recert and this one. If your abbreviated exam or review covers "what's changed," you want to already know the answer rather than discover it during the review.
  • Revisit any method you haven't used recently. If you're certified in MT or PT but your last two years of work have been almost entirely UT, that rarely-used method is where recall gets rusty fastest. A deliberate refresher — even an informal one, working through old procedures and acceptance criteria — closes that gap before a recert exam or a supervisor evaluation exposes it.
  • Get your vision screening done early and on schedule every year. Don't let it become something you only think about when a recert is also due. Keeping the annual screening current and documented removes one entire category of last-minute scrambling.
  • Talk to your Level III if you have questions about your written practice. The interval, the exam format, and the documentation requirements are specific to your employer's program. Someone else's experience at a different company, even in the same method, may not describe your actual requirements.
  • Keep your own copy of your OJT and performance documentation. Don't rely entirely on the company file. If you change employers, your new company's Level III will want evidence of your documented experience, and having your own organized record saves everyone time.

Recertification done well is unremarkable — a scheduled review, a vision screening that was already current, a knowledge refresh that confirms what you already know, and a renewed date that rolls forward without drama. It only becomes a problem when the tracking behind it fails, whether that's an individual technician losing track of their own date or a company relying on a spreadsheet that nobody's opened in months. Building that tracking into your operation, rather than hoping everyone remembers on their own, is what keeps a qualification program audit-ready year-round instead of scrambling every time a customer or code-compliance review comes knocking.

title: NDT Training ROI for Employers: What a Certified Crew Actually Returns
snippet: Why NDT training is a capacity investment, not a cost: fewer missed defects, audit-ready records, bigger bids won, and a crew that isn't one Level II away from crisis.
content:
Training Is a Capacity Decision, Not a Line-Item Cost

Every QA manager along the Gulf Coast has had this conversation with a controller: training budgets get scrutinized as discretionary spend, something to trim when a quarter tightens. That framing gets the accounting backwards. A properly qualified crew isn't overhead sitting next to office supplies — it's what determines which jobs your company can take, how fast those jobs move, and how much rework eats into the margin on jobs you already won. Treat NDT training as a capacity investment and the question changes. You're not asking "what does this course cost." You're asking "what does my company become able to do once this technician holds the qualification, and what does it stay unable to do if they don't."

This matters more in NDT than in most technical trades, because SNT-TC-1A is unusually direct about what a company controls. ASNT SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based recommended practice — ASNT does not certify individual technicians under this scheme. The employer writes its own written practice, follows ASNT's recommended guidelines for training hours, experience, and examination, and certifies its own people against that practice. The program's rigor, its documentation, its coverage across methods and levels, is a direct reflection of decisions the company makes. There's no external body to blame for gaps, and none standing between you and building exactly the qualification bench your contract pipeline requires.

Where the Return Actually Shows Up

ROI on training doesn't land as a single line on an income statement. It shows up distributed across the places where an undertrained crew quietly bleeds money and a well-qualified one quietly protects it. The main drivers, roughly in order of how often they surface in a mid-size inspection company's operations:

  • Fewer missed or misinterpreted defects — properly trained Level II techs catch what undertrained ones miss, avoiding rework and repeat inspections
  • Avoided audit and stop-work exposure — audits and code-compliance reviews check personnel qualification records first; gaps there can halt work regardless of how good the inspection results are
  • Reduced liability and insurance exposure — a documented, defensible qualification program is evidence in exactly the situations where you need evidence
  • Access to larger, more technical contracts — bids requiring multiple methods or higher certification levels in-house get turned away, delayed, or subcontracted out when the bench isn't there
  • Fewer scheduling bottlenecks — a crew with only one Level II per method has a single point of failure that drives overtime and missed deadlines
  • Better technician retention — certification investment is a recognized retention lever in every technical trade, and replacing an experienced tech is slow and expensive
  • Less dependency on subcontracted NDT capability — every method you can perform in-house is scope you keep instead of scope you pay someone else to perform
  • Faster, more consistent onboarding — a structured internal training program beats ad hoc, tribal-knowledge training every time a new hire or promotion happens

None of these show up cleanly as "training saved us $X." They show up as fewer bad days, more contracts won, and a crew that isn't held hostage by one person's calendar.

Fewer Missed or Misinterpreted Defects

The core function of a Level II technician is interpretation — setting up and calibrating equipment, reading the indication, deciding whether it's a rejectable discontinuity or noise. That judgment call costs money twice when it's undertrained. A missed defect that later shows up as an in-service failure or code violation is expensive in ways that dwarf any training budget — repair, downtime, sometimes a full re-inspection of everything that tech ever signed off on. Far more common day to day is the opposite failure: a defect gets called rejectable when it isn't, and a weld gets cut out and re-welded unnecessarily, or a client demands a costly second opinion.

Both failure modes are rework, and rework is the most controllable cost in an inspection business — controllable by the qualification level of the people doing the inspecting. A Level II tech properly trained on the written practice for a given method, who understands the acceptance criteria in the governing code (ASME Section V for the NDE methods themselves, ASME BPVC Section VIII for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping), makes fewer of these calls wrong in either direction. That's precisely why the levels exist: Level I performs to instructions, Level II sets up, calibrates, interprets, and reports. The gap between them is the judgment that prevents rework.

Audit and Stop-Work Exposure Tied to Personnel Records

Any QA manager who has sat through a customer audit on the Houston Ship Channel or in the Baton Rouge–to–New Orleans chemical corridor knows the sequence: the auditor asks for personnel qualification records before a single inspection report. It's the fastest way for a reviewer to assess whether a program is real or paper-thin. A thin written practice, incomplete training-hour logs, or a technician signing off work above their documented level — any of those stops the conversation, and often stops the work. A stop-work finding tied to qualification gaps doesn't just cost the hours lost while it's resolved; it puts the whole contract relationship in question, because the client now has to wonder what else is undocumented.

This is a place where the paperwork is a direct output of the training itself. A structured internal program generates the records an audit is looking for: hours logged against the written practice, exam results, experience documentation, level-to-level progression that's traceable and defensible. Ad hoc training generates none of that, even when the technician doing the work is genuinely skilled. Companies that track certification coverage and expiration systematically — through something like Atlantis NDT ERP rather than a spreadsheet someone updates when they remember — walk into an audit with an answer instead of a scramble. A stop-work order during a turnaround window a refinery scheduled months in advance is one of the more expensive things that can happen to an inspection contract.

Liability and Insurance Exposure

When something goes wrong — a missed defect that leads to a failure, or a dispute over whether an inspection met the applicable code — the qualification records of the technician who performed the work become part of the record almost immediately. A documented, employer-based program under SNT-TC-1A, with a defensible written practice and clean training and experience records, is evidence the company met its obligation to have qualified personnel doing qualified work. An undocumented program, or one where qualification levels don't match what techs are actually assigned to do, is the opposite: a liability finding waiting to happen, and exactly the kind of gap insurers and legal counsel look for when evaluating exposure.

This isn't a once-a-decade consideration. It shapes day-to-day decisions — which tech gets assigned to which job, what gets double-checked, how confidently a QA manager can sign a final report. A crew with a real qualification program behind it operates with less friction, because the qualification structure itself is doing part of the risk management.

Bidding Bigger, More Technically Demanding Work

This is where training stops being risk mitigation and starts being growth. Contracts on the Gulf Coast — turnaround work at Baytown or Deer Park, new construction inspection at a Beaumont–Port Arthur fabrication yard, tank and piping work along the Freeport petrochemical corridor — increasingly specify multiple methods and higher certification levels as a condition of bidding at all. A request for UT and PAUT in-house, or a job requiring a Level III on staff to review procedures and sign technique sheets, excludes companies that don't hold that qualification internally. If the RFQ requires a method or level you don't have, you're not bidding, or you're bidding with a subcontractor baked into the cost structure and your margin already compressed before the job starts.

Every additional method and every additional Level II or Level III your crew holds in-house is scope of work you can capture directly instead of turning away or handing to a competitor as a sub. That's the clearest, least abstract form of training ROI there is: the difference between a bid you can submit and one you can't.

Scheduling Bottlenecks: The Single Point of Failure Problem

A subtler cost shows up in day-to-day scheduling, unnoticed until it actively causes a missed deadline. If a crew has exactly one Level II qualified in a given method, every job requiring that method depends on that one person's availability. They're on vacation — the job waits or gets pushed into overtime. They're out sick during a turnaround window — the crew scrambles for a sub at a premium rate, or the client's schedule slips. They leave the company — the crew's capability in that method disappears overnight, not gradually.

This is a structural fragility, fixed structurally: by qualifying a second and third technician in that method so the crew has redundancy instead of a bottleneck. Companies running multiple crews across several Gulf Coast sites feel this acutely, because a single point of failure in one method can cascade across every site that draws on that technician's schedule. Tracking certification coverage across a crew, by method and level, alongside job assignments and utilization, is exactly the visibility a system like Atlantis NDT ERP gives a QA manager or ops lead — not just who's certified in what, but who's actually free when a job needs them.

Retention: The Certification You Pay For Is the Certification You Keep

Certification investment is a well-understood retention lever in technical trades generally, and NDT is no exception. Technicians who see a clear path from Level I to Level II, and from a single method to multiple methods, have a reason to stay and build that path with the employer investing in it. Technicians who don't see that path — doing the same qualification-limited work year after year — are the ones who take a call from a competitor offering faster qualification, or leave for a company that already has the broader structure in place.

The cost of losing an experienced tech isn't just the search and hiring cost of a replacement. It's the qualification and experience-hour gap that replacement has to close before reaching full productivity, and qualified UT and PAUT techs are in real demand across the Gulf Coast industrial corridor. Every experienced technician retained because the company invested in their qualification path is attrition avoided — real value, even without a precise number attached, because the alternative is a recruiting cycle, a training runway for the replacement, and reduced crew capability in the meantime.

Illustrative Scenario: Insourcing a Missing Method

The following is a hypothetical, illustrative example intended to show the shape of the reasoning — not a real client engagement or a projection of specific results. Consider a crew that currently has to subcontract out UT Level II work because no one on staff holds that qualification. Every job requiring UT either gets turned away, gets delayed waiting on a subcontractor's schedule and travel logistics, or gets performed by the subcontractor at a premium that eats directly into the margin on that portion of the job — the company lives with all three outcomes simultaneously, depending on which subcontractor is available that week.

Now consider what changes if that crew qualifies one or two existing Level I technicians up to UT Level II in-house. Jobs that used to get turned away are now biddable. Jobs that used to wait on a subcontractor's calendar now run on the crew's own schedule, sequenced against other work instead of creating a dependency the company doesn't control. The premium previously paid to a third party stays inside the company — that scope is now performed, billed, and retained internally. And because the qualification sits with an employee rather than a vendor relationship, it doesn't evaporate because a subcontractor is busy with someone else's turnaround the same week yours is scheduled. The shape of the cost changes from a recurring outflow with schedule risk attached to a one-time investment that becomes a standing internal capability — the core logic behind treating training as capacity-building, whether the missing method is UT, PAUT, TOFD, or RT.

Onboarding Consistency vs. Tribal Knowledge

Companies without a structured internal training program tend to onboard new technicians informally: pair them with an experienced tech, have them shadow, let qualification progress happen as opportunity allows. That works, sometimes, but it's inconsistent by nature — different mentors emphasize different things, documentation is incomplete because nobody's tracking it systematically, and when the experienced tech doing the informal mentoring leaves, the institutional knowledge of how techs get trained leaves with them.

A written practice with a real internal training structure behind it standardizes all of that. New hires and internal promotions follow a known path, with known hour requirements, known exam expectations, and documentation generated as a matter of course rather than reconstructed after the fact. That consistency compounds: the second and third technician qualified in a method get there faster and more predictably than the first one did, because the path is now established rather than improvised. That's the difference between NDT training as a structured program and NDT training as whatever happens to occur on a given job site.

Making the Qualification Program a System, Not a File Cabinet

Everything above depends on seeing the qualification picture across a crew at a glance — who's certified in what, at what level, when it needs renewal, and how utilization maps against that coverage. That's operationally difficult with paper files or scattered spreadsheets once a company grows past a handful of techs and a couple of methods. Atlantis NDT ERP was built around this problem for NDT companies specifically — tracking technician certification, training hours, and calibration records alongside project assignments, so a QA manager can answer "do we have coverage for this bid" or "who's actually available for this turnaround" without digging through file folders.

Documentation matters just as much on the delivery end. Inspection results from properly qualified techs are only as valuable as the record-keeping around them — a defect found and correctly characterized needs to be reported clearly and tracked over the asset's life. NDT reporting software that produces clean, code-compliant reports turns qualified work into an asset the client can actually use, not a PDF that gets filed and forgotten. For companies managing complex assets — tank farms, piping networks, pressure vessel fleets — a digital twin platform that ties inspection history to a visual, structured asset model makes that well-documented work far more useful over the asset's lifecycle. Properly certified work, captured in a system built to hold it, is what turns a training investment into a lasting operational asset.

Where Consulting Fits

Not every company needs to build its qualification program from scratch, and not every gap is a training gap — sometimes it's a written practice that hasn't kept pace with the codes it's supposed to satisfy, or a Level III function handled informally when it needs a documented, qualified authority behind it. Companies building out a broader qualification program — writing or revising a written practice under SNT-TC-1A, establishing Level III oversight, or structuring multi-method qualification across a growing crew — often get there faster with ASNT Level III consulting input rather than working it out entirely internally. A training program is only as strong as the written practice governing it, and getting that foundation right the first time avoids rebuilding it under audit pressure later.

Worth stating plainly, since it matters to any company evaluating a training partner: SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based scheme, and Atlantis NDT's training and certification work is built around it — it does not extend to API inspector certifications (510, 570, 653) or to ISO 9712 / PCN credentials, which are administered by their own separate bodies with their own qualification paths. Knowing which credentialing system governs which part of a company's needs is itself part of building the program correctly.

None of these ROI drivers require a leap of faith — they're the ordinary mechanics of how a qualified crew wins more work, moves faster, and holds up better under scrutiny than an unqualified one, and building the systems to track and sustain that qualification is the natural next step.
